primary_reviews.rationale: Every string checks out, the long one included: the full-verse quotation וַיּ֥וֹלֶד אַבְרָהָ֖ם אֶת יִצְחָ֑ק בְּנֵ֣י יִצְחָ֔ק עֵשָׂ֖ו וְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל reproduces MT 1:34 without a character out of place, and בְּנֵ֖י עֵשָׂ֑ו, בְּנֵ֖י אֱלִיפָ֑ז, בְּנֵ֖י רְעוּאֵ֑ל and וּבְנֵ֣י שֵׂעִ֔יר are exact at vv.35, 36, 37 and 38. The opening edge is stronger in Hebrew than the row's own prose lets on. וַיּ֥וֹלֶד is a wayyiqtol hiphil, and sweeping the root across the chapter returns nine occurrences of which this alone is consecutive-preterite and this alone is hiphil; the rest are qatal or pual. A verb form unique to the chapter, standing immediately before a construct-plural head that governs the next three verses, is precisely the double duty the row describes. Nesting is read correctly: Eliphaz and Reuel appear among Esau's sons in v.35, so vv.36-37 are grandson lists under it rather than rivals to it, and Seir is demonstrably absent from v.35's five names, which is the stated reason for stopping short of v.38. The mark cite is accurate and properly hedged — pmarks gives SAMEKH+SAMEKH at 1Chr.1.34, one of the ten doubled verses the strategy names; the doubling is disclosed, the single-witness tag is present, and no driving role is claimed. Keeping the verse whole instead of splitting at 34a/34b honours the mid-verse rule, and medium_low is an honest grade for a seam the strategy itself flags.

v.34's double duty is exactly as described: וַיּוֹלֶד אַבְרָהָם אֶת יִצְחָק closes the Isaac notice deferred since v.28, and בְּנֵי יִצְחָק עֵשָׂו וְיִשְׂרָאֵל in the same breath opens the register that vv.35-37 elaborate — an unsplittable verse correctly anchored forward rather than back.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: No challenge landed on this row and the spot check confirms why: v.34's וַיּוֹלֶד אַבְרָהָם אֶת יִצְחָק בְּנֵי יִצְחָק עֵשָו וְיִשְרָאֵֽל does the double duty the row describes, the doubled samekh at 1.34 is correctly disclosed as single-witness against pmarks_1Chr.json, and Eliphaz and Reuel (vv.36-37) are demonstrably grandsons nested under v.35's Esau list rather than rivals to it. medium_low tracks the strategy's own §7 caution about this exact join.

post_resolution_check.notes: Double-samekh at 1.34 correctly disclosed as 'SAMEKH+SAMEKH, single-witness' in both prose and refs; verified against pmarks_1Chr.json.

primary_reviews.rationale: Transcription is clean — וּבְנֵ֣י שֵׂעִ֔יר, בְּנֵ֖י עֵשָׂ֑ו, וּבְנֵ֥י לוֹטָ֖ן, בְּנֵ֥י עֲנָ֖ה and בְּנֵ֥י דִישׁ֖וֹן ע֥וּץ וַאֲרָֽן all match their verses byte for byte, and the observation that vv.38-42 close with no demonstrative summary is confirmed by sweep: no demonstrative of the אֵ֖לֶּה type occurs anywhere between v.33 and v.43. Three things fail. The tier equation drawn between v.38 and v.35 is contradicted by the morphology of the very two forms set side by side. The Hebrew name at the row's final head is not the name its attached WEB gloss reports, which undercuts the ordering claim carrying the span. And the mark discussion, which this row chooses to open, omits the mark standing at its own closing edge — a pe (single-witness), a different class from the samekh material (single-witness) the row does discuss.

challenges.claim: The row states that v.38 opens on the same tier as v.35, but the two forms it juxtaposes differ morphologically: v.35 reads בְּנֵ֖י עֵשָׂ֑ו, asyndetic, while v.38 reads וּבְנֵ֣י שֵׂעִ֔יר with conjunctive waw. Tier 1 — the text's own morphology. Sweeping all 27 construct-plural “sons of” tokens in MT 1 shows every one of the other ten conjunctive forms in the chapter introducing a sub-branch that continues the preceding head: וּבְנֵ֖י גֹּ֑מֶר (v.6), וּבְנֵ֥י יָוָ֖ן (v.7), וּבְנֵ֣י כ֔וּשׁ (v.9), וּבְנֵ֨י קְטוּרָ֜ה (v.32), וּבְנֵ֥י לוֹטָ֖ן (v.39), וּבְנֵ֥י צִבְע֖וֹן (v.40), וּבְנֵ֣י דִישׁ֔וֹן (v.41), with the remaining three at 9b, 32b and 33 behaving identically. On the cluster's own reading of that morpheme — decision M8-1Chr-004 calls v.32 subordinate precisely because of it — v.38 would be the single conjunctive head in the chapter promoted to a row-opening seam. The converse does not rescue the claim either, since asyndeton carries no tier information here: בְּנֵ֖י אֱלִיפָ֑ז (v.36), בְּנֵ֖י רְעוּאֵ֑ל (v.37) and the asyndetic heads at vv.40, 41 and 42 are all demonstrable sub-branches. The morphology therefore supports neither half of the equation.
challenges.suggested_action: Withdraw the same-tier-as-v.35 warrant and rest the opening edge on the eponym argument the row already possesses (Seir is absent from Esau's five sons in v.35), or argue positively why the waw at v.38 is disjunctive against its in-chapter parallels.

challenges.claim: The row quotes בְּנֵ֥י דִישׁ֖וֹן ע֥וּץ וַאֲרָֽן and glosses it as the sons of Dishan, WEB. The MT form is דִישׁ֖וֹן, written plene with waw — identical to the Dishon of v.41 (וּבְנֵ֣י דִישׁ֔וֹן) — and distinct from the seventh son of v.38, pointed וְדִישָֽׁן there against the fifth son וְדִישֹׁ֥ן in that same verse. WEB v.42 does read Dishan. So a Hebrew quotation naming Dishon has been paired with an English gloss naming a different son, and the structural claim that vv.39-42 expand Seir's seven sons in the order given holds on the WEB reading but not on the MT text actually quoted, where the fifth son's name recurs at v.42 and the seventh is never re-headed. The book strategy's Chronicles hygiene rule is explicit that the witness actually cited must be quoted and that name variants are never harmonised inside a quote.
challenges.suggested_action: Disclose the Dishon/Dishan divergence at v.42 as a witness variant, restate the seven-sons-in-order claim as a WEB-based reading with the MT departure noted or drop the ordering phrase, and keep Hebrew quote and English gloss visibly attributed to their own witnesses.

challenges.claim: Having elected to argue about the mark field — a real formal gap, not filled by the double samekh, since that mark falls mid-run — the row reports that field incompletely. pmarks_1Chr.json keys PE to 1Chr.1.42 (single-witness), standing at this row's own closing edge and belonging to a different mark class from every samekh discussed; it also keys SAMEKH to 1Chr.1.39 and 1Chr.1.40 (single-witness), which are mid-run on exactly the same footing as the v.41 doubled mark singled out. The v.41 cite itself is type-accurate: pmarks does give SAMEKH+SAMEKH there, the doubling is disclosed and the single-witness tag is present. This is a disclosure gap rather than a boundary problem — the omitted pe is weak tier-3 corroboration of the row's own edge and drives nothing.
challenges.suggested_action: Add oshb:1Chr.1.42 (pe, single-witness) to the mark discussion and the evidence refs, note the vv.39-40 samekhs alongside the v.41 doubled mark, and keep all of them explicitly non-driving.

primary_reviews.rationale: The row's candid admission of a 'real formal gap' checks out: unlike Ishmael and Keturah just above, Seir's seven-son expansion running vv.39-42 never receives an אֵלֶּה closing tally, so the row's end is carried entirely by v.43's fresh register (kings), not by any closural device inside 38-42 — an honest asymmetry rather than a glossed-over one.

The mark report is now complete for the span and type-accurate at every point: pmarks keys SAMEKH to 1:39, SAMEKH to 1:40, SAMEKH+SAMEKH to 1:41 and PE to 1:42, with no mark keyed to 1:38, which is exactly the four-item picture the row gives, doubling flagged and class distinction preserved. Its companion claim also verifies — no token of the elleh family occurs anywhere in 1:38-42, so the missing closure the row calls a real formal gap really is missing, and the pe cannot be smuggled in to fill it. On the name question the disclosure is more scrupulous than the original challenge required. The v.42 form is written with waw, consonantally identical to Anah's son three words into 1:41; the seventh son at 1:38 is written without it. Worth adding that the MT distinguishes Seir's fifth and seventh sons at 1:38 by pointing alone, both being consonantally d-y-s-n, which makes the row's concession — that the orderly seven-son reading depends on WEB's differentiated naming — stronger rather than weaker than it needed to be. Nine Hebrew citations, all byte-exact; WEB at 1:38 and 1:43 verbatim. Nothing here calls for a fresh item. The samekh keyed to 1:37 sits at the opening edge but outside the span, and the row's disclosure scope is verses inside the row, applied consistently.

This is the most heavily repaired row in the cluster and the most improved. The morphological argument that used to do real work (same-tier waw) is gone, replaced by the eponym-absence point, which I confirmed independently: v.35's five sons of Esau do not include Seir. The Dishon/Dishan disclosure is likewise accurate on inspection -- v.38's fifth and seventh sons are pointed differently in MT, and vv.41-42 do repeat the fifth son's plene spelling, so flagging the ordering claim as WEB-dependent rather than MT-native is the right call, not overcaution. Mark disclosure is now complete for the row's own span.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: All three OL challenges verify against the sliced text and I rule each supported; none touches where the row starts or ends. OL-M8-1Chr-006-1 exposes a real morphological mismatch: v.35's בני עשו is asyndetic while v.38's ובני שעיר carries a conjunctive waw, and sweeping the chapter's ten other conjunctive 'sons of' tokens (vv.6, 7, 9 twice, 32 twice, 33, 39, 40, 41) shows every one continuing a head already on the page, unlike Seir at v.38, which the row itself calls 'an unrelated eponym' -- so the 'same tier as v.35' phrasing is the wrong warrant even though the eponym-absence argument the row also gives remains sound on its own. OL-M8-1Chr-006-2 catches a genuine witness-fidelity slip: the Hebrew quoted for v.42's closing clause, בני דישון עוץ וארן, is spelled plene with vav exactly as v.41's Dishon and distinct from either spelling of v.38's fifth or seventh son, yet the row glosses it 'sons of Dishan' following WEB -- a harmonization the book strategy's own Chronicles-hygiene rule forbids ('never harmonize names across witnesses in a quote'). OL-M8-1Chr-006-3 is lower-stakes but accurate: pmarks_1Chr.json keys a pe to the row's own closing verse (1.42) and samekh to vv.39 and 40, none of which the row's mark discussion mentions alongside the v.41 double samekh it does discuss; all are tier-3, single-witness, and non-driving, so this is a completeness gap in disclosure rather than a boundary defect.

challenge_responses.response: Accepted (peer-ruled supported): v.35 is asyndetic and v.38 carries a conjunctive waw, so 'same tier as v.35' was the wrong warrant. Withdrew it and rest the opening edge solely on the eponym-absence argument -- Seir is not one of the five sons of Esau v.35 names -- which the row already possessed.

Accepted (peer-ruled supported): the MT at v.42 names דִישׁ֖וֹן (plene vav, identical to Anah's son at v.41), not the pointed form used for Seir's own seventh son at v.38; WEB's 'Dishan' at v.42 is a disambiguating English gloss, not a distinct Hebrew name. Disclosed the divergence and noted that the row's seven-sons-in-order framing rests on WEB's differentiated naming rather than on the MT spelling alone.
Accepted (peer-ruled supported, low severity): added the pe at v.42 and the samekh at vv.39-40 alongside the already-disclosed double samekh at v.41, all tier-3, single-witness, non-driving.

boss_ruling.reasoning: Three sound amendments: the v.35/v.38 'same tier' warrant is withdrawn for the true asyndetic-versus-conjunctive contrast, the Dishon/Dishan witness divergence is now quoted per witness instead of harmonized, and the mark field carries the full pe/samekh inventory. The Seir register's edges were never in doubt; medium stands.

post_resolution_check.notes: All four marks in span (1.39 samekh, 1.40 samekh, 1.41 double-samekh, 1.42 pe) correctly typed, single-witness tagged, doubling disclosed; explicit non-driver disclaimer present; Dishon/Dishan gloss claim verified against oshb (1.41 and 1.42 share the Dishon spelling; WEB renders 1.42 as 'Dishan' by translator choice).

primary_reviews.rationale: This row's load-bearing claims are the kind that can be settled by counting, and every count falls its way. The refrain is real and breaks precisely where the row puts the break: stripping accents (necessary, since v.50 points the verb differently) and testing all 54 verses for the death verb וַיָּ֖מָת alongside the succession clause וַיִּמְלֹ֣ךְ תַּחְתָּ֔יו returns both elements at vv.44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49 and 50, while at v.51 the death verb recurs and the succession clause appears nowhere in the verse. That is a positive pattern-break in the text's own syntax, not an inference from silence. The synchronism is likewise unique here: לִפְנֵ֥י מְלָךְ מֶ֖לֶךְ לִבְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל occurs at v.43 only, and it is the sole אֲשֶׁ֤ר clause of its kind in the sequence. So is the wife notice — וְשֵׁ֨ם אִשְׁתּ֤וֹ מְהֵיטַבְאֵל֙ בַּת מַטְרֵ֔ד בַּ֖ת מֵ֥י זָהָֽב carries the one occurrence of אִשְׁתּ֤וֹ in 1 Chronicles 1, and it does name three successive forebears, so the claim is accurate as scoped. Quotations are exact at vv.43, 44, 50 and 51, the truncated refrain among them being a contiguous prefix of v.44 rather than a stitched composite. Numbering is one-to-one, so no dual citation is owed. I probed for a concealed internal seam and found none worth raising: vv.44-50 form one formulaic cycle, and the granularity rule treats an internally formulaic sequence as a single row. High confidence is warranted.

The refrain-break argument is precise: every death notice from v.44 through v.49 pairs וַיָּמָת X with וַיִּמְלֹךְ תַּחְתָּיו Y, but v.51's וַיָּמָת הֲדָד drops the 'reigned in his place' half entirely and instead opens the chiefs' title-list — a hard formal edge, not a stylistic variant of the same device.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Unchallenged, and the spot check confirms the row's own reasoning: the וימת X וימלך תחתיו Y refrain runs unbroken across vv.44-50 and drops the succession half entirely at v.51 (וימת הדד with no תחתיו clause following), a hard break rather than a stylistic variant on the same device. The wife's three-generation lineage at v.50 and the unique synchronism opening v.43 are both accurately scoped by the row without overreach. High confidence is earned here.

post_resolution_check.notes: Ellipsis-compressed WEB refrain quote ('Bela died, and ... reigned in his place') accurately represents the recurring formula rather than any single verse verbatim (see aggregate class B); underlying Hebrew fragment byte-matches 1.44.

primary_reviews.rationale: The three quotations — the opening stretch of v.51, the whole of v.52, and the closing formula אֵ֖לֶּה אַלּוּפֵ֥י אֱדֽוֹם at v.54 — are byte-exact, and the assertion that v.54 carries the last of the chapter's closure formulas survives a sweep: genuine demonstratives of the אֵ֖לֶּה type fall at vv. 23, 29, 31, 33, 43 and 54, and v.54's is indeed final. I find the boundary itself well placed, and keeping v.51 undivided respects the mid-verse rule the strategy imposes on this transition. The trouble is that the row's positive evidence is a count, and the count is wrong in both directions — it undercounts the verse it is defending and overstates the reach of the pattern. Repairing the first would strengthen the row; repairing the second trims a claim it never needed.

challenges.claim: The row calls v.51's contribution the first named chief, and its rejected alternative calls it the chiefs' register head and first name. MT 1:51 in fact names three: אַלּ֥וּף תִּמְנָ֛ע אַלּ֥וּף עליה עַֽלְוָ֖ה אַלּ֥וּף יְתֵֽת. Counting the chief title (אַלּ֥וּף, accents stripped since the pointing varies) verse by verse gives 51 = 3, 52 = 3, 53 = 3, 54 = 2. The Hebrew quote stops at Timna, which is where the singular description originates; the truncation conceals the row's own best evidence, since a three-chief count at v.51 matches vv.52-53 exactly and is a stronger reason to attach the verse forward than the one actually given. The second chief also carries an undisclosed ketiv/qere — the source line reads ketiv עליה followed by qere עַֽלְוָ֖ה — and WEB's Aliah follows the ketiv form, exactly the kind of witness divergence the strategy requires a row to surface rather than smooth over.
challenges.suggested_action: Extend the v.51 quotation through its three chiefs, replace the first named chief with the actual three-name count, and disclose the ketiv/qere at the second chief, identifying the WEB form as following the ketiv.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative appeals to a three-per-verse chieftain pattern said to continue in vv.52-54, but v.54 breaks that count: it reads אַלּ֥וּף מַגְדִּיאֵ֖ל אַלּ֣וּף עִירָ֑ם — two chiefs — followed by the closure אֵ֖לֶּה אַלּוּפֵ֥י אֱדֽוֹם. The three-per-verse arithmetic holds for vv.51, 52 and 53 and stops there, v.54 being a two-name entry plus summary rather than a fourth triplet.
challenges.suggested_action: Restate the pattern as three chiefs each in vv.51-53 with v.54 as a two-name entry closed by the summary formula, so the count claim matches the text it cites.

primary_reviews.rationale: v.51 is correctly kept whole and assigned forward: its second clause, וַיִּהְיוּ אַלּוּפֵי אֱדוֹם אַלּוּף תִּמְנָע, is itself the chiefs' register head and first name, not a coda appended to the kings' chain, and the row's own arithmetic (three chiefs each in vv.51-53, two more plus the closing tally in v.54) accounts for all eleven names before אֵלֶּה אַלּוּפֵי אֱדוֹם shuts the register.

Counting the chief title verse by verse confirms the arithmetic the repair now advertises: three tokens at 1:51, three at 1:52, three at 1:53, two at 1:54, with the construct plural standing separately in the register head of 1:51 and in the closure of 1:54 — the row keeps those two apart correctly. The source line at 1:51 does carry the unpointed ketiv followed by its pointed qere, and WEB's Aliah does follow the ketiv consonants, so that disclosure is accurate as written. Six Hebrew quotations collate byte-for-byte; 'Then Hadad died,' and 'These are the chiefs of Edom,' reproduce WEB exactly, and the closure at 1:54 is indeed the last of the chapter's four summary formulas, the others falling at 1:23, 1:31 and 1:33. What the row leaves out is the witness field at the one place its own argument is contested. From 1:43 through 1:54 the single-witness marks are sparse rather than dense — two in twelve verses — and one of them falls after 1:51, precisely the seam the rejected alternative proposes and rejects.

challenges.claim: The row argues at length that v.51 attaches forward to the chiefs rather than back to the kings, sets its confidence at medium_low, and builds a rejected alternative around opening the chiefs at v.52 — yet it never touches the mark field, which speaks at exactly that seam. pmarks_1Chr.json keys SAMEKH to 1Chr.1.51 and PE to 1Chr.1.54, and those are the only two marks anywhere in 1:43-1:54, so unlike the crowded samekh runs elsewhere in this chapter neither can be waved off as list-item bookkeeping. The samekh sits between v.51 and v.52, which is where the rejected alternative wants its seam, and is therefore weak tier-3 single-witness evidence running against the row's reading; the pe sits at the row's own closing edge and runs weakly for it. A row that argues a contested attachment ought not to pass over the one witness signal standing at that attachment, in either direction.
challenges.suggested_action: Disclose both marks as tier-3, single-witness, non-driving: the samekh after 1:51 as weak signal toward the rejected v.51|v.52 seam, the pe after 1:54 as weak corroboration of the row's close, and state that neither displaces the tier-1 case built on the three-per-verse count and the register head inside v.51.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both repairs are load-bearing rather than cosmetic. Extending the v.51 quotation through all three chiefs actually strengthens the row's own case (three-per-verse matches vv.52-53), which the original truncated quote had been hiding rather than helping. I checked the ketiv/qere claim against the source line myself: WEB's 'Aliah' does track the ketiv עליה rather than the qere עַֽלְוָ֖ה, so the disclosure is accurate, not just plausible-sounding. The v.54 count correction is a clean, verifiable fix -- two chiefs plus the closing formula, not a fourth triplet.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Both OL challenges check out arithmetically and I rule each supported; neither disputes the boundary itself, which the OL primary's own rationale already calls well placed. OL-M8-1Chr-008-1 is correct that v.51 names three chiefs, not one -- אלוף תמנע אלוף עליה/עלוה אלוף יתת -- so the row's truncated quotation and 'first named chief' phrasing understate the verse's own best evidence for the three-per-verse count it wants (51=3, 52=3, 53=3), and the row also passes over an undisclosed ketiv/qere at the second name (ketiv עליה, qere עלוה) that WEB's 'Aliah' resolves toward the ketiv, exactly the divergence the strategy's Chronicles-hygiene rule expects surfaced. OL-M8-1Chr-008-2 is correct that v.54 breaks the three-per-verse pattern the rejected_alternative claims continues through 'vv.52-54': v.54 in fact names two chiefs (Magdiel, Iram) before the closing tally, not three. Both are evidentiary corrections to how the row reports the text it already relies on, not challenges to where the row starts or ends, so the frozen span and confidence stand; only the supporting count needs tightening, an author/boss-level edit.

challenge_responses.response: Accepted (peer-ruled supported): v.51 names three chiefs, not one; extended the quotation to all three and disclosed the undisclosed ketiv/qere at the second name (ketiv and qere stand consecutively in the source), noting WEB's 'Aliah' follows the ketiv consonants.

Accepted (peer-ruled supported, low severity): v.54 in fact names two chiefs before the closing tally, not three. Fixed the strongest_rejected_alternative's count claim, which had been the specific sentence carrying the error, to state the three-per-verse pattern runs vv.51-53 with v.54 closing on two names plus the summary formula.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both edges hold when read off the consonantal text. אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל sits at word 0 of MT 2:1 with all six of that verse's names trailing it, and 2:2 stops on גָּ֥ד וְאָשֵֽׁר with nothing left to gather; the roll is arithmetically whole at six plus six. The narrowing at 2:3 is genuine — בְּנֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֗ה is a bare construct head naming one tribe. Numbering needs no dual-cite here: ch 2 lies outside all three declared offset zones and MT and WEB both run 55 verses. Mark citation is accurate against pmarks (samekh after 2:2, single-witness, not doubled). My objection is not to the span, which I think is secure, but to the book-level generalisation the row rests its opening on, which a full sweep of that formula does not bear out.

challenges.claim: Tier 1, and it fails as stated: the row licenses its opener as an "aleph-plus-benei head pattern" that the book supposedly uses "to launch a fresh register", but 1 Chronicles mostly uses that formula to close. A consonantal sweep of every aleph-lamed-he (+ hayu) + benei sequence in the book returns 23 hits, of which 16 stand after the names they gather — כָּל אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֥י יָקְטָֽן (oshb:1Chr.1.23), אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֥י יַפְלֵֽט (oshb:1Chr.7.33), כָּל אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֥י אָצַֽל (oshb:1Chr.8.38), and 2:33's own אֵ֥לֶּה הָי֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י יְרַחְמְאֵֽל (oshb:1Chr.2.33) — against only 7 standing verse-initial with the list following (2:1, 2:50, 3:1, 5:14, 6:35, 8:6, 23:24). What makes 2:1 a head is its position at word 0 plus the twelve names that follow inside the same verse, not the identity of the formula.
challenges.suggested_action: Re-ground the opening edge positionally (verse-initial formula with its list following) and either drop the book-wide 'launch' generalisation or disclose the 16:7 anaphoric-to-cataphoric split when the formula is cited as an opening signal.

primary_reviews.rationale: The national headline formula אֵּלֶּה בְּנֳֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל at 2:1 and the narrowing head בְּנֳֵי יְהוּדָה at 2:3 bracket this span exactly as claimed, and the twelve names in 2:1-2 are a flat, undeveloped roll with no internal head to contest. The samekh cited after 2:2 checks out against pmarks_1Chr.json as a single, non-doubled mark. The rejected alternative (reading 2:1-4 as an 'introduction to Judah') is the genuine rival and is fairly dismissed: 2:1-2 names all twelve sons of Israel, not a Judah-only preface.

I re-ran the book-wide sweep rather than take it on trust, and it reproduces: reading the construction as the row defines it — elleh, optionally with hayu, immediately followed by benei — 1 Chronicles yields twenty-three occurrences, seven of them verse-initial (2:1, 2:50, 3:1, 5:14, 6:35, 8:6, 23:24) and sixteen standing later in their verse, overwhelmingly after the names being gathered. Widening the pattern by one variant, the elleh hem benei of 1:31, would give twenty-four; the row's figure is the figure its own stated construction produces. Both named exemplars are anaphoric as described, and the tribal roll counts to twelve across the two verses, six in each. The samekh after 2:2 is in pmarks as claimed and is properly weighted as weak corroboration of a break the wording already makes. WEB at 2:1, 2:2 and 2:3 is quoted verbatim, and all four Hebrew strings are byte-exact. One sentence in the disclosure, though, hands a verse from another row's territory to this one.

challenges.claim: The sweep disclosure describes אֵ֥לֶּה הָי֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י יְרַחְמְאֵֽל (oshb:1Chr.2.33) as “this row's own closing device at 2:33.” This row is 1Chr.2.1-1Chr.2.2. The formula at 2:33 closes the Jerahmeel register thirty-one verses downstream and belongs to a different row entirely, and the rationale contradicts itself two clauses later by describing this row's actual stop at 2:2 as a bare enumeration with nothing to gather — that is, as having no closing device of this kind at all. The quotation and its reference are both accurate; what is wrong is the ownership attached to them, and the slip was introduced by the repair, since the sweep sentence is new text.
challenges.suggested_action: Re-label 2:33 as the book's — or the chapter's — anaphoric exemplar rather than this row's, keeping it in the sweep evidence where it belongs, and leave the statement that 2:2 closes on bare enumeration standing as the row's actual account of its own edge.

primary_reviews.rationale: The repair correctly demotes the formula's identity as the load-bearing signal and puts the verse-initial position plus the trailing twelve names in its place -- a more defensible warrant, since the same formula closes lists far more often than it opens them elsewhere in the book. I did not take the row's 'most of them... stand after' claim on faith; a book-wide sweep for the construction returns totals consistent with that description under a reasonable reading of which forms count as 'benei sequences.' The argument now matches the evidence rather than outrunning it.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: OL-M8-1Chr-009-1 is correct: I independently swept 1Chr_oshb.txt for the elleh(+hayu)+benei construction and, once a false hit at 25:2 (אַשְׁרֵאָלָה, a proper name whose tail merely looks like אלה) is excluded, get the same 23-verse field OL reports. Sorting those by position confirms the ratio the challenge describes: the great majority — 1:23, 1:33, 2:23, 2:33, 4:4, 4:6, 4:18, 7:8, 7:11, 7:17, 7:33, 8:38, 9:44, 23:10, 24:30 among them — stand AFTER the names they gather (anaphoric close), while only a handful, including 2:1 itself plus 2:50, 3:1 and 6:35, stand at word 0 with the list following (cataphoric open). The row's claim that this formula is a book-wide device for launching a register therefore overstates the pattern; what actually licenses 2:1 as an opening is its verse-initial position plus the twelve trailing names, not the formula's identity, exactly as the challenge argues. This does not touch the span: both edges (the 2:1 headline and the 2:3 narrowing to בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה) remain solid on their own terms, and the challenge itself disclaims any span objection.

challenge_responses.response: Accepted (peer-ruled supported): a book-wide sweep confirms the elleh(+hayu)+benei construction totals 23 occurrences and stands mostly anaphoric (closing a list already given, as at 1:23 and this chapter's own 2:33), not cataphoric. Dropped the book-wide 'launch' generalization and re-grounded 2:1 as an opening on positional grounds -- verse-initial placement plus the twelve names following in the same verse -- rather than on the formula's identity.

Micro round (author_sonnet_1chr_micro_r2) applied the peer-reconciled remedy: In boundary_rationale, change 'this row's own closing device at 2:33' to attribute 2:33's אֵ֥לֶּה הָי֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י יְרַחְמְאֵֽל to the book's/chapter's anaphoric exemplar class generally, not to this row (span 2:1-2:2). Leave unchanged the statement that this row's own edge at 2:2 is a bare enumeration with nothing to gather.

rulings.remedy: In boundary_rationale, change 'this row's own closing device at 2:33' to attribute 2:33's אֵ֥לֶּה הָי֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י יְרַחְמְאֵֽל to the book's/chapter's anaphoric exemplar class generally, not to this row (span 2:1-2:2). Leave unchanged the statement that this row's own edge at 2:2 is a bare enumeration with nothing to gather.

boss_ruling.reasoning: The elleh-launch generalization inverted the book's own usage (mostly anaphoric); the amendment re-grounds the opener on 2:1's actual position after 1:54's Edomite close. A two-verse all-Israel head list is not otherwise contestable; high stands.

post_resolution_check.notes: Book-wide sweep claim ('23 occurrences of elleh(+hayu)+benei') not independently re-derivable with a simple regex (confound with elohim); core tier-1 argument (verse-initial position + 12 names) does not depend on that count and is independently sound.

primary_reviews.rationale: Everything quoted here slices exactly, and the count the row leans on survives arithmetic: 2:3 lists Er, Onan and Shelah and labels them שְׁלוֹשָׁה֙, 2:4 adds Perez and Zerah, so כָּל בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה חֲמִשָּֽׁה is a true total rather than a rhetorical flourish. The Er notice is quoted from the predicate onward (רַ֛ע בְּעֵינֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה וַיְמִיתֵֽהוּ); its governing form is the wayyiqtol וַיְהִ֞י earlier in the verse, so the fragment starts mid-clause — I record that as an observation, not a defect, since the row's description of an interposed death notice is exactly what 2:3 does. The closing edge is confirmed by בְּנֵי פֶ֖רֶץ at 2:5, a fresh construct head that cannot be read as a continuation of the five-count. I also credit the row for not hiding the mark field: samekh do follow 2:3, 2:5, 2:6 and 2:7 as well as 2:4 (single-witness), and the one after 2:3 falls inside the span itself, which the row's 'immediate stretch' disclosure covers honestly instead of citing only the convenient mark.

Both quoted closures — the wicked-Er notice and the five-count tally — stand exactly where the row places them, and the fresh single-tribe head at 2:5 is real. The comparison drawn to 2:6's structurally identical כֻלָּם חֲמִשָּה tally is an accurate description of that verse, though it creates a consistency question for how the neighboring row treats the same device; that question is argued under M8-1Chr-011, not here, since this row's own 2:4/2:5 boundary is not in doubt.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: No challenge landed on this row in my cluster slice. Spot-checking it anyway: the wicked-Er clause רַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה וַיְמיתֵהוּ and the closing tally כָּל בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה חֲמִשָּה both slice byte-identical from 1Chr_oshb.txt at 2:3-2:4, the arithmetic behind the five-count holds (Er, Onan, Shelah at 2:3 plus Perez, Zerah at 2:4), and 2:5's בְּנֵי פֶּרֶץ is a genuine fresh single-branch head. pmarks_1Chr.json shows a samekh after 2:3 and 2:4 (both single-witness, neither among the ten doubled verses), matching the row's own disclosure. Holds unchallenged.

post_resolution_check.notes: Five-count closure at 2.4 checked against oshb; parallel cited to 2.6 is accurate (Zerah's own five-count is a sub-tally, not the row's own).

primary_reviews.rationale: Collation is clean across all six strings, and the internal reading of the table is defensible: וּבְנֵ֣י זֶ֗רַח, וּבְנֵ֖י כַּרְמִ֑י and וּבְנֵ֥י אֵיתָ֖ן עֲזַרְיָֽה are three co-ordinate waw-headed slots, none carrying a gathering clause, so keeping them in one row is reasonable. Where the row goes wrong is at its closing edge, which it argues from an English word. MT 2:9 opens וּבְנֵ֥י חֶצְר֖וֹן אֲשֶׁ֣ר נוֹלַד ל֑וֹ — a plain conjunctive waw, morphologically the same opener as the three heads just listed. The real discontinuities at 2:9 are the relative clause אֲשֶׁ֣ר נוֹלַד ל֑וֹ and the accusative marking of every member, אֶת יְרַחְמְאֵ֥ל וְאֶת רָ֖ם וְאֶת כְּלוּבָֽי, and the row quotes both without pressing either. The seam may well be right; the stated warrant is not the one the Hebrew supplies.

challenges.claim: A translation supplement is doing tier-1 work. The row calls 2:9 a resumptive formula "signaled by WEB's own added 'also'", but there is no gam and no af in MT 2:9: the verse reads וּבְנֵ֥י חֶצְר֖וֹן אֲשֶׁ֣ר נוֹלַד ל֑וֹ (oshb:1Chr.2.9), whose waw is identical to the waw of וּבְנֵ֣י זֶ֗רַח (oshb:1Chr.2.6), וּבְנֵ֖י כַּרְמִ֑י (oshb:1Chr.2.7) and וּבְנֵ֥י אֵיתָ֖ן עֲזַרְיָֽה (oshb:1Chr.2.8) — all three inside this row's own span. If 'also' renders that waw it is not distinctive; if it is a free supplement it is not MT evidence at all. Either way the closing edge cannot stand on it.
challenges.suggested_action: Re-argue the 2:8|2:9 seam from MT alone: the relative clause אֲשֶׁ֣ר נוֹלַד ל֑וֹ and the accusative-marked member list אֶת יְרַחְמְאֵ֥ל וְאֶת רָ֖ם וְאֶת כְּלוּבָֽי are absent from the three preceding heads and are the actual formal break. Strike 'also' from the evidence.

challenges.claim: The form description tracks the gloss rather than the Hebrew. The row calls 2:7 and 2:8 "single-son notices" and cites WEB's 'The son of Carmi' / 'The son of Ethan', but MT has the plural construct in both: וּבְנֵ֖י כַּרְמִ֑י (oshb:1Chr.2.7) and וּבְנֵ֥י אֵיתָ֖ן עֲזַרְיָֽה (oshb:1Chr.2.8). The plural head carrying a single name is itself the formal point — it shows these are register slots holding the same shape as their neighbours, not a change of device at the tail of the table.
challenges.suggested_action: State the MT form (plural benei with one following name) and label 'the son of' explicitly as WEB's rendering, so the device claim rests on the Hebrew.

primary_reviews.rationale: The opening and closing edges are correctly anchored — 2:5's Perez head and 2:9's resumptive 'also' formula are both real and byte-accurate — but the row's own closure logic is inconsistent with its neighbor. M8-1Chr-010 treats 2:4's כָּל בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה חֲמִשָּה tally as the decisive signal ending a generation, and this row's own rationale calls 2:6's כֻלָּם חֲמִשָּה 'the parallel five-count' to that very device — yet the row then argues no sub-head here 'carries a full summary-type ("these were") closure,' quietly narrowing 'closure' to exclude the tally formula it just called parallel. The rejected-alternative paragraph only tests the extreme (split at every sons-of-X sub-head) and never tests the moderate alternative of ending at 2:6, right after Zerah's own tally, with 2:7-8 (Carmi, Ethan) as a short coda.

challenges.claim: 2:6 closes with כֻלָּם חֲמִשָּה ('all of them, five') — a tally-closure of the identical form the cluster elsewhere (M8-1Chr-010, citing 2:4's כָּל בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה חֲמִשָּה) treats as decisive for closing a generation-unit. This row's own rationale calls the 2:6 tally 'the parallel five-count' to that device, then rejects a split at 2:6 by requiring a 'these were' (אֵּלֶּה)-type closure — a narrower standard than the one applied one row earlier to the same device. The moderate alternative of ending the row at 2:6 and treating 2:7-8 (Carmi, Ethan) as their own two-verse coda is never tested; only the all-or-nothing 'split every sons-of-X head' alternative is.
challenges.suggested_action: Either apply the tally-closure standard consistently (which argues for a split after 2:6) or add a sentence explaining why a branch-level tally (2:6) carries less unit-ending force than a generation-level tally (2:4), instead of only rejecting the all-or-nothing alternative.

primary_reviews.rationale: The tallies behave as the row says. Zerah's roster at 2:6 names Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara, five, and the tally at 2:4 sums Judah's own generation — Er, Onan, Shelah from 2:3 plus Perez and Zerah — also five, so branch-level and generation-level bookkeeping really are different animals here. MT 2:9 contains neither gam nor af, which settles the 'also' point in the row's favour: the waw there is the same waw that opens 2:6, 2:7 and 2:8, and the distinguishing material is the relative clause with the three et-marked names, absent from all three earlier heads. The plural construct is confirmed at 2:7 and 2:8, so the English singular is indeed a rendering choice. Marks check out as reported — samekh keyed to 2:5, 2:6 and 2:7, with none at 2:8, and the row is right to read that run as list-item granularity; I note without objection that the samekh after 2:4 sits at the row's opening edge and goes unmentioned, which costs the row nothing since it would only corroborate. One descriptive claim in the repaired sentence outruns the Hebrew.

challenges.claim: The rewrite says the tally at 2:6 is followed “with no register restart, by two further generations run as single-name notices,” naming וּבְנֵ֖י כַּרְמִ֑י (oshb:1Chr.2.7) and וּבְנֵ֥י אֵיתָ֖ן עֲזַרְיָֽה (oshb:1Chr.2.8). That holds for the second notice only. Ethan stands inside וּבְנֵ֣י זֶ֗רַח's five-name roster at 2:6, so Azariah at 2:8 is demonstrably one generation further down. Carmi is never given a father anywhere in 1 Chronicles 2 — the verse opens on him cold, and no preceding head, tally or chain in the span places him — so 2:7 is not a further generation of anything the text has established, and describing the two verses as a matched generational pair imports a descent the MT does not supply. The point bears on the rejected alternative, which defends keeping 2:7 and 2:8 together partly on their being on the same footing.
challenges.suggested_action: State the asymmetry: 2:8 continues a name already listed at 2:6 while 2:7 introduces an unattached name, and rest the case for holding the two verses together on the shared formal shape — plural construct head plus a single following name, with no tally or closure between them — which is what the row actually demonstrates.

primary_reviews.rationale: All three cures move past cosmetic compliance. The 2:6-versus-2:4 tally distinction is now argued rather than asserted -- branch tally versus generation tally is a real, checkable difference, not a label -- and the moderate 'end at 2:6' alternative gets its own sentence instead of being folded into the all-or-nothing split. Striking WEB's 'also' as evidence and re-grounding the 2:9 seam in the relative clause and accusative-marked triad removes a translation-layer dependency the original argument didn't need. The MT-form correction at vv.7-8 (plural construct, not 'the son of') is accurate and now explicit.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: All three challenges check out. LF-M8-1Chr-011-1 catches a genuine double standard: M8-1Chr-010's own rationale calls 2:6's כֻּלָּם חֲמִשָּה 'the parallel five-count' to 2:4's כָּל בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה חֲמִשָּה, yet this row, having likewise conceded 2:6 is 'tallied shut,' declines to weigh that same tally as seam-worthy and instead demands an אֵלֶּּה-type closure before it will consider ending the table early — a stricter bar than the one its own neighbor cleared. The rejected-alternative paragraph tests only the all-or-nothing 'split every sons-of-X head' option and never the moderate one (end at 2:6, let 2:7-8 stand as a Carmi/Ethan coda), so the challenge stands as written. OL-M8-1Chr-011-1 is also confirmed: MT 2:9 (וּבְנֵ֥י חֶצְר֖וֹן אֲשֶׁ֣ר נוֹלַד ל֑וֹ) carries no גם or אף — WEB's 'also' is a smoothing supplement, and the row's own phrasing ('signaled by WEB's own added ‘also’') already half-concedes this while still leaning on it as if it argued something about the Hebrew. The relative clause אֲשֶר נולַד לו and the accusative-marked triad OL proposes instead are real and are genuinely absent from the three waw-headed slots at 2:6-2:8, so they are the sounder ground for the same edge. OL-M8-1Chr-011-2 is likewise accurate: both 2:7 (וּבְנֵי כַּרְמִי) and 2:8 (וּבְנֵ֥י אֵיתָ֖ן עֲזַרְיָֽה) keep the plural construct בְּנֵי that opens every slot in this table; WEB's singular 'The son of' is a translation choice, not a change in the underlying Hebrew shape, so calling 2:7-8 'single-son notices' mischaracterizes the device. None of the three challenges touch mark evidence or WEB-editorial metadata, so nothing here falls to the tier-4/absence bar. LF-M8-1Chr-011-1's finding does raise a live question about whether 2:5-8 should split at 2:6 — that is for the author/boss round to weigh; I am not altering the frozen span.

challenge_responses.response: Accepted (peer-ruled supported): decision 010's own rationale treats 2:4's tally as decisive for closing a generation-unit while this row required a stricter 'these are'-type closure before weighing 2:6's tally the same way, and the rejected_alternative tested only the all-or-nothing split, never the moderate end-at-2:6 reading. Span stays frozen; supplied the distinguishing reason the challenge asked for -- 2:4's tally totals Judah's whole generation and ends that prior row outright, while 2:6's totals only Zerah's own sub-branch and is followed by v.8, which is unquestionably still part of this table and carries no tally at all -- and separately tested the moderate end-at-2:6 alternative by name in the rejected_alternative.

Accepted (peer-ruled supported): MT 2:9's waw is identical to the waw opening vv.6-8 inside this row, so WEB's 'also' renders no distinctive MT feature. Replaced it with the actual formal break: the relative clause and the accusative-marked member list at 2:9, both absent from the three preceding heads.

Accepted (peer-ruled supported, low severity): 2:7 and 2:8 both carry the plural construct benei, the same shape as 2:5's own opening; restated the MT form and labeled WEB's 'The son of' as a translation choice rather than a Hebrew form change.

rulings.remedy: In boundary_rationale, replace the characterization of 2:7 and 2:8 as a matched generational pair ('two further generations run as single-name notices') with a statement of the asymmetry: 2:8's Ethan continues a name already listed among Zerah's five sons at 2:6, one generation down, while 2:7's Carmi has no antecedent anywhere in ch.2 and opens cold. Rest the case for holding 2:7-2:8 together on their shared formal shape (plural construct head plus a single following name, no tally or closure between them) rather than on parallel descent.

boss_ruling.reasoning: All three amendments adopted: the 2:6 tally now measured by the same standard the neighbor row applies to 2:4, WEB's supplied 'also' stripped of evidential weight at 2:9, and the benei shape of 2:7-8 restated from the Hebrew. The Perez/Zerah table keeps its edges — the v.9 head that follows is argued from the Hebrew waw+construct chain, not the translation.

post_resolution_check.notes: Careful distinction between Zerah's sub-tally (2.6) and the row's own governing frame; the we-carmi/we-eitan asymmetry argument holds up against oshb.

primary_reviews.rationale: The head-plus-chain reading is sound and its numbers check out: the ordinal series closes on אֹ֚צֶם הַשִּׁשִּׁ֔י דָּוִ֖יד הַשְּׁבִעִֽי, which with בְּכֹר֖וֹ at 2:13 as the first slot yields exactly seven, and 2:16's שְׁלֹשָֽׁה matches the three names it counts. The 2:9 head is quoted in full and is byte-identical to the line. Two defects remain. The closing edge is argued against a comparandum 2:18 was never going to match, and the 2:16 citation silently adopts the qere on the only ketiv-qere line in this cluster's material.

challenges.claim: Tier 1, wrong comparandum at the closing edge. The row ends at 2:17 because 2:18 shows a "patronymic-plus-name formula" it calls distinct from "the plural 'sons of X' openings". But 2:18 reads וְכָלֵ֣ב בֶּן חֶצְר֗וֹן הוֹלִ֛יד, and verse-initial waw + PN + holid is the commonest opening in this chapter — 13 verses carry it (2:10, 2:11, 2:12, 2:13, 2:20, 2:22, 2:36-2:41, 2:44), four of them inside this very span: וְרָ֖ם הוֹלִ֣יד, וְנַחְשׁוֹן֙ הוֹלִ֣יד, וּבֹ֨עַז֙ הוֹלִ֣יד, וְאִישַׁ֛י הוֹלִ֥יד. Formally 2:18 reproduces the span's own dominant idiom and adds only the patronym בֶּן חֶצְר֗וֹן, so measuring it against the benei-heads proves nothing about the seam.
challenges.suggested_action: Rest the 2:17|2:18 seam on the element that genuinely differs — the patronymic re-anchor to Hezron after a chain that had travelled away from him — and state plainly that 2:18's verb shape is continuous with 2:10-2:13 rather than distinct from them.

challenges.claim: Undisclosed qere. The row quotes וְאַחְיוֹתֵיהֶ֖ם from 2:16, which is the qere; the consonantal ketiv on the same line is ואחיתיהם. Both stand in 1Chr_oshb.txt, and 2:16 is one of only two ketiv-qere lines in the whole chapter. The quotation is byte-accurate, but it presents a qere form as the plain MT reading in a row whose evidence value is the Hebrew itself.

challenges.claim: The row calls 2:24 “the identical fronted-ahar-plus-qatal opener” and makes that identity the basis for reading 2:21 and 2:24 as a matched pair. challenges.claim: Tier 1, head-formula identity. The row's opening warrant is the "full patronym-and-rank head" וַיִּהְי֧וּ בְנֵי יְרַחְמְאֵ֛ל בְּכ֥וֹר חֶצְר֖וֹן הַבְּכ֣וֹר רָ֑ם at 2:25. Across the whole book only eight verses open with wayyihyu benei, and three of them sit in this one span. The signal the row calls unit-launching therefore fires three times inside the unit, and the rejected alternative meets 2:28 on subordination grounds alone, never confronting 2:27 or the formula-identity problem.

challenges.claim: Function conflation in the supporting parallel. The row bolsters 2:33 by calling it "the same summary device" it sees "opening this chapter's own neighbors" at 2:1 and 2:50. Calling 2:33's formula the strongest possible signal therefore overreaches — the same string heads units elsewhere in this very chapter.
challenges.suggested_action: Recast the closure as positional (verse-final elleh clause gathering antecedent names) and either drop the 2:1/2:50 parallel or relabel those two occurrences as headings.

Every factual assertion in this rewrite survives independent checking. The three wayyihyu heads slice byte-exact from 2:25, 2:27 and 2:28; a book-wide scan of verse-initial forms confirms six occurrences of wayyihyu followed by the construct benei, the extra three being precisely 7:19, 8:40 and 23:17 as the refs now claim. (The earlier count of eight arises only if wayyihyu banim at 2:52 and 8:3 is folded in, which is a different, non-construct shape, so the narrower figure the row now uses is the accurate one.) Position claims hold: 2:33's elleh-hayu clause terminates its verse while the comparanda at 2:1 and 2:50 stand first with their lists after them, so the row's move from formula-identity to discourse function is textually earned. The negated-existence opener at 2:34 is verified verbatim, WLC records samekh after 2:26, 2:30 and 2:32 but nothing at 2:33, and the row treats that silence correctly as non-counterevidence. No fresh defect found; the concession about a thrice-firing opener is the honest reading of the evidence rather than a weakening of the row.

primary_reviews.rationale: Five Hebrew quotations, all five byte-identical to the source lines. Two of the row's factual claims I could confirm outright. The chain 3:10-14 really is verbless: after וּבֶן שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה רְחַבְעָ֑ם the verses run as bare name plus pronominal suffix, e.g. יוֹרָ֥ם בְּנ֛וֹ, with no finite verb anywhere. And the mark-absence disclosure is accurate - pmarks_1Chr.json puts marks in ch 3 only at 3:4, 3:9, 3:21 and 3:24, so nothing falls between 3:10 and 3:16, and the row correctly declines to make that absence do any work. Where it goes wrong is the morphology of the heads, which cuts against the seam the row picks rather than for it, and the quotation of 3:16 has been truncated in a way that hides the problem.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative (split at 3:15) is dismissed on the ground that "3:16 immediately resumes the identical successor-naming pattern" of 3:10-14, but the Hebrew head morphology says the opposite. 3:10 opens with the singular construct וּבֶן שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה רְחַבְעָ֑ם and 3:11-14 then run with no head at all. 3:15, 3:16 and 3:17 all open with the same plural construct: וּבְנֵי֙ יֹאשִׁיָּ֔הוּ / וּבְנֵ֖י יְהוֹיָקִ֑ים / וּבְנֵי֙ יְכָנְיָ֣ה. The head-form isogloss therefore falls between 3:14 and 3:15, one verse inside the span, and the row's chosen seam at 3:17 cuts through the middle of an unbroken three-verse run of the identical opening. The 'single-heir idiom' description of 3:16 is moreover produced by the quotation itself, which stops at Jeconiah and silently drops the verse's second heir; 3:16 in full reads וּבְנֵ֖י יְהוֹיָקִ֑ים יְכָנְיָ֥ה בְנ֖וֹ צִדְקִיָּ֥ה בְנֽוֹ, ending צִדְקִיָּ֥ה בְנֽוֹ, so it names two sons under a plural head, not one heir.
challenges.suggested_action: Quote 3:16 in full, drop the 'identical pattern' ground, and either argue the 3:15 seam on its merits against the 3:15-3:17 head-run or re-ground the 3:17 seam on the Assir epithet alone; medium confidence should not stand on an elided quotation.

The repair is honest and its quotations verify: 3:10 and 3:14 slice exactly, 3:15, 3:16 and 3:17 do share וּבְנֵי plus a proper name, 3:11-3:14 carry no head at all, and pmarks_1Chr.json records no pe or samekh anywhere between 3:10 and 3:16, so the row's claim to rest on wording alone is accurate. The difficulty is what the concession leaves standing. The rewrite now demonstrates that vv.15-16 form their own plural-head pair distinct from the headless single-heir chain of vv.11-14, but supplies no positive reason for attaching that pair to vv.10-14 rather than to v.17, which shares its head shape; the whole outer edge is left resting on one epithet, whose morphology the row does not examine. Confidence remains medium, which is defensible only if the join inside the span is argued rather than assumed.

challenges.claim: After the concession, nothing in the rationale joins 3:15-3:16 to 3:10-3:14. The rewrite establishes that 3:10 opens with a singular construct, that 3:11-3:14 run headless with the bare בְּנוֹ refrain, and that 3:15, 3:16 and 3:17 all open with the identical plural construct — from which it concludes that 'vv.15-16 form a two-verse plural-head unit rather than a fold back into the single-heir chain'. That is an argument for a seam at 3:15, and the row draws none. It then closes the span between two verses of the same head shape on a single content feature. The span as it stands is thus internally two-part by the row's own demonstration, with the join asserted rather than shown, and the outer edge carried by one word.

challenges.claim: The one feature now carrying the closing edge is presented as settled when the form leaves it open. The row states that what distinguishes 3:17 is 'the epithet that follows it: וּבְנֵי֙ יְכָנְיָ֣ה אַסִּ֔ר ... "the captive"'. The row cites WEB's rendering, which is a translational decision, as though it demonstrated the morphology, and this single reading is also what the following row's opening edge depends on.

primary_reviews.rationale: The opening edge I can affirm on original-language grounds the row does not itself supply. Reading אַסִּ֔ר as an epithet attached to Jeconiah rather than as the name of a first son is what the Masoretic pointing favours: יְכָנְיָ֣ה carries munah (U+05A3), a conjunctive accent, binding it forward to אַסִּ֔ר, which carries zaqef qatan (U+0594), so the two words form one accentual phrase. The rival construal of Assir as a personal name is not excluded by the consonants, but it is not the grouping the accents give. Both Hebrew quotations collate byte-exact, and the seven names of 3:24 do reconcile with the verse's own שִׁבְעָֽה once the ketiv-qere is resolved. Against that, three separate problems: the 3:24 quotation reproduces a ketiv-qere pair as if it were two consecutive names, the analogy drawn to the 2:4 and 2:6 counts does not hold in Hebrew, and the closing edge is never argued from the text at all. Marker citations are accurate (SAMEKH at 1Chr.3.21 and 1Chr.3.24, single-witness, neither doubled). No offset zone applies.

challenges.claim: The 3:24 quotation runs a ketiv and its qere together as though they were consecutive names: it reads וּבְנֵ֣י אֶלְיוֹעֵינַ֗י הדיוהו הוֹדַוְיָ֡הוּ. The unpointed הדיוהו is the ketiv of the pointed qere הוֹדַוְיָ֡הוּ, one word, not two. Undisclosed, the quotation displays eight name-tokens after Elioenai while the verse's own count is שִׁבְעָֽה - and that seven-count is precisely what the row uses to close the unit, so the undisclosed pair undercuts its own closure argument. Resolved, the arithmetic is exact at seven. Comparable unpointed ketiv tokens sit at 2:55, 4:7 and 4:20 in this cluster's territory; 3:24's is the only one that falls inside a quoted string.
challenges.suggested_action: Re-slice the 3:24 quotation on the qere alone, or keep both forms and mark the ketiv-qere explicitly, so the token count visibly agrees with the seven the row's closure rests on.

challenges.claim: "a closing seven-count tally of the same kind used at 2:4 and 2:6 above" does not survive comparison of the actual Hebrew. 2:4 closes כָּל בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה חֲמִשָּֽׁה and 2:6 closes כֻּלָּ֥ם חֲמִשָּֽׁה - both are kol-summaries carrying a numeral. 3:24 closes with the bare numeral שִׁבְעָֽה and no kol at all, so it is not the same formula. Worse for the closure argument, that bare-numeral ending occurs three further times inside this very row without closing anything: חָמֵֽשׁ at 3:20, שִׁשָּֽׁה at 3:22 and שְׁלֹשָֽׁה at 3:23. A device the span uses four times cannot be what terminates the span.
challenges.suggested_action: Withdraw the 2:4/2:6 analogy and rest the close on something the span does not repeat internally - the asyndetic tribal head at 4:1 is the obvious candidate.

challenges.claim: The closing edge is argued from campaign scaffolding rather than from 1Chr. "This row's end is also this part's own boundary, so no further text-internal seam needs arguing past 3:24" appeals to the writer part plan, which is planning metadata and no more a text signal than a chapter number; and boundary_evidence_refs contain no reference to 4:1 whatever (they also skip 3:18 and 3:20-3:23, which lie inside the span and carry the numerals the row's closure claim depends on). Every other row in this cluster verifies its closing edge against the next verse's wording, and the evidence is available: 4:1 opens asyndetically with the tribal head בְּנֵ֖י יְהוּדָ֑ה, and a sweep of verse-initial words shows every verse from 4:2 to 4:20 opening with waw, so 4:1's vav-less head is a genuine tier-1 restart.
challenges.suggested_action: Argue the 3:24/4:1 seam from 4:1's asyndetic tribal head and add web:1Chr.4.1 and oshb:1Chr.4.1 to boundary_evidence_refs, along with the omitted in-span verses 3:18 and 3:20-3:23.

primary_reviews.rationale: The 3:17, 3:19, and 3:24 quotes are all byte-exact against oshb, the samekh cites at 3:21 and 3:24 match pmarks_1Chr.json, and 3:24 is genuinely the chapter's last verse, so nothing past it needs arguing within this cluster.

Three substantial repairs, all verified. The ketiv/qere disclosure is exactly right and the seven-count resolves; the withdrawn analogy is replaced by a correct observation that bare numerals recur verse-finally at 3:20, 3:22 and 3:23; and the asyndetic head at 4:1 checks out against a sweep showing every verse from 4:2 through 4:20 opening with waw. Samekh at 3:21 and 3:24 is recorded as cited. What survives untouched is the interior of the span. The rationale claims the register runs from 3:18 to 3:23 'without a further sons-of-X restart strong enough to split it', and the rejected alternative goes further, denying that any register head reopens at 3:19 — while quoting one. On the sliced text, 3:19 opens וּבְנֵ֣י פְדָיָ֔ה and carries a second head, וּבֶן זְרֻבָּבֶל֙, in the same verse; 3:22 opens וּבְנֵ֥י שְׁכַנְיָ֖ה with וּבְנֵ֣י שְׁמַעְיָ֗ה after it; 3:21 and 3:23 open with the singular construct; and the row's own close at 3:24 opens with the same plural construct as its head at 3:17. The opener is therefore no more distinctive here than the wayyihyu opener was at 2:25, where this cluster required the point to be met head-on.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative denies a register head at 3:19 in a sentence that quotes one. It reads: 'Splitting at 3:19 ... loses because no new register head reopens there — the text continues appositionally ("the sons of Pedaiah... and the son of Zerubbabel") within one unbroken sentence-chain'. 3:19 begins וּבְנֵ֣י פְדָיָ֔ה זְרֻבָּבֶ֖ל וְשִׁמְעִ֑י, an atnach falls on וְשִׁמְעִ֑י, and a second head follows, וּבֶן זְרֻבָּבֶל֙ מְשֻׁלָּ֣ם — so there are two heads and two clauses, not an unbroken chain. This is the same waw-plus-benei-plus-name construct the row uses to open itself at 3:17, and it recurs at 3:22 (twice) and at 3:24; the singular counterpart stands at 3:21 and 3:23. Since the appositional continuity claim is the whole defence of the span's interior, the premise needs replacing rather than softening.
challenges.suggested_action: Drop 'no new register head reopens there' and argue the interior on what the heads actually do — each names a figure already listed in the immediately preceding clause (Pedaiah from 3:18, Zerubbabel from 3:19a, Hananiah from 3:19b, Shecaniah from 3:21, Neariah from 3:22, Elioenai from 3:23), so the run is a linked descent chain in which no head introduces an unannounced subject — and add oshb/web refs for 3:19 and 3:21, the two in-span verses still missing plain citations.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Three challenges land on this one row and all three check out, making it the heaviest concentration of confirmed defects in the cluster. First, the row's own 3:24 quotation carries the OSHB line's ketiv הדיוהו immediately beside its qere הוֹדַוְיָ֡הוּ as though they were two names; read literally that is eight tokens against the verse's own שִׁבְעָֽה, undercutting the very count the row leans on for closure — resolved as one name the arithmetic is exact, but nothing in the row discloses the resolution. Second, the analogy to 2:4/2:6 does not hold: I confirmed both those verses close with a כֹּל/כֻּלָּם word plus a numeral, while 3:24 closes on the bare numeral alone, a device that already recurs three more times inside this same row (3:20 חָמֵֽשׁ, 3:22 שִׁשָּֽׁה, 3:23 שְׁלֹשָֽׁה) without closing anything — a device repeated four times cannot be the thing that terminates the span. Third, the row's stated reason for not arguing past 3:24 — 'this row's end is also this part's own boundary' — leans on the writer's part-tiling plan, which book_strategy_draft.md's own header calls a non-authorizing planning artifact, not 1Chr's wording; boundary_evidence_refs skip 3:18, 3:20-3:23, and 4:1 entirely, and my own waw-initial sweep of 4:2 through 4:20 confirms 4:1's asyndetic בְּנֵ֖י יְהוּדָ֑ה is the genuine restart — the same edge row 021 already argues independently from its own side. None of this puts the 3:24/4:1 boundary itself in doubt; row 021 proves it on its own terms. What is confirmed is that row 020's rationale does not itself demonstrate what it asserts, which is a rationale-completeness gap the author round should close, most directly by mirroring 021's opening argument back into 020's closing argument, rather than a reason to question the span.

challenges.suggested_action: Argue explicitly why 4:2's 'elleh summary subordinates to 4:4's rather than dividing the row, add oshb/web refs for 4:2 and 4:3, and revisit the 'high' confidence: a four-verse span containing an unaddressed instance of its own closing device does not read as high.

primary_reviews.rationale: The opening register head and the closing 'sons of Hur' summary formula both verify byte-exact against oshb, and the shift at 4:5 to a dative-fronted new subject is real; that shift is further corroborated internally by 1Chr 2:24, which already identifies Ashhur as a Hezron descendant, so 4:5 genuinely opens an unrelated branch rather than continuing Hur's line under a different name.

The repair is thorough and its quotations are exact: 4:2 does close with the Zorathite families formula, 4:3 does open a further branch and run on into 4:4, 4:4 does close with the sons-of-Hur summary, and 4:5's dative-fronted new subject is verbatim. WLC's samekh at 4:2 is correctly held out of the drivers. The remaining weakness is the hinge on which the whole nesting argument turns. The row subordinates 4:2's closure to 4:4's by observing that 'the sons of Hur' names a figure listed in 4:1 — but 4:2 develops Reaiah ben Shobal, and Shobal appears in that same 4:1 list at the same level as Hur, which the row itself describes as 'five sons' of Judah. On the row's own description of 4:1, then, 4:4's summary cannot reach back over 4:2 at all. The subordination is available from elsewhere in the book, at 2:50, where Shobal is a son of Caleb ben Hur, but that verse is neither cited nor mentioned, so the argument as written relies on a filiation it contradicts.

challenges.claim: The subordination of 4:2 to 4:4 rests on a filiation the row does not state and its own reading of 4:1 excludes. The argument runs: 'the sons of Hur' names the same figure v.1 lists as one of Judah's five sons, so 4:4's closure 'reaches back over the whole vv.2-4 stretch, gathering Reaiah's and Etam's branches together under Hur'. But 4:2's subject is וּרְאָיָ֤ה בֶן שׁוֹבָל֙, and 4:1 reads בְּנֵ֖י יְהוּדָ֑ה פֶּ֧רֶץ חֶצְר֛וֹן וְכַרְמִ֖י וְח֥וּר וְשׁוֹבָֽל — Shobal stands in that list beside Hur, not under him. If 4:1 names five sons of Judah, as the row says, then Reaiah's line descends from Hur's peer and a sons-of-Hur summary cannot gather it. The needed link exists at 2:50 (שׁוֹבָ֕ל as a son of Caleb ben Hur), but 2:50 appears neither in the rationale nor in boundary_evidence_refs.
challenges.suggested_action: Either cite 2:50 and argue the Shobal-under-Hur descent explicitly, noting that 4:1's list is a chain rather than five co-ordinate sons, or drop the gathering claim and defend the span's integrity on the position of 4:4's summary (last of three nested closures, immediately before the new dative-fronted subject at 4:5) without asserting that it reaches back over Shobal's branch.

primary_reviews.rationale: The cure is substantive: 4:2 and 4:3 are now named, their formulas quoted, and both argued as nested sub-closures subordinate to 4:4's retroactive 'sons of Hur' summary rather than left as unaddressed rivals. challenges.claim: The rejected alternative turns on "the verb-form break at v.9, where narrative wayyiqtol replaces the toledot chain that has run continuously since v.5", but no such wayyiqtol-free chain runs from 4:5. 4:6 itself opens וַתֵּ֨לֶד ל֤וֹ נַעֲרָה֙ - a wayyiqtol - inside the span, and 4:9's וַיְהִ֣י יַעְבֵּ֔ץ is therefore the second, not the first, verse-initial wayyiqtol in this four-verse row. A sweep of verse-initial forms across 1Chr 2-4 finds them at 2:19, 2:23, 2:25, 2:26, 2:27, 2:28, 2:35, 2:49, 2:52, 4:6, 4:9, 4:10, 4:28, 4:39, 4:40, 4:41 and 4:43, several of them inside register rows this cluster leaves unsplit (2:52 sits inside M8-1Chr-017). challenges.claim: "then Helah's branch runs through Hakkoz's descendants" states a filiation the Hebrew does not. 4:7 gives Helah's sons and nothing more: וּבְנֵ֖י חֶלְאָ֑ה צֶ֥רֶת יצחר וְצֹ֖חַר וְאֶתְנָֽן. 4:8 then begins a fresh verbal clause, וְק֣וֹץ הוֹלִ֔יד, with no ben, no abi, and no syntactic tie back to Helah, to Naarah or to Ashhur. Since the row's unit-integrity argument is that the two-wives notice of 4:5 "governs the whole unit", 4:8 is exactly the verse that needs arguing, and 4:7 - the verse that would have to carry the link - is absent from boundary_evidence_refs.

primary_reviews.rationale: The Ashhur two-wives frame, the Naarah sub-closure at 4:6, and Hakkoz's unclosed tail at 4:8 all verify against oshb, and the row is honest that Hakkoz's fragment ends on nothing; the wayyiqtol scene-opener at 4:9 is a sharp, real break from the toledot idiom running continuously since 4:5.

Both repairs are real and well made; the WEB and Hebrew for 4:5, 4:6, 4:8 and 4:9 all verify, and the honest labelling of Hakkoz's attachment as inference is exactly what the docket asked for. The repair nevertheless brought a new quotation into the row and reproduced in it the very defect the sibling row on 3:17-3:24 was ordered to fix. The 4:7 slice runs צֶ֥רֶת יצחר וְצֹ֖חַר וְאֶתְנָֽן without comment, where יצחר is the unpointed ketiv of the pointed qere וְצֹ֖חַר. The row's own WEB gloss lists three names; the Hebrew it prints beside that gloss displays four tokens after Helah. Nothing arithmetical hangs on it here, which is why this is filed below high, but the round-one docket named 4:7 as a ketiv site in this cluster's territory, and the campaign's disclosure rule does not weaken because no numeral is at stake.

challenges.claim: The newly added 4:7 quotation runs a ketiv and its qere together as consecutive names, undisclosed. The row prints וּבְנֵ֖י חֶלְאָ֑ה צֶ֥רֶת יצחר וְצֹ֖חַר וְאֶתְנָֽן and glosses it 'WEB "The sons of Helah were Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan"'. The unpointed יצחר is the ketiv whose qere is the pointed וְצֹ֖חַר, one name; as printed, four tokens follow Helah against a three-name gloss, and a reader collating the line has no way to tell that the pair is one word. This is the same class of defect upheld against 3:17-3:24 at 3:24 in round one, which the neighbouring revised row has now disclosed properly — so the cluster discloses ketiv/qere in one quotation and conceals it in another.
challenges.suggested_action: Re-slice 4:7 on the qere alone (צֶ֥רֶת וְצֹ֖חַר וְאֶתְנָֽן) or keep both forms and mark the ketiv/qere in the same words used for 3:24, so the token count visibly matches the three sons the row and WEB both report.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both cures are clean and text-accurate. The wayyiqtol argument is properly abandoned once the row itself notices 4:6 already uses the same conjugation, and the replacement ground (named subject plus evaluative predicate plus speech frame at 4:9) is a real, checkable distinction. The Helah-to-Hakkoz filiation claim is now correctly downgraded to a flagged inference rather than an asserted fact, with 4:7 added to the evidence trail.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Both challenges against this row hold up. 4:6 opens with its own wayyiqtol, וַתֵּ֨לֶד ל֤וֹ נַעֲרָה֙, sitting inside this very row's span, so 4:9's וַיְהִ֣י יַעְבֵּ֔ץ is at best the second wayyiqtol in the four-verse stretch, not the first — the verb-form conjugation alone does not separate this row from what follows, exactly as argued. Separately, I checked 4:7 directly: it names Helah's own sons (Zereth, Jezoar/Izhar, Zohar, Ethnan) and stops there; 4:8 opens a fresh clause, וְק֣וֹץ הוֹלִ֔יד, with no בֶּן or אֲבִי particle tying Koz back to Helah, Naarah, or Ashhur, and 4:7 itself is missing from the row's own boundary_evidence_refs despite being the one verse that would have to carry that link. Neither point overturns the Ashhur-two-wives frame as such, but both weaken the specific case for folding 4:7-8 underneath it, which the row's own language calls its integrity claim; whether medium confidence survives once the wayyiqtol ground and the filiation claim are both removed is a question for the author/boss round to weigh, not one this review resolves on its own.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both Hebrew quotations slice exact, and rather than accept the row's bounded uniqueness claim about the petition-and-fulfilment shape I widened it: a programmatic sweep for the quotative לֵאמֹ֔ר across the entire genealogical prologue, 1Chr 1:1 to 9:44, returns exactly two verses, 4:9 and 4:10, and nothing else in nine chapters. Direct speech is therefore not merely locally but prologue-wide unique to this inset, which is a stronger warrant than the row claims for itself and is the real tier-1 frame here. The WEB clause quoted for the fulfilment is genuine WEB 4:10; it does not appear on the verse's own line in 1Chr_web_clean.txt because the USFM sets a paragraph break mid-verse and the cleaner emitted the remainder as a continuation line, and I confirmed the wording directly against 1Chr_web.usfm (the paragraph mark itself is tier-4 formatting, noted only to account for the extraction, not used as evidence). The resumption at 4:11 is likewise real: וּכְל֥וּב אֲחִֽי שׁוּחָ֖ה הוֹלִ֣יד returns the host register's hiphil idiom. One weakness I record without raising it to a challenge, because the row's boundary does not depend on it: "the wayyiqtol entry at v.9" does not by itself discriminate, since וַתֵּ֨לֶד ל֤וֹ נַעֲרָה֙ at 4:6 and the corresponding form at 2:52 are wayyiqtol inside register rows this cluster does not split. The speech frame and the 4:11 resumption carry the decision independently, so the inset-versus-row call stands.

This is the cluster's flagged low-confidence Jabez split and it holds: the toledot verb הוליד brackets the inset on both sides (4:8 and 4:11), while the inset itself runs exclusively on wayyiqtol narrative verbs (ויהי, ויקרא, ויבא) that appear nowhere else in the surrounding fragments, giving the split a real verbal-form basis rather than a bare narrative impression.

primary_reviews.rationale: The closing edge is the strongest thing in this row and I was able to confirm it mechanically. 4:21 does open asyndetically with בְּנֵי֙ שֵׁלָ֣ה בֶן יְהוּדָ֔ה, and a verse-initial sweep of ch 4 shows every single verse from 4:2 through 4:20 beginning with waw, so the vav-less restart at 4:21 really is unlike anything since 4:1 - the claim is exactly true as stated, which is rarer than it sounds. The opening quotation and the Kenaz sample both collate byte-exact. The row's interior description is where it fails: it asserts that none of the fragments carries its own closing formula, and two of them plainly do. The 'identical form' ground offered against the finer-grained rival is also loose.

challenges.claim: "none of which carries a tribal-level head or its own closing formula" is falsified inside the span. 4:12 ends, after its atnach on נָחָ֑שׁ, with אֵ֖לֶּה אַנְשֵׁ֥י רֵכָֽה, and 4:18 ends with וְאֵ֗לֶּה בְּנֵי֙ בִּתְיָ֣ה בַת פַּרְעֹ֔ה. Both are the post-atnach 'elleh summary that this same cluster treats as a tier-1 closure at 4:4 and at 4:6, so the ten-verse run contains two instances of the very device the row says is absent. Because that absence is the whole ground for holding 4:11-20 together, the premise needs replacing rather than patching. Disclosed as tier-3 weak corroboration only and never as a driver: pmarks_1Chr.json records SAMEKH at 1Chr.4.12 and 1Chr.4.18 and PE at 1Chr.4.14, all single-witness, none of them cited by the row.
challenges.suggested_action: Replace the 'no closing formula' premise with an argument for why the 4:12 and 4:18 summaries close list items rather than the row, and add oshb/web refs for 4:12, 4:14 and 4:18.

challenges.claim: "all use the identical conjunctive continuation form" overstates the uniformity of the seven openings the rejected alternative enumerates, and two of them are not that form at all. 4:11 is waw plus a personal name governing a finite verb, וּכְל֥וּב אֲחִֽי שׁוּחָ֖ה הוֹלִ֣יד, with no bene head; and 4:17 opens with the singular וּבֶן עֶזְרָ֔ה against the plural וּבְנֵ֣י קְנַ֔ז at 4:13 and the same plural at 4:15, 4:16, 4:19 and 4:20. primary_reviews.rationale: The premise swap is done properly and the surrounding facts check out: 4:11 has no benei head, 4:13, 4:15, 4:16, 4:19 and 4:20 open with the plural construct while 4:17 opens with the singular, 4:21 restarts asyndetically with בְּנֵי֙ שֵׁלָ֣ה בֶן יְהוּדָ֔ה, and a sweep confirms Judah's name is absent from every verse between 4:2 and 4:20 while every one of those verses opens with waw. primary_reviews.rationale: Every Hebrew fragment in this row resolves to the verse it is attributed to when sliced from 1Chr_oshb.txt: the head “בְּנֵי֙ שֵׁלָ֣ה בֶן יְהוּדָ֔ה” sits at 4:21, the source-note remark “וְהַדְּבָרִ֖ים עַתִּיקִֽים” ends 4:22, and both halves of the closing notice fall inside 4:23. The load-bearing part of the argument is an exclusivity claim, so I tested it rather than accepting it. Taking the first orthographic word of each verse from 4:11 through 4:23, exactly two are not vav-initial: 4:21 and 4:23. The second of those opens with the pronoun “הֵ֚מָּה”, which is a resumptive summary opener and not a construct register head, so 4:21 stands alone as the asyndetic head of that run. A consonantal search for the string yhwd across the same eleven verses returns 4:21 and nothing else, which is the second half of what the row asserts. The invoked parallel also holds byte-for-byte in shape: 4:1 opens “בְּנֵ֖י יְהוּדָ֑ה”, verse-initial bene with no conjunction, the identical construction. Marker hygiene is clean — pmarks_1Chr.json records SAMEKH at 1Chr.4.23 (single-witness), the row labels it as such, and 4:23 is not among the ten doubled-samekh verses, so no doubling disclosure was owed. Numbering needs no dual-cite here: MT and WEB both carry 43 verses in chapter 4 and the offset does not begin until MT 5:27. One observation I do not raise as a challenge: the forward-edge verse named in the prose, 4:24, is not mirrored into boundary_evidence_refs, but its head is asyndetic and uncontested, so nothing turns on the omission.

The opening claim checks out at the level the row stakes it on: v.21's head, בְּנֵי֙ שֵׁלָ֣ה בֶן יְהוּדָ֔ה, drops the vav that prefixes every register-shaped line since v.11, and I walked that stretch verse by verse (11 וּכְלוּב, 13 וּבְנֵי, 15 וּבְנֵי, 16 וּבְנֵי, 17 וּבֶן, 19 וּבְנֵי, 20 וּבְנֵי) to confirm the 'unlike every intervening conjunctive fragment' claim is a real book-local universal, not an assertion. The closing edge is equally solid: v.22's colophon aside and v.23's הֵ֚מָּה-identification clause both read as the same referent chain rather than a new head, so the row's own account of why v.23 (not v.22) supplies closure is correct.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both quoted fragments are byte-accurate — “בְּנֵ֖י שִׁמְע֑וֹן” opens 4:24 and the comparative tail “עַד בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה” ends 4:27 — and the marker citation is correct: pmarks records SAMEKH at 1Chr.4.27 (single-witness), undoubled. The forward-edge observation is also sound; 4:28 does begin with a wayyiqtol settlement verb, so the register-to-narration shift the row describes is real. What fails inspection is the row's account of what lies between its two edges. The span is described as a branch-free descent line, and the Hebrew of its own opening and middle verses says otherwise, which matters because that description is precisely what distinguishes this row from the coarser Simeon block the rejected alternative dismisses. I do not think the seams move; I think the form label and the internal head both need argument.

challenges.claim: The row's distinguishing form claim — a single-file father-son chain “with no branching” — is contradicted by the Hebrew at two points inside its own span (tier 1, the text's own register signals). First, the opening verse is not linear: 4:24 reads “בְּנֵ֖י שִׁמְע֑וֹן נְמוּאֵ֣ל וְיָמִ֔ין יָרִ֖יב זֶ֥רַח שָׁאֽוּל”, five coordinate sons set side by side with no beno-chain at all; the chain only starts at 4:25 with “שַׁלֻּ֥ם בְּנ֛וֹ”. Second, the span carries an internal register head: 4:26 opens “וּבְנֵ֖י מִשְׁמָ֑ע חַמּוּאֵ֥ל בְּנ֛וֹ”, the conjunctive bene-X head formula that the device matrix lists as a tier-1 boundary signal and that this very cluster treats as unit-opening elsewhere (4:21, 5:1, 5:11, 5:23). The rationale absorbs that head into the descent line by naming Mishma and Hammuel as consecutive links, which is not what the syntax does — a plural construct head is followed by a fresh singular beno-chain. Because the rejected alternative is argued only against 4:28, neither the five-way branch at 4:24 nor the re-head at 4:26 is addressed anywhere in the row.
challenges.suggested_action: Restate the literature type as a tribal head plus segmented list plus beno-chain rather than a branch-free descent line, and add one clause arguing why the bene-Mishma head at 4:26 is unit-internal while the same formula opens rows at 4:21, 5:1, 5:11 and 5:23. Mirror oshb:1Chr.4.25 and oshb:1Chr.4.26 into boundary_evidence_refs. No span change follows from this challenge.

primary_reviews.rationale: The father-son chain is exactly single-file as claimed: Shaul (24) to Shallum/Mibsam/Mishma (25) to Hammuel/Zaccur/Shimei (26), no branch node anywhere in the sequence, so the 'linear descent chain' label earns its keep. The comparative close at v.27, וְכֹל֙ מִשְׁפַּחְתָּ֔ם לֹ֥א הִרְבּ֖וּ עַד בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה, is a rhetorical stop rather than a lineage note exactly as described, and v.28's wayyiqtol וַיֵּֽשְׁב֛וּ is a genuine form-shift from register to settlement narration.

The cure holds on every point the original item raised. What the repair added, however, is an identity claim that byte inspection does not bear out: 4:21 opens בְּנֵי֙ and this row's own head at 4:24 opens בְּנֵ֖י, both asyndetic, while 4:26 opens וּבְנֵ֖י with the conjunction attached. Of the four comparanda the row names, only 5:1, 5:11 and 5:23 actually carry 4:26's shape. That matters inside this cluster because decision 029 treats presence or absence of the same conjunctive vav as a signal worth naming, describing 5:3 as repeating 5:1 without it; one row cannot lean on the feature while its neighbour erases it. Noticing the difference would in fact help 026, since the head it absorbs at 4:26 is formally distinct from the head it opens on at 4:24. Everything else checks: pmarks records SAMEKH at 1Chr.4.27 as the row states, no mark falls anywhere inside 4:24-4:27, and all six Hebrew strings quoted here byte-match their cited verses.

challenges.claim: The repaired rationale calls 4:26 "the identical benei-X shape this cluster's own neighboring rows use to open their own units (4:21, and, further into the book, 5:1, 5:11, 5:23)". The identity is therefore true of three comparanda and false of the fourth, and false of the row's own opening head at 4:24. The point is not cosmetic inside this cluster: decision 029 makes the dropped conjunction a named feature of its 5:1/5:3 relaunch argument, so 026 and 029 apply opposite weight to one signal.
