primary_reviews.rationale: Quote fidelity is not the problem here: “וַיֵּֽשְׁב֛וּ” does open 4:28, the two fragments of the 4:38 summary are contiguous with the text, and the observation about 4:34 is exactly right — that verse begins “וּמְשׁוֹבָ֣ב”, a bare vav-plus-name with no head formula. The difficulty is that the row builds its case on the absence of a head at 4:34 while saying nothing about the presence of a closure at 4:33, and then treats its own forward edge as a clean break when the following narrative reaches back across it by name. Two challenges follow, one internal and one at the outer edge; together they mean the medium confidence recorded here is, if anything, generous. Marker check: none of 4:28-4:38 carries a pe or samekh in pmarks, which under the Writings policy is neither evidence for nor against any of this, and I draw nothing from it.

challenges.claim: The span swallows a demonstrative summary closure without argument (tier 1). 4:33 ends “זֹ֚את מוֹשְׁבֹתָ֔ם וְהִתְיַחְשָׂ֖ם לָהֶֽם” (WEB: “These were their settlements, and they kept their genealogy”), a zot-plus-summary-noun formula of the same closure class the row itself leans on at 4:38; and 4:31 already ends “אֵ֥לֶּה עָרֵיהֶ֖ם עַד מְלֹ֥ךְ דָּוִֽיד” (WEB: “These were their cities until David's reign”). So the row asserts that 4:38 supplies a single closing formula for the whole span while that span in fact contains three demonstrative summary formulas, two of them unmentioned. This also means the rejected alternative is not engaged at its strongest: the rival split at 4:33/4:34 does not depend on finding a head at 4:34 (there is none, as the row correctly says) but on the closure that stands immediately before it. Note further that 4:38's summary is about persons listed by name, which caps the roster of 4:34-4:37, not the place-lists of 4:28-4:33 that 4:33 has already capped.
challenges.suggested_action: Either argue explicitly why the zot-formula at 4:33 does not close the settlement register, or re-span to 1Chr.4.28-1Chr.4.33 and let the name roster stand as its own decision. Either way add oshb:1Chr.4.31 and oshb:1Chr.4.33 to boundary_evidence_refs, which at present omit 4:33 entirely.

challenges.claim: The forward-edge argument — that 4:39 opens an “unrelated expedition” — is contradicted by an explicit lexical anaphora across that seam. 4:38 opens “אֵ֚לֶּה הַבָּאִ֣ים בְּשֵׁמ֔וֹת” and 4:41 opens “וַיָּבֹ֡אוּ אֵלֶּה֩ הַכְּתוּבִ֨ים בְּשֵׁמ֜וֹת”: the same demonstrative elleh, the same root bw' (participle at 4:38, wayyiqtol at 4:41), and the same adverbial beshemot. A consonantal sweep of the book returns beshemot at five verses only (4:38; 4:41; 6:50; 12:32; 16:41), and this pair is the only place where it combines with elleh and with bw'. The expedition is therefore not unrelated to the roster this row ends on — 4:41 names that roster as its own grammatical subject.
challenges.suggested_action: Argue the 4:38/4:39 seam against this anaphora rather than by asserting unrelatedness, or record the roster's forward attachment as a live unresolved rival; mirror oshb:1Chr.4.41 into boundary_evidence_refs as the argued comparandum.

primary_reviews.rationale: The outer edges hold: v.28's וַיֵּֽשְׁב֛וּ opens settlement narration and v.38's אֵ֚לֶּה הַבָּאִ֣ים בְּשֵׁמ֔וֹת summary closes the roster. But the row's rejected-alternative argument only tests v.34's OPENING (no head formula there) and never engages that v.33 already carries its OWN closing formula, זֹ֚את מוֹשְׁבֹתָ֔ם וְהִתְיַחְשָׂ֖ם לָהֶֽם, of the same class this cluster elsewhere treats as sufficient by itself to end a row (v.23, v.27) regardless of whether the next unit opens with a head.

challenges.claim: The rejected-alternative sentence rests entirely on v.34's missing head formula and never addresses that v.33 already carries its own tier-1 closure, 'זֹ֚את מוֹשְׁבֹתָ֔ם וְהִתְיַחְשָׂ֖ם לָהֶֽם' (WEB 'These were their settlements, and they kept their genealogy'). This cluster treats a bare closure as sufficient to end a row without requiring the following unit to open with its own head at both 4:23 (potters coda, no fresh head follows until 4:24) and effectively at 4:27 (Judah comparison, followed immediately by 4:28's verb-form shift rather than a head). By that same standard v.33's closure is a live candidate for ending 4:28-33 as its own settlement register, leaving 4:34-38 as a separately-closed (v.38) roster -- a second internal closure at v.31 (אֵ֥לֶּה עָרֵיהֶ֖ם עַד מְלֹ֥ךְ דָּוִֽיד) compounds the point.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both formal requirements are met, so I record all three items cured. The whole weight of the high-severity cure, though, now rests on one lexical reading that the repair supplies without evidence: that וְהִתְיַחְשָׂ֖ם לָהֶֽם at 4:33 is promissory and forward-points to 4:34-38. I swept the root across the book. Ten verses in 1 Chronicles carry a hitpael of yod-het-sin, and the notice is overwhelmingly retrospective: 5:17, 7:5, 7:7, 7:9, 7:40 and 9:1 are each followed by a pe or a samekh, and 5:17 is treated as precisely such a terminal dated closure by decision 030 in this same cluster. The reading the row wants is nonetheless attested once, at 5:7, where בְּהִתְיַחֵ֖שׂ does introduce the roster that runs on into 5:8, and that verse sits inside sibling decision 029's span. It is neither quoted nor mirrored. A second asymmetry cuts the other way and also goes unmentioned: 4:33 is the one yahas notice in the book with no paragraph mark after it, which is weak but genuine corroboration for the row's own conclusion. The row is left arguing a minority sense of a book-internal formula with none of the book-internal data on the page. Confidence at medium_low is appropriate; the evidence trail is not.

primary_reviews.rationale: All four fragments collate exactly, and the second episode's opener “וּמֵהֶ֣ם מִן בְּנֵ֣י שִׁמְע֗וֹן הָלְכוּ֙” is quoted with its full construct string intact. challenges.claim: The inclusio that binds the two episodes rests on the refrain being “identical”, and the witness does not support that word. At 4:41 the phrase reads “עַד הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה” and at 4:43 it reads “עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה”: the consonants agree but the pointing does not (4:41 carries U+05B7/U+05B7/U+05BC/U+05A3/U+05B9/U+05B7/U+05BC/U+05B6/U+0594, 4:43 carries U+05B7/U+0596/U+05B7/U+05BC/U+05A5/U+05B9/U+05B7/U+05BC/U+05B6/U+05BD). More decisively, the 4:41 occurrence is not where its episode ends — six words follow it in the same verse, “וַיֵּשְׁב֖וּ תַּחְתֵּיהֶ֑ם כִּֽי מִרְעֶ֥ה לְצֹאנָ֖ם שָֽׁם”, so the Gedor episode closes on a pasture note, not on the refrain. A book-wide consonantal sweep finds the phrase at 4:41, 4:43, 5:26, 13:11 and 17:5, and the verse-final form at 4:43 is byte-identical to those at 5:26 and 13:11, so it is a recurring Chronicler closure rather than a device shaped for this pair.

challenges.claim: The repair states that the Gedor episode closes "not on a verse-final refrain but mid-clause", and later that 4:43's occurrence, "unlike v.41's, is genuinely clause-final". primary_reviews.rationale: This row's repair is the strongest of the cluster: it corrects a genuine misdescription (the day-formula is not verse-final at v.41) and a genuine overclaim ('identical' refrain), replacing both with claims the Hebrew actually supports. primary_reviews.rationale: The relaunch argument is the strongest original-language observation in this cluster and it verifies cleanly. Stripping points from the two heads shows 5:1's “וּבְנֵ֨י רְאוּבֵ֥ן בְּכֽוֹר יִשְׂרָאֵל֮” and 5:3's “בְּנֵ֥י רְאוּבֵ֖ן בְּכ֣וֹר יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל” are consonantally identical once the initial vav is removed, so “literally repeating its own head phrase, now without the conjunctive vav” is exact, and the row discloses the one difference rather than glossing over it. The closing quote sits at 5:10 as claimed, the mark file carries a PE there (1Chr.5.10, single-witness) with no doubling, and the WEB gloss preserves the lower-case opening of 5:3, which is careful. I still challenge, on two counts of unevenness: a head of the row's own diagnostic shape is passed over inside the span, and the tier-3 disclosure is one-sided. The first of these sits awkwardly with a confidence of high.

challenges.claim: The criterion the row uses to identify its relaunch — verse-initial bene with the conjunction dropped — applies unchanged to 5:4, which the span absorbs in silence. A sweep of chapters 4 and 5 for verse-initial asyndetic bene returns exactly seven verses: 4:1, 4:21, 4:24, 5:3, 5:4, 5:18, and MT 5:27 (= WEB 6:1, inside offset zone A). Six of the seven are treated as heads by the rows of this cluster or open the unit that follows it; only 5:4 is neither argued nor named, although it reads “בְּנֵ֖י יוֹאֵ֑ל שְׁמַֽעְיָ֥ה בְנ֛וֹ” and introduces a Joel who is not connected to any of the four sons just listed at 5:3. This is a tier-1 register signal of the row's own preferred shape, left unaddressed inside a span carrying high confidence.
challenges.suggested_action: Argue 5:4 explicitly — either as a sub-head continuing the Reuben register or as a genuine internal seam — then carry 5:4 into the boundary refs under both sigla, web:1Chr.5.4 alongside oshb:1Chr.5.4. If it cannot be argued down, the confidence should not remain high.

challenges.claim: Tier-3 disclosure is asymmetric. Under the Writings policy neither mark can drive a boundary and neither is counterevidence, so this does not decide anything; but citing the mark that corroborates the chosen edge while passing over the mark standing at the rejected one is selective use of weak evidence.

challenges.claim: The repair argues 5:4 down by calling it "the same class of internal pivot this campaign already treats as staying inside one row elsewhere in this cluster (4:26's construct-plural reopening within a single register)". Under 026's rule 5:4 is the branch-introducing case, not the continuation case, so the analogy runs backwards while high confidence rests on it. challenges.suggested_action: Say the head phrase recurs consonantally, identical apart from the conjunction and repointed for its new position, and drop "literally" and "verbatim". The relaunch argument survives unchanged.

primary_reviews.rationale: Three fragments, three exact hits: the Gad head at 5:11, the two-king dated closure filling 5:17 in its entirety, and the joint-tribe opener of 5:18 quoted as the outer edge. challenges.claim: One tier-1 form is treated two ways inside this cluster without acknowledgement. I tested the one claim in the row that could be over-reach, that the numbered-muster form has no counterpart in the single-tribe heads of 5:1-17. First, the syntax binds 5:18 to 5:19: “וַיַּעֲשׂ֥וּ מִלְחָמָ֖ה עִם הַֽהַגְרִיאִ֑ים” has no nominal subject of its own and takes it from the muster clause, which argues for keeping the census and the war together far more directly than the appeal to form-distinctness. Second, the witness itself distinguishes this war from the Saul-era Hagrite notice that closes the preceding row: 5:10 spells the gentilic defectively, “הַֽהַגְרִאִ֔ים”, while 5:19 and 5:20 spell it plene, “הַֽהַגְרִיאִ֔ים”. challenges.claim: The rejected alternative is defeated by a grammatical assertion the Hebrew does not support: that 5:26 “continues the same wayyiqtol chain begun at v.25 with the same subject”. At 5:25 the verbs are third-person plural with the tribes as subject — “וַיִּֽמְעֲל֔וּ” and “וַיִּזְנ֗וּ”. At 5:26 the chain continues but the subject switches: “וַיָּעַר֩ אֱלֹהֵ֨י יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל” is third-person masculine singular with a new explicit nominal subject, and the two following verbs “וַיַּגְלֵם֙” and “וַ֠יְבִיאֵם” are likewise singular, carrying the tribes as pronominal object suffixes rather than as subject. The subject demonstrably changes at the one verse the row says it cannot change at. The span is probably still right, on the sin-and-consequence sequence and the shared triad of names, but the stated reason for it is false and cannot be left standing in a row marked high confidence.

primary_reviews.rationale: Four Hebrew citations, four exact substring hits on the lines the row names: בְּנֵ֖י לֵוִ֑י and גֵּרְשׁ֕וֹן resolve to oshb 1Chr.5.27, וּבְנֵ֖י קְהָ֑ת to 1Chr.5.28, וּבְנֵ֣י עַמְרָ֔ם to 1Chr.5.29, with no normalization needed to make them land. Morphology tightens the row's case rather than loosening it. The block-opening head is asyndetic while the two narrowing heads carry a conjunctive waw, so what the row calls a cascade is graded in the consonants themselves; and all three verses are verbless nominal clauses, which is precisely the observation the row makes when it says no head predicates anything of its members. The first finite verb of the sequence arrives only at oshb 1Chr.5.30 (אֶלְעָזָר֙ הוֹלִ֣יד), so the pivot the row locates between web:1Chr.6.3 and web:1Chr.6.4 is a real verbal onset, not a rhetorical one. I tested the anchor claim rather than accepting it: a token sweep of every form beginning gimel-resh-shin across all of 1 Chronicles returns the nun-final spelling exactly once, at oshb 1Chr.5.27, while the mem-final name is written two ways elsewhere (גֵּרְשֹׁ֕ם at oshb 1Chr.6.1 and 1Chr.6.28; a waw-spelled variant at 1Chr.6.2, 1Chr.6.5, 1Chr.6.47, 1Chr.6.56). The orthographic spread on the Gershom side leaves the nun/mem discriminator the row depends on intact. Mark data checks out: pmarks carries SAMEKH+SAMEKH keyed to 1Chr.5.29 (single-witness), matching the doubling the row discloses; a further SAMEKH keyed to 1Chr.5.28 (single-witness) falls between web:1Chr.6.2 and web:1Chr.6.3, inside the span, and being tier-3 it neither supports nor undercuts anything. One nuance I note without pressing it: oshb 1Chr.5.29 carries a fourth instance of the register device mid-verse (וּבְנֵ֣י אַהֲרֹ֔ן), which the row surfaces as a clause it opens into rather than labelling as a head — mid-verse and therefore unsplittable under the strategy's own hold rule. Offset arithmetic on all five refs is right under WEB 6:v = MT 5:v+26.

The three cascading register heads (בְּנֵ֖י לֵוִ֑י oshb 5:27; sons-of-Kohath וּבְנֵ֖י קְהָ֑ת oshb 5:28; sons-of-Amram וּבְנֵ֣י עַמְרָ֔ם oshb 5:29) genuinely narrow generation by generation and none predicates a fathering act, so grouping them under one row that stops the instant the fathering-verb chain begins at 5:30 is the reading the text supports; the double-samekh disclosure at 5:29 is correctly flagged.

primary_reviews.rationale: The terminal quotation is byte-perfect against oshb 1Chr.5.41, and the mark attached to it is right in both type and placement: pmarks keys SAMEKH to 1Chr.5.41 (single-witness), which under the follows-the-verse convention divides web:1Chr.6.15 from web:1Chr.6.16 — the closing edge the row is arguing. The aside is analysed correctly too — ה֚וּא אֲשֶׁ֣ר כִּהֵ֔ן at oshb 1Chr.5.36 is a pronoun plus relative clause hanging off the preceding object, which leaves the chain's syntax undisturbed. primary_reviews.rationale: Collation is clean — all four Hebrew strings sit exactly where the row puts them — and the reopening thesis is actually better supported than the row realises. Searching the whole book for the head string בְּנֵ֖י לֵוִ֑י returns two verses, oshb 1Chr.5.27 and oshb 1Chr.6.1, meaning the opening of this row is byte-identical to the opening of the row at web:1Chr.6.1 apart from the son's name; the same test on וּבְנֵ֖י קְהָ֑ת again returns a pair, oshb 1Chr.5.28 and oshb 1Chr.6.3, where the two verses differ by a single conjunctive waw on the second son (יִצְהָ֔ר against וְיִצְהָ֔ר). A near-verbatim doublet at both the head and the second tier is the strongest available in-book argument that the text is restarting rather than continuing, and it is available without touching numbering. The handoff claim also holds: oshb 1Chr.6.5 opens with a lamed-prefixed patronymic rather than another register head. Two problems remain. The device inventory misdescribes the unit's own middle, and the closural argument rests on a formula the row has already used as an opener four verses earlier; separately, a universal-sounding claim goes out unscoped. Both are set out below. Neither touches the span's edges, which I think are correctly placed.

challenges.claim: web:1Chr.6.17 = oshb:1Chr.6.2 is counted among “three further ‘sons of X’ heads”, yet the string the row itself reproduces disproves the label: וְאֵ֛לֶּה שְׁמ֥וֹת בְּֽנֵי גֵרְשׁ֖וֹם is an elleh-plus-shemot naming formula, a different tier-1 device from the bare construct heads at oshb 1Chr.6.3 and בְּנֵ֥י מְרָרִ֖י at oshb 1Chr.6.4. This is not pedantry about labels — the row's closure argument treats וְאֵ֛לֶּה מִשְׁפְּח֥וֹת הַלֵּוִ֖י לַאֲבוֹתֵיהֶֽם at oshb 1Chr.6.4 as distinctively sealing, while the identical elleh element opens the unit at oshb 1Chr.6.2. The distinction that would rescue the argument is cataphoric versus anaphoric reference (names follow at oshb 1Chr.6.2; nothing is enumerated after the clause at oshb 1Chr.6.4), and the row never draws it. A second error rides along: “at the same generational depth as decision 01's cascade” is wrong in both directions, since the earlier row's heads descend Levi to Kohath to Amram whereas oshb 1Chr.6.2, 1Chr.6.3 and 1Chr.6.4 head three brothers standing at one level.
challenges.suggested_action: Reclassify oshb:1Chr.6.2 (= web:1Chr.6.17) as an elleh naming formula, ground the closural reading of oshb 1Chr.6.4 on the absence of any following enumeration rather than on the elleh element alone, and correct the depth statement to sibling-level heads.

challenges.claim: “no counterpart until the next register closes” is asserted without a scope and fails when swept book-wide. The same formula stands at oshb 1Chr.4.2, אֵ֖לֶּה מִשְׁפְּח֥וֹת הַצָּֽרְעָתִֽי, also sealing a register. Read forward the claim does survive: the lexeme's next closural use is the settlement total at web:1Chr.6.60 = oshb:1Chr.6.45, and the possessive tail of oshb 1Chr.6.4 is a genuine hapax in 1 Chronicles — it occurs there and nowhere else in the book, which is a sharper fact than the one claimed.
challenges.suggested_action: State the scope (“nothing of this shape recurs before oshb:1Chr.6.45 = web:1Chr.6.60”), cite oshb 1Chr.4.2 as in-book corroboration that the formula does closural work in this book, and use the hapax status of the closing word rather than a bare “no counterpart”.

primary_reviews.rationale: The Gershon/Gershom spelling contrast the row leans on for the crosswalk anchor is real in the text (defective גֵּרְשֹׁ֕ם at 6:1 vs גֵּרְשׁ֕וֹן at 5:27), the three sibling-clan sons-lists sit at one generational depth unlike decision 033's nested cascade, and the 6:19b toledot-style seal genuinely has no counterpart until the register closes again later — a stronger closural anchor than 033 had, which explains the confidence gap between the two rows.

Both original items were repaired on their own terms and the two programmatic claims the repair installed survive independent re-execution: לַאֲבוֹתֵיהֶֽם really is a one-off in 1 Chronicles, and the אלה-משפחות formula really does stand at oshb 1Chr.4.2 doing closural work with no offset. The samekh newly attached to the 4:2 citation is genuine (pmarks_1Chr.json: 1Chr.4.2 SAMEKH). What the repair did not touch is the sentence that anchors the whole row, and that sentence quotes the wrong words. The row builds its opening on a Gershom/Gershon spelling pair but reproduces לֵוִ֑י for both members, a form that is byte-identical across the two verses and is neither name. primary_reviews.rationale: Quote fidelity is not the problem here — the string attributed to MT 6:50 = WEB 6:65 matches the witness exactly, the WEB-to-MT pairings all resolve at the +15 offset that governs this zone, and pmarks confirms SAMEKH (not pe) trailing MT 6:50 = WEB 6:65, disclosed as single-witness. The trouble is what the row does with the syntax of that verse. Read whole, it is a wayyiqtol clause of giving: וַיִּתְּנ֣וּ בַגּוֹרָ֗ל, then the source tribes מִמַּטֵּ֤ה בְנֵי יְהוּדָה֙ וּמִמַּטֵּ֣ה בְנֵי שִׁמְע֔וֹן וּמִמַּטֵּ֖ה בְּנֵ֣י בִנְיָמִ֑ן, then the object phrase אֵ֚ת הֶעָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה אֲשֶׁר יִקְרְא֥וּ אֶתְהֶ֖ם בְּשֵׁמֽוֹת. Two things follow from that shape, and both cut against reading WEB 6:64-65 as this unit's retrospective colophon. I also checked the row's account of its middle: the Gershom tally at MT 6:47 = WEB 6:62 carries no בגורל at all, so the 'plain by-lot tally' description covers two of the three sub-grants, not three.

challenges.claim: The device is misidentified. The row calls the ending of MT 6:50 = WEB 6:65 “an 'these are'-style summary closure”, but אֵ֚ת הֶעָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה is an attributive demonstrative modifying the definite object of וַיִּתְּנ֣וּ — 'they gave ... these cities' — not the nominal אלה clause the strategy's matrix lists as a summary/closure formula. The genuine article appears inside this very cluster at MT 7:17 (no offset there), אֵ֚לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י גִלְעָ֔ד, a verbless 'these are the sons of X' clause; that row demotes it to internal bookkeeping while this row promotes a demonstrative embedded in a verbal clause to a unit-sealing device. The two rows cannot weigh the same tier-1 device in opposite directions on weaker grammar.
challenges.suggested_action: Either restate the closure claim on a device the Hebrew supports (e.g. the shift to the collective giving verb and the all-Israel subject at MT 6:49 = WEB 6:64) or withdraw the 'these are' label; if the אלה-summary label is retained anywhere in this book, apply the same threshold to MT 7:17.

challenges.claim: The relative clause has no antecedent inside the span. אֵ֚ת הֶעָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה אֲשֶׁר יִקְרְא֥וּ אֶתְהֶ֖ם בְּשֵׁמֽוֹת means the cities 'which they call by names', yet MT 6:46-48 = WEB 6:61-63 name no city at all: they give tribes and bare numerals (בַּגּוֹרָ֖ל עָרִ֥ים עָֽשֶׂר ... עָרִ֖ים שְׁלֹ֥שׁ עֶשְׂרֵֽה ... עָרִ֖ים שְׁתֵּ֥ים עֶשְׂרֵֽה). The cities that are called by name stand on the other side of the proposed seam, in MT 6:51-66 = WEB 6:66-81. Worse for the closure reading, the three source tribes listed in MT 6:50 = WEB 6:65 — מִמַּטֵּ֤ה בְנֵי יְהוּדָה֙ וּמִמַּטֵּ֣ה בְנֵי שִׁמְע֔וֹן וּמִמַּטֵּ֖ה בְּנֵ֣י בִנְיָמִ֑ן — are precisely the tribes of the Aaronic grant two decisions back (Hebron אֶת חֶבְר֖וֹן בְּאֶ֣רֶץ יְהוּדָ֑ה at MT 6:40 = WEB 6:55; וְאֶת עָשָׁן֙ at MT 6:44 = WEB 6:59, which 1Chr's own Simeon register lists as Simeonite at oshb:1Chr.4.32 = web:1Chr.4.32, וְעָשָׁ֑ן עָרִ֖ים חָמֵֽשׁ; וּמִמַּטֵּ֣ה בִנְיָמִ֗ן at MT 6:45 = WEB 6:60) and appear nowhere among the tribes of MT 6:46-48 = WEB 6:61-63. So WEB 6:64-65 does not summarize what this span contains, and the forward-facing reading the row dismisses in one line is at least as strong as the one it adopts.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: All three challenges against this row's closing colophon claim are borne out, and two of them (LF's and OL's second) converge on the same underlying defect from different angles, so I am treating the tribe-mismatch point as one finding with one remedy rather than double-counting it. I sliced MT 6:46-6:50 directly: v46 מִֽ֠מַּחֲצִית מַטֵּ֨ה חֲצִ֧י מְנַשֶּׁ֛ה, v47 מִמַּטֵּ֣ה יִ֠שָׂשכָר / אָשֵׁ֜ר / נַפְתָּלִ֗י / מְנַשֶּׁה֙ בַּבָּשָׁ֔ן, v48 מִמַּטֵּ֣ה רְ֠אוּבֵן / גָ֞ד / זְבוּלֻן֙ — Manasseh, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, Reuben, Gad, Zebulun, and nothing else. V50's own tribe list is מִמַּטֵּ֤ה בְנֵי יְהוּדָה֙ וּמִמַּטֵּ֣ה בְנֵי שִׁמְע֔וֹן וּמִמַּטֵּ֖ה בְּנֵ֣י בִנְיָמִ֑ן — Judah, Simeon, Benjamin — none of which appears in this row's own material. Judah and Benjamin sit instead in decision 041's span (Hebron בְּאֶ֣רֶץ יְהוּדָ֑ה at MT 6:40, Benjamin's cities at MT 6:45), and Simeon reaches it through Ashan: MT 6:44's וְאֶת עָשָׁן֙ is listed as Simeonite at MT 4:32 (וְעָשָׁ֑ן עָרִ֖ים חָמֵֽשׁ), which I confirmed by direct lookup. So the colophon's named tribes track decision 041's grant, not this row's 61-63. OL's first challenge catches a separate, compounding problem in how the row types the device: אֵ֚ת הֶעָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה at v50 is an attributive demonstrative on the direct object of a wayyiqtol giving-verb (וַיִּתְּנ֣וּ בַגּוֹרָ֗ל ... אֵ֚ת הֶעָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה), not the verbless predicate-nominal 'these are the sons of X' closure the strategy's matrix actually catalogs — the genuine article of that formula sits three verses into the next decision, at MT 7:17's אֵ֚לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י גִלְעָ֔ד, which this same cluster correctly treats as internal bookkeeping rather than a seal. And the relative clause that follows, אֲשֶׁר יִקְרְא֥וּ אֶתְהֶ֖ם בְּשֵׁמֽוֹת ('which they call by names'), has no antecedent inside 61-63 at all — v46/47/48 give tribes and bare numerals, never a city name; the named cities start only at MT 6:51 = WEB 6:66, on the far side of this row's own closing edge. Three independent readings of the same two verses (61-65's colophon) all point the same way: the row's claim that 64-65 seals 61-63 specifically is not what the Hebrew supports. I am not moving the span myself, but the author/boss round should treat this as a live seam question — whether 64-65 belongs with 041's grant, heads toward 043's named lists, or the whole 54-65 run is better argued as one row with 61 as an internal sub-head, exactly as the LF challenge's suggested_action itself floats.

OL's two challenges are substantive and both hold. The first: MT 6:56 = WEB 6:71 opens לִבְנֵי֮ גֵּרְשׁוֹם֒ and MT 6:62 = WEB 6:77 opens לִבְנֵ֣י מְרָרִי֮ הַנּוֹתָרִים֒ — I confirmed both by direct slice — and these are the identical לבני X formula the immediately preceding decision (042) treats as constituting its own rows at MT 6:47 = WEB 6:62 and MT 6:48 = WEB 6:63. Decision 044, one row over in this same cluster, already gets this right — its own boundary_rationale calls v6 'the bare tribe name... with no syntactic tie-back,' pointedly noting the absence of בני as part of its own case for closing at v5. Decision 045 then turns around and calls the identical verse 'a tribal head' and leans on 'the single '"'sons of Benjamin"' head at v6' to reject a three-way clan split — treating as a matrix-grade register-head formula the very thing decision 044 correctly flagged as lacking one. Meanwhile the three clan sub-heads this row is arguing should stay subordinate do carry the formula: וּבְנֵ֣י בֶ֗לַע at v7, וּבְנֵ֣י בֶ֗כֶר at v8, וּבְנֵ֥י יְדִיעֲאֵ֖ל בִּלְהָ֑ן at v10, all confirmed against the witness. The rationale needs rewriting from what the Hebrew actually shows at v6, and the description of v6 needs to be reconciled with decision 044's own (correct) description of the same clause so the cluster does not carry two contradictory readings of it. Whether a corrected rationale still supports keeping the span at one row, or whether the internal לבני-headed sub-lists should be weighed differently, is for the author/boss round.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Two challenges converge on the row's flat 'no textual link' claim and I am ruling them together with one remedy that folds in both data points; the third challenge is a separate, narrower fix to the row's stated criterion and stands on its own. On the recurrence question: LF caught that MT 7:7 lists וְעִירִ֜י (Iri) among Bela's sons, one final yod away from MT 7:12's עִ֔יר (Ir) — a genuine near-homograph, though a different word, and I confirmed by sweep it is the only עירי in the book. OL's version of the same objection is the stronger one and changes the picture more: a consonantal sweep for חפים/חפם turns up exactly two hits in the whole book, MT 7:12 and MT 7:15, and MT 7:15 — three verses later, inside this same cluster's Manasseh row (048) — reads וּמָכִ֞יר לָקַ֤ח אִשָּׁה֙ לְחֻפִּ֣ים וּלְשֻׁפִּ֔ים, naming Huppim and Shuppim outright as people Machir found wives for. That is not a near-miss like Iri/Ir; it is the same two names recurring verbatim, close by, inside a named genealogical transaction. Neither observation settles where v12 belongs — and the row's own honesty about not being able to adjudicate Ir/Aher's tribal identity is, if anything, reinforced by there now being two candidate attachments instead of one, not weakened by it — but a row whose entire case rests on 'no textual link' has to name and argue past both, and as written it addresses neither. The 'strongest_rejected_alternative' should at minimum add the Manasseh-side attachment via the 7:15 recurrence alongside the Benjamin-side one it currently names alone. Separately, the row's 'carries no register-head formula of its own' is imprecise on its own terms: MT 7:12 contains בני twice, בְּנֵ֣י עִ֔יר and בְּנֵ֥י אַחֵֽר, just never in clause-initial position — confirmed against the witness — and the real distinguishing criterion is fronting, sharpened by MT 7:13 next door, which opens with fronted בְּנֵ֣י נַפְתָּלִ֗י but also ends in the identical predicate-position pattern, בְּנֵ֥י בִלְהָֽה. None of these three corrections moves this row out of low confidence or off its own span; if anything the added data makes the case for holding it exactly where it is, unresolved, stronger rather than weaker.

primary_reviews.rationale: This row survives every check I can put to it. The full-verse citation of MT 7:13 and the head quoted from MT 7:14 both collate byte-exact; the head בְּנֵ֣י נַפְתָּלִ֗י is genuinely clause-initial, unlike the fragment before it; the mark trailing MT 7:13 is PE in pmarks, correctly typed, correctly tagged single-witness, and correctly demoted to weak corroboration rather than made a driver; and בְּנֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה does open a new tribal entry at MT 7:14. The comparative claim is the part most exposed to falsification, so I tested it: Issachar closes with שְׁמוֹנִ֤ים וְשִׁבְעָה֙ אֶ֔לֶף הִתְיַחְשָׂ֖ם לַכֹּֽל at MT 7:5, Benjamin's clans close with three census figures at MT 7:7, 7:9 and 7:11, and Asher closes with אֲנָשִׁ֔ים עֶשְׂרִ֥ים וְשִׁשָּׁ֖ה אָֽלֶף at MT 7:40, whereas MT 7:13 carries neither a sub-list nor a numeral. The row names only those three tribes and does not generalize across the chapter, which is the right scoping since Manasseh and Ephraim also lack totals — so the comparison is accurate as written rather than accidentally true. No dual-cite is owed anywhere here, chapter 7 being outside both offset zones, and the medium confidence looks calibrated for a one-verse span whose only real risk is attachment to its neighbours.

Naphtali's one-verse entry is the strongest-edged of the two fragments in this stretch: it has its own unambiguous head formula, a tier-3 pe right at its close, and a genuinely unrelated Manasseh head immediately after, so separating it from v12 rather than lumping the two together as one leftover appendix is the better reading.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: No challenge was raised against this row by either primary, and it is the one clean edge-pair in this cluster's run of fragments. The pe cited at MT 7:13 is confirmed in pmarks and correctly held to weak corroboration rather than promoted to a driver. Both quoted strings collate exactly against 1Chr_oshb.txt. Nothing here needs correcting.

post_resolution_check.notes: Single-verse span; register-head-vs-fragment contrast with v.12 checked against oshb; pe mark correctly single-witness tagged.

primary_reviews.rationale: Four Hebrew strings, four exact matches; the pe after MT 7:19 is confirmed and properly typed; and וּבְנֵ֥י אֶפְרַ֖יִם at MT 7:20 is the clean outer head the row says it is. I think the row's central judgment is right and better founded than it realises: MT 7:18 opens וַאֲחֹת֖וֹ הַמֹּלֶ֑כֶת יָלְדָה֙ and MT 7:19 opens with a wayyiqtol, so neither verse fronts a competing register head, which is a stronger reason for keeping v17's אֵ֚לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י גִלְעָ֔ד internal than the row actually gives. Both my objections are about citation and construal precision rather than about where the edges fall, and I would not move this span.

challenges.claim: The closing citation is clipped in a way that costs the row its best evidence. MT 7:19 begins וַיִּהְי֖וּ בְּנֵ֣י שְׁמִידָ֑ע, but the row quotes only from בני onward while pairing it with the WEB gloss 'the sons of Shemida were ...', whose 'were' renders the very verb the Hebrew citation drops. That wayyiqtol is what formally separates MT 7:19 from a fresh בני X head of the kind found at MT 7:13, 7:14 and 7:20, so citing it would have answered the obvious objection that a fourth register head is being absorbed without argument.
challenges.suggested_action: Extend the MT 7:19 citation to include the clause-initial verb and use it affirmatively: v19 is a verbal continuation clause, not a fronted register head, which is why it closes the Manasseh unit instead of opening a new one.

challenges.claim: “Tracing the concubine-born line” over-reads MT 7:14. The Hebrew runs בְּנֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה ... פִּֽילַגְשׁוֹ֙ הָֽאֲרַמִּיָּ֔ה יָלְדָ֕ה אֶת מָכִ֖יר: in the sequence אַשְׂרִיאֵ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָלָ֑דָה the verb carries no expressed subject, and פילגשו הארמיה stands as the explicit subject of the following verb, bearing Machir. Making the concubine the mother of Asriel is WEB's construal at web:1Chr.7.14, not a statement of the witness, and the row presents it as description rather than as a gloss-dependent reading.
challenges.suggested_action: Either mark the concubine-to-Asriel connection as a WEB construal, or restate the opening neutrally as the Manasseh head running to Machir and Gilead — the boundary argument does not depend on resolving the subject of the first verb, and the row already concedes that this region's internal relationships are not fully recoverable.

primary_reviews.rationale: The v17 "these are the sons of Gilead" formula reads as internal bookkeeping rather than a competing register head, since vv18-19 keep naming the same Machir-Gilead circle without ever restarting with a new tribal name, and the true outer edge at v20's "sons of Ephraim" head is unambiguous.

The v19 repair is the strongest part of this revision and is right on the merits: וַיִּהְי֖וּ carries the prefix-conjugation preformative that בְּנֵ֣י נַפְתָּלִ֗י (7:13), בְּנֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה (7:14) and וּבְנֵ֥י אֶפְרַ֖יִם (7:20) have no verb to bear, so the contrast is real, and pmarks_1Chr.json puts PE at 1Chr.7.19 where the row places it. Six Hebrew runs, all byte-exact; the WEB strings for vv14, 17, 19 and 20 are verbatim. The defect sits in the other repair. To mark WEB's reading of v14 as a construal the row had to say which verb lacks an expressed subject, and it named the wrong token. MT 7:14 runs בְּנֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה אַשְׂרִיאֵ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָלָ֑דָה פִּֽילַגְשׁוֹ֙ הָֽאֲרַמִּיָּ֔ה יָלְדָ֕ה אֶת מָכִ֖יר, where the token named is in fact the relative marker; the suffix-conjugation form left without a subject is יָלָ֑דָה directly after it, and פִּֽילַגְשׁוֹ֙ הָֽאֲרַמִּיָּ֔ה is supplied only for the second occurrence of that verb. The substantive observation survives correction, which is why this is a labelling failure rather than a boundary problem.

challenges.claim: The rationale calls the relative particle a verb and glosses it "she bore": "the first verb, אֲשֶׁ֣ר (\"she bore\"), has no expressed subject of its own in the Hebrew." MT 7:14 reads בְּנֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה אַשְׂרִיאֵ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָלָ֑דָה פִּֽילַגְשׁוֹ֙ הָֽאֲרַמִּיָּ֔ה יָלְדָ֕ה אֶת מָכִ֖יר. אֲשֶׁ֣ר is the relative particle; the verb whose subject goes unexpressed is יָלָ֑דָה immediately following it, and פִּֽילַגְשׁוֹ֙ הָֽאֲרַמִּיָּ֔ה is supplied as subject only for the second form of that verb. The observation the row wants is sound, but it is hung on a particle, so as written the row plants a false tier-1 morphological identification inside the very sentence meant to correct one.
challenges.suggested_action: Name יָלָ֑דָה as the subjectless verb and leave אֲשֶׁ֣ר as the relative particle introducing it; the conclusion that WEB's extension of the concubine to Asriel is a construal is unaffected.

primary_reviews.rationale: The v14 crux (a verse widely regarded as syntactically difficult) is now handled with appropriate hedging rather than an asserted grammatical claim, consistent with the row's own acknowledged limits on recovering this family's internal relationships. One loose label worth noting but not rising to a challenge: 'the first verb, אֲשֳֶר יָלָֽדָה' treats a two-word span (relative particle plus the actual verb) under one 'verb' label; since the row explicitly declines to resolve subject attribution either way, this doesn't affect the conclusion.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Both challenges here are precision fixes that OL itself flags as not moving the span, and I confirm both against the witness. First: MT 7:19 begins וַיִּהְי֖וּ בְּנֵ֣י שְׁמִידָ֑ע, and the row's boundary_evidence quotes only from בני onward, even while pairing it with a WEB gloss whose 'were' is exactly the wayyiqtol verb the trimmed citation drops. That verb is the reason v19 does not read as a fourth fronted register-head alongside MT 7:13/7:14/7:20 — an argument the row could have made explicitly with the fuller citation and currently does not. Second: MT 7:14 reads בְּנֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה אַשְׂרִיאֵ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָלָ֑דָה פִּֽילַגְשׁוֹ֙ הָֽאֲרַמִּיָּ֔ה יָלְדָ֕ה אֶת מָכִ֖יר — the first יָלָ֑דָה, inside its own relative clause, has no subject expressed there; 'his Aramean concubine' is stated as subject only of the second verb, bearing Machir. WEB's rendering ('Asriel, whom his concubine the Aramitess bore') resolves that gap by extending her as mother of Asriel too, which is WEB's construal, not something the clause itself states, and the row's 'tracing the concubine-born line' presents that construal as plain description. Neither fix touches the outer edges: MT 7:19's pe is correctly cited, and MT 7:20's וּבְנֵ֥י אֶפְרַ֖יִם is exactly the clean outer head both primaries and I agree closes this row. These are citation and construal precision corrections to be made inside the existing span, nothing more.

primary_reviews.rationale: The two outer edges survive collation: the opening slice at 7:20 and the closing נ֥וֹן בְּנ֖וֹ / יְהוֹשֻׁ֥עַ בְּנֽוֹ pair at 7:27 are both byte-exact, and 7:28's וַאֲחֻזָּתָם֙ וּמֹ֣שְׁבוֹתָ֔ם really does change device. The row's account of what happens at v21b does not survive it. וַהֲרָג֗וּם is labelled a wayyiqtol, but strip its pointing and the skeleton is והרגום, whose second consonant is the first radical of the root; there is no prefix-conjugation preformative anywhere in the form. Contrast the verbs the row then quotes from the same inset, where a preformative sits in exactly that slot: וַיִּתְאַבֵּ֛ל and וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ in v22, וַיָּבֹא֙, וַתַּ֖הַר and וַיִּקְרָ֤א in v23, וַתִּ֧בֶן in v24. The form is a suffix conjugation with a 3mp object suffix carrying a waw pointed patah, and calling it a wayyiqtol misstates the one piece of morphology the row uses to locate the seam. The seam itself is real on other grounds the row could have used — a finite clause with the new grammatical subject אַנְשֵׁי גַת֙ displaces the nominal X-plus-son chain — so this is a defective demonstration of a defensible break, not a wrong span. Two smaller gaps sit behind it. v24 is the only verse inside the span with neither a quoted form nor an oshb ref, and it is exactly where the register's participant turns from sons to a daughter acting under her own finite verb (וּבִתּ֣וֹ שֶׁאֱרָ֔ה וַתִּ֧בֶן); the row's inset argument reaches it only by implication. And the refrain lemma is cited in a shape that does not occur in the source file at all (see collation_tally): the file spells the refrain word with cantillation and with dagesh preceding shewa, and in v20 not even uniformly — בְּנוֹ֙ beside the spirantized בְנ֖וֹ.

challenges.claim: Tier-1 morphological claim is wrong. The row argues the break at 7:21b from "the syntax breaks into wayyiqtol narrative, וַהֲרָג֗וּם". וַהֲרָג֗וּם is not a wayyiqtol: its consonantal skeleton is והרגום, i.e. waw followed immediately by the three root consonants, with no preformative. Every wayyiqtol the row goes on to quote from the same inset has one — וַיִּתְאַבֵּ֛ל, וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ (7:22); וַיָּבֹא֙, וַיִּקְרָ֤א (7:23); וַתִּ֧בֶן (7:24). The form is the suffix conjugation plus 3mp object suffix under a waw pointed patah.
challenges.suggested_action: Re-argue the v21b seam from what the Hebrew does show — a finite verbal clause introducing the new subject אַנְשֵׁי גַת֙ where the preceding text ran a nominal X-plus-son sequence — and either drop the verb-class label or restate it accurately as a waw-plus-suffix-conjugation form. Genuine wayyiqtol narration in this inset begins at v22, not v21b.

primary_reviews.rationale: This row absorbed the most repair and carries the most repair damage. What worked: the v24 gap is closed with a full quotation and a stated reason; the settlement-device contrast is accurate, since וַאֲחֻזָּתָם֙ וּמֹ֣שְׁבוֹתָ֔ם carries third-person plural suffixes and v29 closes on בְּאֵ֨לֶּה֙ יָשְׁב֔וּ בְּנֵ֥י יוֹסֵ֖ף בֶּן יִשְׂרָאֵֽל; the v23/v24 rival is argued rather than omitted; and wayyiqtol onset is correctly relocated to וַיִּתְאַבֵּ֛ל. Fifteen Hebrew runs, thirteen byte-exact, the two failures being the composed refrain lemma covered by the dismissed docket item, and every WEB-labelled string reproduces its verse. What broke: three separate Hebrew tokens are attached to descriptions belonging to other words, all three inside sentences the repair rewrote. The refrain noun is called a verb with a plural object suffix; וְעֵ֣זֶר וְאֶלְעָ֑ד is called the incoming subject and glossed "the men of Gath"; and אֶת, the definite-object marker, is named as one term of the Beriah sound-play. None of the three unseats the boundary, which is exactly why they are easy to miss and worth filing one by one.

challenges.claim: The rationale states that "the verb בְּנוֹ itself is a waw-plus-suffix-conjugation form with a 3mp object suffix, not a wayyiqtol (it carries no prefix-conjugation preformative)." That word is not a verb of any conjugation: it is the noun for son with a third-masculine-singular possessive suffix, and it is the refrain the row elsewhere makes the backbone of its unity argument, attested across MT 7:20, 7:21, 7:25, 7:26 and 7:27 in the forms בְּנוֹ֙, בְּנ֔וֹ, בְנ֖וֹ, בְּנֽוֹ and their neighbours. The form the description actually fits is וַהֲרָג֗וּם in MT 7:21, waw plus the three root consonants plus a plural object suffix. The prior round upheld a challenge against a false verb-class label at this exact seam; the repair lifted the label off וַהֲרָג֗וּם and set it down on a noun, so a false tier-1 morphology still stands, two clauses from where it stood before, and now collides with the row's own nominal use of the same word later in the paragraph.
challenges.suggested_action: Put וַהֲרָג֗וּם back as the subject of the morphological sentence and let the refrain word be described as the noun it is; both the seam argument and the v22 wayyiqtol onset stand unchanged once the two are returned to their places.

challenges.claim: The rationale has the v21b clause "introducing the new subject וְעֵ֣זֶר וְאֶלְעָ֑ד (\"the men of Gath\")," pairing a Hebrew string with a gloss of a different phrase. In MT 7:21 וְעֵ֣זֶר וְאֶלְעָ֑ד are the last two names of the nominal sequence and the antecedents of the plural object suffix on וַהֲרָג֗וּם -- they are killed, not acting -- while the incoming subject is אַנְשֵׁי גַת֙, which is what "the men of Gath" renders and what the row's own full-verse quotation contains. web:1Chr.7.21 agrees: "Ezer, and Elead, whom the men of Gath ... killed."
challenges.suggested_action: Substitute אַנְשֵׁי גַת֙ for וְעֵ֣זֶר וְאֶלְעָ֑ד in the new-subject clause, which is what the upheld prior item asked for and what makes the nominal-to-verbal shift argument work.

challenges.claim: The row claims tier-1 visibility for the Beriah etymology -- "the naming itself plays on the sound of אֶת against בְּרִיעָ֔ה, visible directly in the Hebrew text, not asserted from any footnote" -- but אֶת is the definite-object marker standing before the word for his name, and has no phonetic bearing on the name. MT 7:23 supplies both terms of the play in its own words, וַיִּקְרָ֤א אֶת שְׁמוֹ֙ בְּרִיעָ֔ה כִּ֥י בְרָעָ֖ה הָיְתָ֥ה בְּבֵיתֽוֹ, i.e. בְּרִיעָ֔ה against בְרָעָ֖ה. As written, the row's demonstration that it is independent of the footnote at web:1Chr.7.23 rests on the one word in the clause that cannot carry it.
challenges.suggested_action: Replace אֶת with בְרָעָ֖ה as the second term of the play, which makes the independence-from-footnote point self-evident from the verse already quoted.

primary_reviews.rationale: The v21b seam argument now contains two new, independently confirmable Hebrew errors introduced while repairing the wayyiqtol mislabel. בְנוֹ ('his son,' a possessive noun with a 3ms suffix, quoted four times as the row's own patrilineal refrain) is called 'the verb' carrying a '3mp object suffix.' Immediately before that, וְעֵֶזֶר וְאֶלְעֳָד is glossed '(the men of Gath)' and called 'the new subject,' though the row's own WEB quote two clauses earlier reads 'Ezer, and Elead, whom the men of Gath...killed' -- making Ezer and Elead the object of the killing, not its subject; אַנְשֵׁי גַתֹעֶץ is the actual subject. The word that needed the corrected grammatical description in the first place, וַהֲרָגְוּם, is never itself given one. This is precisely the second-generation-regression pattern this round exists to catch: a repair-time edit that removes one error but plants two more at the identical seam. The row's other three repairs (the rejected-alternative rival, the v24 quote and binding argument, and the retained-but-unowed בְנוֹ gloss) are sound.

challenges.claim: Repairing OL-M8-1Chr-049-1's wayyiqtol mislabel introduced two new errors in the same sentence. The row now states 'the verb בְנוھ itself is a waw-plus-suffix-conjugation form with a 3mp object suffix' -- but בְנוֹ ('his son') is a noun bearing a 3ms possessive suffix, not a verb, and carries no 3mp feature under any reading; it is the row's own named patrilineal refrain from v20-21a. Just before that, the row glosses וְעֵֶזֶר וְאֶלְעֳָד as '("the men of Gath")' and calls it 'the new subject' -- but Ezer and Elead are personal names (per the row's own WEB quote three lines earlier: 'Ezer, and Elead, whom the men of Gath...killed'), and grammatically they are the object of וַהֲרָגְוּם, not its subject. וַהֲרָגְוּם itself -- the word that needed the corrected description -- is never given one.
challenges.suggested_action: Rewrite the sentence to attach the corrected grammatical description to וַהֲרָגְוּם itself -- e.g. 'the verb וַהֲרָגְוּם is a waw-plus-suffix-conjugation form with a 3mp object suffix (referring back to Ezer and Elead), not a wayyiqtol' -- and correct the subject gloss so עֵֶזֶר וְאֶלְעֳָד is identified as the two named sons (object of the killing) while אַנְשֵׁי גַתֹעֶץ הַנּוֹלָדִִם בָּאָרֶץ is identified as the subject.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Four items target this row and none reaches its outer edges. LF-049-1 and OL-049-2 converge on the same real gap from different directions: v24's daughter-builds-towns notice (וּבִתּ֣וֹ שֶׁאֱרָ֔ה וַתִּ֧בֶן אֶת בֵּית חוֹר֛וֹן...וְאֵ֖ת אֻזֵּ֥ן שֶׁאֱרָֽה) sits inside the decided span but carries no oshb citation anywhere in boundary_evidence_refs (it is the only verse in the span with a web ref and no oshb ref) and is never engaged by the rejected_alternative, even though its place-naming interest echoes 7:28's settlement formula closely enough to invite a rival reading. Per the book strategy's own block map, the Beth-horon building notice is already named as a distinct item from the bereavement inset (line 116), so this is a live seam question, not a stretch. OL-049-1 is independently correct on morphology alone: וַהֲרָג֗וּם has no prefix-conjugation preformative anywhere in its consonant skeleton (ה-ר-ג-ו-ם), unlike every genuine wayyiqtol the row itself quotes one clause later (וַיִּתְאַבֵּ֛ל, וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ, וַיָּבֹא֙, וַתַּ֖הַר, וַיִּקְרָ֤א, וַתִּ֧בֶן); labeling it 'wayyiqtol narrative' misnames the form, though the seam it marks (the new subject אַנְשֵׁי גַת֙ displacing the nominal chain) is real on the grounds OL itself supplies. OL-049-3 fails: the two bare 'בְּנוֹ' mentions it flags are lemma-labels naming a recurring refrain word, sitting beside or referring back to already-cited, fully accented, byte-exact occurrences of that same word (v20's בְּנוֹ֙, v25/27's בְּנ֗וֹ / בְּנ֖וֹ / בְּנֽוֹ) rather than independent evidentiary slices — exactly the disclosed vowel-pointed, accent-free citation-form convention already accepted at freeze time under the campaign's 2Kgs precedent, so 'quote not byte-exact' does not hold against that ground. I make no span call, but the author/boss rounds may want to weigh whether v24 belongs with the vv21b-23 aside or anticipates 7:28-29, since that is what LF-049-1 and OL-049-2 jointly put in play.

primary_reviews.rationale: Everything this row asserts about the Hebrew checks out. The opening וַאֲחֻזָּתָם֙ וּמֹ֣שְׁבוֹתָ֔ם בֵּֽית אֵ֖ל and the closing בְּאֵ֨לֶּה֙ יָשְׁב֔וּ בְּנֵ֥י יוֹסֵ֖ף בֶּן יִשְׂרָאֵֽל are exact slices, the next register head בְּנֵ֣י אָשֵׁ֗ר stands where the row puts it, and pmarks_1Chr.json records PE keyed to 1Chr.7.29 (single-witness) — mark type correct, and not one of the ten verses the strategy lists as doubled. Chapter 7 is 'identical' in the verse crosswalk, so the row is right not to dual-cite. On the supra-tribal reading I went looking for a reason to push back and found the opposite: the warrant is stronger than the row's own argument for it. The row reasons that Joseph's sons are Ephraim and Manasseh together, which is knowledge the verse does not state; but v29 opens וְעַל יְדֵ֣י בְנֵי מְנַשֶּׁ֗ה, so Manasseh is named inside the very notice that closes on Joseph, and the two-tribe scope falls out of the verse's own wording. A book-wide sweep for the name confirms 1 Chronicles nowhere spells out the paternity relation: it surfaces at 2:2, at MT 5:1 and MT 5:2 (which map to web 5:1 and web 5:2, short of the offset that begins at MT 5:27), at 7:29 itself, and then at 21:3, 25:2 and 25:9, none of them a statement that Ephraim and Manasseh are Joseph's sons — so the inference route the row chose is the weaker of the two available. That is an under-citation of evidence the row already had, not a defect in the decision, and it does not reach the threshold for a challenge.

The 'sons of Joseph' closing scope is not merely asserted -- the row's own evidence shows v28's town list sitting on Ephraimite ground while v29 explicitly marks its towns as 'by the borders of the children of Manasseh' before summarizing under Joseph, so the supra-tribal reach of the closing line is demonstrated from the geography named in the text itself, not read into it.

primary_reviews.rationale: The span is sound and its best argument verifies. Two claims outrun their evidence. The first is the inference hinged on 'thereby'. v40 reads כָּל אֵ֣לֶּה בְנֵי אָ֠שֵׁר, which names the immediate tribe and nothing wider — the same move 7:5 makes for מִשְׁפְּח֣וֹת יִשָׂשכָ֔ר. High confidence remains defensible for the edges.

primary_reviews.rationale: Quotes all collate, and the row earns credit twice over. The ordinal chain is exactly as described (בְּכֹר֑וֹ / הַשֵּׁנִ֔י / הַשְּׁלִישִֽׁי in v1; הָֽרְבִיעִ֔י / הַחֲמִישִֽׁי in v2), and the refusal to explain Ehud is vindicated by a book-wide sweep: the name-form in v6 occurs once in the whole of 1 Chronicles, so leaving the Bela-Ehud relation at insufficient_evidence is the evidenced call, not mere caution. The problem is the word 'explicitly'. The row makes וְאֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י אֵח֑וּד point backwards over vv1-5, and that anaphoric reading is asserted, never shown. Distribution in this book runs the other way. The exact form occurs 23 times; 17 of those are verse-initial, and in all sixteen other than 8:6 the demonstrative introduces the list that follows in its own verse. The closest control is decisive: MT 6:35 opens וְאֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י אַהֲרֹ֑ן אֶלְעָזָ֥ר בְּנ֛וֹ — identical to 8:6 through both words including their accents, tipeha then munah with the following name under atnach — and there the sons plainly follow. In fairness the construction is attested anaphorically at 4:18, וְאֵ֗לֶּה בְּנֵי֙ בִּתְיָ֣ה, where the preceding three sons are retitled; but that instance is mid-verse, positioned after the list it relabels, which 8:6 is not. So the reading the row needs is possible and is the minority pattern, while the row presents it as explicit. Note also that v6's second clause, אֵ֣לֶּה הֵ֞ם, is bare demonstrative plus pronoun — a different formula that can look backwards without help, and a better place to rest the argument.

challenges.claim: The row's binding argument rests on an undemonstrated and minority syntactic reading. It says v6 'explicitly retitles the entire preceding list', taking וְאֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י אֵח֑וּד as anaphoric. Across 1 Chronicles the exact form appears 23 times, 17 of them verse-initial, and every verse-initial instance except 8:6 introduces the list that follows it. The one exact control for the construction demonstrative-plus-construct-plural-plus-name in verse-initial position is MT 6:35, וְאֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י אַהֲרֹ֑ן אֶלְעָזָ֥ר בְּנ֛וֹ (dual-cite web:1Chr.6.50), byte-identical to 8:6 through both words and their accents, and unambiguously forward-pointing. The construction does occur anaphorically at 4:18, וְאֵ֗לֶּה בְּנֵי֙ בִּתְיָ֣ה, but mid-verse and after the list it relabels. (Counts are over MT numbering; the ch.6 and ch.12 members fall in the offset zones.)
challenges.suggested_action: Drop 'explicitly' and move the retroactive argument onto v6's second clause, אֵ֣לֶּה הֵ֞ם, whose bare demonstrative plus pronoun genuinely can summarize; or state the anaphoric reading of וְאֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י אֵח֑וּד as a contested minority option, citing 4:18 for it and MT 6:35 (= web:1Chr.6.50) against it. The span's outer edges are unaffected — the exile notice still closes at v7 and וְשַׁחֲרַ֗יִם הוֹלִיד֙ still opens a new genitor at v8 — so this bears on the rationale and on the rejected alternative, not on the seam.

primary_reviews.rationale: v6's retroactive אלה-label genuinely binds vv1-5 to vv6-7 -- 'these are the sons of Ehud' is exactly the kind of summary-closure device this book uses to seal a register even when, as here, no Ehud was named in the list it retitles -- and the honest disclosure of that naming gap as insufficient_evidence rather than a harmonized guess is the correct discipline.

The single upheld item is fully discharged, and the replacement argument survives independent checking at every point I could test. The dual-cite is arithmetically right: the offset zone maps MT 6:1-66 onto WEB 6:16-81, a shift of fifteen, so MT 6:35 is web:1Chr.6.50, and that verse does read "These are the sons of Aaron: Eleazar his son ...", forward-pointing as the row says. The byte-identity claim is literally true at codepoint level -- the opening two words of MT 8:6 and of MT 6:35 (וְאֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י אֵח֑וּד against וְאֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י אַהֲרֹ֑ן) share the sequence U+05D5 U+05B0 U+05D0 U+05B5 U+0596 U+05DC U+05BC U+05B6 U+05D4 and U+05D1 U+05BC U+05B0 U+05E0 U+05B5 U+05A3 U+05D9, accents included. MT 4:18 does place וְאֵ֗לֶּה בְּנֵי֙ בִּתְיָ֣ה after the three sons its opening clause names, and mid-verse, exactly as characterised. All eight Hebrew runs are byte-exact and the four WEB-labelled strings reproduce web:1Chr.8.1, 8.6, 8.7 and 8.8 without drift. Holding v6's first clause undecided while resting the summary work on אֵ֣לֶּה הֵ֞ם is the right disposition for a gap the book's own wording does not close. peer_crosscheck.assessment: One item targets this row and it is right in substance while overreaching in its own supporting count. OL-052-1 correctly shows the row's claim that v6's וְאֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י אֵח֑וּד 'explicitly retitles' vv1-5 outruns what the wording alone can carry: MT 6:35 (= web:1Chr.6.50) opens with the byte-identical construction including cantillation, וְאֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י אַהֲרֹ֑ן, and there the demonstrative unambiguously introduces the descendants that follow in the same verse rather than retitling anything prior — a genuine, verified forward-pointing control for the identical opening two words. 4:18's וְאֵ֗לֶּה בְּנֵי֙ בִּתְיָ֣ה is a real anaphoric parallel, but positioned mid-verse, immediately after the three sons it relabels, structurally closer than 8:6's reach back over five prior verses. Both comparanda collate clean against 1Chr_oshb.txt and both support the core point that the row's anaphoric reading is asserted rather than demonstrated. Where the challenge overstates its own case is the book-wide tally: it reports the exact demonstrative-plus-construct-plural-plus-name form occurring 23 times, 17 verse-initial, sixteen of those forward-pointing. A programmatic sweep of 1Chr_oshb.txt for the consonant-skeleton sequence אלה/ואלה directly followed by בני returns 20 occurrences with only 5 verse-initial (1Chr.2.1, 5.14, 6.35, 8.6, 23.24); loosening the search to any verse containing both a demonstrative and any בני-form anywhere returns 36 occurrences with 13 verse-initial. Neither reproduces 23/17, so that statistic is unverified as stated. See the correction below; this is an argumentation matter only — v6's second clause אֵ֣לֶּה הֵ֞ם remains an available anchor, and the row's own edges (v1 opening, v7 exile-notice closing, v8's new genitor opening 'sons of Joseph' at M8-1Chr-053) and its medium confidence are untouched.

challenge_responses.response: Peer-corrected: accepted the corrected form. The core point holds -- MT 6:35 (= web:1Chr.6.50) is a byte-exact, unambiguously forward-pointing control for 8:6's opening two words and accents, and 4:18 is a genuine but mid-verse anaphoric parallel, so v6's 'retitles' reading was asserted, not demonstrated. Dropped the challenge's own unverified 23/17 book-wide tally (an independent sweep of 1Chr_oshb.txt for the demonstrative-plus-bene bigram found 20 total/5 verse-initial on strict adjacency, not 23/17) and rest the argument on the two verified comparanda only; v6's second clause is now offered as an alternative anchor that works regardless of how the first clause is read.

primary_reviews.rationale: All five quoted forms collate exactly, the samekh keyed to 8:28 is correctly typed and correctly flagged single-witness, and medium_low is an honest confidence for a twenty-one-verse register held together as one row. But the row states a universal about its own span — 'the only closing device is at v28' — and that is falsifiable and false. A formula sweep of 8:8-28 returns three loci, not one. 8:10 ends אֵ֥לֶּה בָנָ֖יו רָאשֵׁ֥י אָבֽוֹת, a demonstrative summary of the Hodesh sub-list, and the strategy's own device matrix lists the demonstrative summary as a tier-1 closure signal. 8:13 carries הֵ֚מָּה רָאשֵׁ֣י הָאָב֔וֹת לְיוֹשְׁבֵ֖י אַיָּל֑וֹן, which is the same construction — heads-of-fathers plus the preposition plus a toponym — that decision M8-1Chr-052 treats as the closing device at 8:6 (רָאשֵׁ֤י אָבוֹת֙ לְי֣וֹשְׁבֵי גֶ֔בַע). The two rows therefore read one formula two ways without saying so. I also note, in the row's favour, that the sub-lists it calls 'sub-heads' at vv16-27 are nothing of the kind: 8:16 ends בְּנֵ֥י בְרִיעָֽה and the parallel tags at vv18, 21, 25 and 27 likewise trail their lists rather than heading them, which makes them even less capable of restarting a register than the row claims. The closing quote at אֵ֖לֶּה יָשְׁב֥וּ בִירוּשָׁלִָֽם and the following settlement head וּבְגִבְע֥וֹן יָשְׁב֖וּ are both sound.

challenges.claim: The span-internal universal is false as stated. The row holds that 'the only closing device is at v28'. Inside 8:8-28 two further closure formulas stand: 8:10 closes with אֵ֥לֶּה בָנָ֖יו רָאשֵׁ֥י אָבֽוֹת, a demonstrative summary of the Hodesh list, and 8:13 carries הֵ֚מָּה רָאשֵׁ֣י הָאָב֔וֹת לְיוֹשְׁבֵ֖י אַיָּל֑וֹן. The latter is the same heads-of-fathers-plus-toponym construction that M8-1Chr-052 identifies as the closing device of its own row at 8:6 (רָאשֵׁ֤י אָבוֹת֙ לְי֣וֹשְׁבֵי גֶ֔בַע), so the formula is being read as closural in one row and as unremarkable inside another.
challenges.suggested_action: Withdraw the 'only closing device' wording and argue instead why the 8:10 and 8:13 formulas are subordinate to v28 — for instance that neither carries the settlement clause v28 pairs with, and that 8:13's group is resumed at 8:16 — or, if that cannot be sustained, disclose 8:13 as a live rival seam. Since this is the row's stated granularity justification, medium_low confidence should be re-examined against it.

primary_reviews.rationale: Running this Shaharaim complex as a single register-dominant row rather than fragmenting at every internal 'sons of X' sub-head is the right granularity call, and treating the v28 samekh as tier-3 seconding rather than a driver is exactly right; what falls short is which internal rival the row actually argues against.

Fourteen Hebrew runs, all byte-exact; WEB strings verbatim; the samekh at 1Chr.8.28 is attested in pmarks_1Chr.json. The other half did not land. The universal the prior round asked to have withdrawn still stands word for word in the closing sentence, next to the new sentence conceding that v10 closes something, and the same sentence's "formulaic throughout" passes over v12's building notice and v13's Gath clause. primary_reviews.rationale: Edges verified and marks verified. וּבְגִבְע֥וֹן יָשְׁב֖וּ opens the span, כָּל אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֥י אָצַֽל closes it, וּבְנֵ֖י עֵ֣שֶׁק אָחִ֑יו opens the next, and pmarks carries samekh at both 8:32 and 8:34, correctly typed, correctly disclosed as single-witness, neither doubled. The row also handles the 9:35-44 resumption exactly as the strategy requires, declaring it background and keeping it out of the edge argument. One collation subtlety worth recording: the v33 quotation is not unique in the book, since the identical string also stands at 9:39 — the row cites it to 8:33, which is right for this span. What fails is the uniformity claim. I counted the genitor verb across 8:29-38 and it is absent from vv29, 30, 31, 35 and 38 — four of the ten verses, including the whole opening stretch. The chain does not begin at the Gibeon head: v29 is a settlement clause, vv30-31 are a plain name list (וּבְנ֥וֹ הַבְּכ֖וֹר עַבְדּ֑וֹן ... וּגְד֥וֹר וְאַחְי֖וֹ וָזָֽכֶר), and the first genitor clause is וּמִקְל֖וֹת הוֹלִ֣יד at v32. The pattern also breaks before the end, since v37 leaves the genitor verb for the patrilineal refrain (רָפָ֥ה בְנ֛וֹ אֶלְעָשָׂ֥ה בְנ֖וֹ אָצֵ֥ל בְּנֽוֹ) and v38 opens on a counted-sons construction (וּלְאָצֵל֮ שִׁשָּׁ֣ה בָנִים֒). Separately, the row's distinction at v32 does hold and I checked it: יָשְׁב֥וּ בִירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם עִם אֲחֵיהֶֽם lacks the demonstrative that makes v28 a summary, so treating it as list-internal is defensible.

challenges.claim: The 'unbroken X fathered Y chain' is not what the span contains, and the rejected alternative depends on it. The row says the line 'runs unbroken as an "X fathered Y" chain' from v29, and defeats a split at v33 because v33 'continues the same unbroken chain begun at the Gibeon settlement head in v29'. A count of the genitor verb across 8:29-38 gives zero occurrences in vv29, 30, 31, 35 and 38. v29 is a settlement clause (וּבְגִבְע֥וֹן יָשְׁב֖וּ), vv30-31 are an uninflected name list (וּבְנ֥וֹ הַבְּכ֖וֹר עַבְדּ֑וֹן ... וּגְד֥וֹר וְאַחְי֖וֹ וָזָֽכֶר), and the first genitor clause is וּמִקְל֖וֹת הוֹלִ֣יד in v32. The pattern also lapses at the close, v37 reverting to the patrilineal refrain (רָפָ֥ה בְנ֛וֹ אֶלְעָשָׂ֥ה בְנ֖וֹ אָצֵ֥ל בְּנֽוֹ) and v38 opening וּלְאָצֵל֮ שִׁשָּׁ֣ה בָנִים֒.

primary_reviews.rationale: A two-verse row with nothing loose in it. וּבְנֵ֖י עֵ֣שֶׁק אָחִ֑יו opens on a fresh head naming the brother, כָּל אֵ֖לֶּה מִבְּנֵ֥י בִנְיָמִֽן closes, both byte-exact; pmarks records PE keyed to 8:40 (single-witness), correctly typed and undoubled, and the row is right that it adds nothing the formula had not already established. The absence of a v41 is a fact about the chapter, not an argument, and the row does not lean on it. I pressed the scope claim and it survives, though with a qualification worth recording. The closing formula carries a partitive prefix — מִבְּנֵ֥י, not the bare construct that stands at 8:38's כָּל אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֥י אָצַֽל — so v40 strictly says the men listed are drawn from among Benjamin's sons rather than declaring the register exhausted. That qualifies the 'closing bracket' language without defeating it, because the tribal name it reaches for is the same name that heads the register at 8:1 (וּבִ֨נְיָמִ֔ן), so the lexical link the row needs is genuinely there. I have challenged the parallel scope claim in M8-1Chr-051 and deliberately do not challenge this one: at 7:40 the summary names only the immediate tribe and so cannot reach the roster, whereas here the summary names the very head the row is closing back to. The further reach 'as far back as 7:6' is hedged as a tribal-level aside and is the one argued comparandum not mirrored into the refs — בִּנְיָמִ֗ן stands at 7:6 — which is a housekeeping matter rather than an evidentiary defect.

The scope-widening move at the close -- from Eshek's and Azel's branches to 'sons of Benjamin' broadly -- is read directly off v40's own wording rather than assumed, and a fresh-brother head genuinely opens the coda at v39 rather than continuing Azel's just-closed line.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both halves of 9:1 collate exactly, the glosses are marked as glosses per the citation policy, the mark WLC places after this verse is indeed a samekh as cited and is disclosed single-witness, and the row is honest about sitting in a disputed hinge. Its morphological descriptions are also right as far as they go: הִתְיַחְשׂ֔וּ is a finite suffix-conjugation form, and וְהַיּוֹשְׁבִים֙ הָרִ֣אשֹׁנִ֔ים is genuinely participial. The claim that fails is 'exactly like'. The three later heads adduced are not one shape and v2 is not any of them: 9:10 is וּמִן הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים and 9:14 is וּמִֽן הַלְוִיִּ֑ם, both partitive preposition plus definite class noun; 9:17 is וְהַשֹּׁעֲרִים֙, conjunction plus definite class noun; v2 is conjunction plus definite participle plus definite adjective plus a relative clause. Worse for the argument, the verse that does share the partitive construction with 9:10 and 9:14 is the one the row excludes — 9:3, וּבִירוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ יָשְׁב֔וּ מִן בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה. And v2's own tail is a four-item enumeration, יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ הַכֹּ֣הֲנִ֔ים הַלְוִיִּ֖ם וְהַנְּתִינִֽים, naming precisely the classes that vv3, 10, 14 and 17 then unpack, which patterns v2 with v1 as summary rather than with the heads as a head. Since the row says v2's class-head function 'is what ultimately decides it', the deciding evidence is the weakest part of the row. The v1/v2 split may still be right — the exile clause is closural in its own terms — but the rival grouping the row itself raises is stronger than it allows. A refs defect sits alongside: 9:1's Hebrew is quoted twice yet the refs carry no plain oshb entry for it, only the mark-annotated form.

challenges.claim: The deciding argument overstates a formal parallel. The row holds that v2 functions as a class-head 'exactly like' 9:10, 9:14 and 9:17. Those three are not a single shape and v2 matches none: 9:10 וּמִן הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים and 9:14 וּמִֽן הַלְוִיִּ֑ם are partitive preposition plus definite class noun, 9:17 וְהַשֹּׁעֲרִים֙ is conjunction plus definite class noun, and 9:2 is conjunction plus definite participle plus definite adjective plus relative clause. The partitive construction those heads share appears instead at 9:3, וּבִירוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ יָשְׁב֔וּ מִן בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה, which the row excludes from the series; and v2's tail יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ הַכֹּ֣הֲנִ֔ים הַלְוִיִּ֖ם וְהַנְּתִינִֽים enumerates the four classes that vv3, 10, 14 and 17 subsequently detail, which aligns v2 with v1 as scope-setting summary.
challenges.suggested_action: Re-argue the v1/v2 seam on the closural force of the exile clause and the shift from finite summary to participial description, dropping the 'exactly like' parallel; or, if the class-head series is retained, begin it at 9:3 where the partitive actually starts and re-test whether vv1-2 then belong together. Confidence should not rise above medium while the deciding evidence is this weak.

primary_reviews.rationale: Isolating v1 as its own hinge is defensible on this book's own terms: the device matrix names 9:1b specifically as an exile/return closure type distinct from the settlement-class-head that opens v2, and v2's participial 'וְהַיּוֹשְׁבִים֙ הָרִ֣אשֹׁנִ֔ים' genuinely patterns with the later class-heads at v10, v14, and v17 rather than being asserted to.

Both original defects are repaired, and the morphology behind the repair is right: v2 is conjunction plus definite participle plus definite adjective plus relative clause, and the partitive construction genuinely first appears at v3. I also tested the offset handling, since this row reaches into the zone. WEB 6:1-15 maps to MT 5:27-41, an offset of 26, so WEB 6:15 maps to MT 5:41; the row dual-cites it correctly as 'web:1Chr.6.15 = oshb:1Chr.5.41 (MT)', and the content confirms the mapping because both carry the Jehozadak deportation notice. The 5:25 and 5:26 citations rightly take no dual-cite, the offset beginning only at WEB 6:1. Verse counts corroborate: MT ch.5 runs to 41 against WEB 26, MT ch.6 to 66 against WEB 81. The difficulty lies with what the repair moved into the deciding position. Having dropped the class-head parallel, the row now rests both the v1/v2 seam and the rejection of the vv1-3 rival on a device-pair precedent said to close 5:25-26 and 6:15 (MT 5:41). MT 5:41 supplies only the exile member, its predecessor MT 5:40 being a genitor clause; and at 5:25-26 the first member is a trespass notice rather than the registration summary 9:1 pairs with its exile clause. So the precedent has no clean instance, and the attached book-wide negative is unswept.

challenges.claim: The precedent now carrying the decision is not attested at either citation it names. The row grounds the seam, and rejects the vv1-3 hinge, on 'v1's own device-pair closure (finite-verb summary plus exile notice), the same pairing this book uses to close 5:25-26 and 6:15 (MT 5:41)'. At MT 5:41 only the exile member is present -- וִיהוֹצָדָ֣ק הָלַ֔ךְ בְּהַגְל֣וֹת יְהוָ֔ה אֶת יְהוּדָ֖ה וִירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם בְּיַ֖ד נְבֻכַדְנֶאצַּֽר -- and the verse before it is וַעֲזַרְיָה֙ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת שְׂרָיָ֔ה וּשְׂרָיָ֖ה הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת יְהוֹצָדָֽק, a genitor clause, so nothing pairs with the deportation there. At 5:25-26 the opening member is the trespass notice וַיִּֽמְעֲל֔וּ בֵּאלֹהֵ֖י אֲבוֹתֵיהֶ֑ם, which yields a sin-plus-exile pair rather than the registration-summary-plus-exile pair 9:1 exhibits. OL-056-1 shows the row's deciding claim overstates a formal parallel: it treats v2's וְהַיּוֹשְׁבִים֙ הָרִ֣אשֹׁנִ֔ים as a class-head 'exactly like' the later heads at 9:10, 9:14, and 9:17, but those three do not even share one shape among themselves (9:10 וּמִן הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים and 9:14 וּמִֽן הַלְוִיִּ֑ם are partitive-מן plus a definite class noun; 9:17 וְהַשֹּׁעֲרִים֙ is conjunction plus a definite class noun with no partitive at all), and v2 (conjunction + definite participle + definite adjective + relative clause) matches none of them. The partitive construction 9:10 and 9:14 actually share turns up instead at 9:3 (וּבִירוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ יָשְׁב֔וּ מִן בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה...), a verse the row's own comparanda set excludes, and v2's four-class tail (יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ הַכֹּ֣הֲנִ֔ים הַלְוִיִּ֖ם וְהַנְּתִינִֽים) previews exactly the classes vv3, 10, 14, and 17 go on to unpack, aligning v2 with v1 as scope-setting summary at least as plausibly as with the class-head series. Because the row itself says v2's class-head function 'is what ultimately decides it,' this lands on the deciding evidence, not a peripheral point -- though the v1/v2 split may still hold on the exile clause's own closural force, which the challenge does not contest. OL-056-2 is a smaller, cleanly verified citation-hygiene gap: boundary_evidence_refs carries only 'oshb:1Chr.9.1 (samekh, single-witness)' with no plain 'oshb:1Chr.9.1', even though both halves of the verse are quoted in the rationale -- checking all six other rows in this cluster confirms this is the only one where the mark-annotated cite substitutes for the plain text cite rather than standing alongside it. primary_reviews.rationale: Collation first: the five pointed runs in this row (two from 9:2, one each from 9:3, 9:4, 9:9) are byte-exact substrings of the verses they are hung on, and the WEB renderings quoted alongside them match 1Chr_web_clean.txt. Numbering is safe here, since 1Chr 9 carries 44 verses in both witnesses and lies outside both verified offset zones, so the row is right not to dual-cite. The mark cite is also accurate: pmarks_1Chr.json keys 1Chr.9.9 to a single SAMEKH, the verse is not among the ten doubled ones, and the row flags it single-witness and treats it as ornament rather than as a driver, which is what the Writings tier-3 rule requires. Where I part company is the premise the whole span hangs on. A consonantal sweep of all 943 MT verses of 1 Chronicles returns the root n-t-y-n exactly once, in this very verse (וְהַנְּתִינִֽים); the fourth class v2 names is never given a register anywhere in the book, and the class the cluster in fact places fourth (וְהַשֹּׁעֲרִים֙, 9:17) is not in v2's list at all. So v2's roll cannot be doing the architectural work claimed for it. Second, the row defends the 9:3/9:4 seam but says nothing about three verse-initial partitive heads it swallows, וּמִן הַשִּׁ֣ילוֹנִ֔י (v5), וּמִן בְּנֵי זֶ֖רַח (v6), וּמִן בְּנֵ֖י בִּנְיָמִ֑ן (v7), which are the same shape the next row reads as a class-opening formula at 9:10. Both objections are tier-1, resting on the text's own class roll and its own register heads, so they cut in the same direction they would if aimed at me.

primary_reviews.rationale: Quotation fidelity is clean: 9:10's head is reproduced as the whole verse and matches character for character, 9:13's closing phrase matches, and 9:14's וּמִֽן הַלְוִיִּ֑ם matches including the meteg. The grammar of the argument is where it slips. The row says v10's head matches 'the same' partitive shape as 'the laity's implicit scope in v2', but v2 contains no such particle whatever; the chapter's first partitive is 9:3's מִן בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה. And the shape is not class-selective: a verse-initial partitive stands seven times in this chapter (9:5, 9:6, 9:7, 9:10, 9:14, 9:30, 9:32), five of those inside spans that other rows of this cluster keep whole. A second, smaller point runs the other way: the row says v13's tag 'does not repeat' v9's wording, but the two openings are וַאֲחֵיהֶ֗ם רָאשִׁים֙ לְבֵ֣ית אֲבוֹתָ֔ם against וַאֲחֵיהֶם֙ לְתֹ֣לְדוֹתָ֔ם ... רָאשֵׁ֥י אָב֖וֹת לְבֵ֥ית אֲבֹתֵיהֶֽם, sharing the brother-formula, the chiefs construct and the household phrase. The row is understating evidence that favours it.

rulings.remedy: The row’s single phrase ‘fourteen named individuals across eleven begetting steps’ conflates three distinct counts, which must be kept separate: (1) NAMES — the printed Ner-to-Azel list is 14 named individuals (confirmed by direct count); (2) TOTAL LINKS — connecting those 14 names as one continuous line, mixing the הוליד-verb steps with the nominal joins (8:34/9:40’s ובן יהונתן מריב בעל and 8:37/9:43’s ...בנו...בנו...בנו chain), yields 13 links, not 11; (3) HOLID-LINKS — the count of הוליד (‘fathered’) verb tokens actually printed in 9:35-44 is 9 total (verified by token sweep), of which 1 (v38, מִיקְלוֹת הולִישׁ) belongs to the Mikloth side-branch outside the Ner-Kish-Saul line, leaving 8 הוליד tokens strictly on that line. ‘Eleven’ correctly describes only the narrower 12-name Saul-through-Azel sub-count (11 links). Replace the sentence with a formulation that keeps these three counts distinct: either keep the fourteen-name list and say ‘thirteen links’, or narrow the printed list to the twelve Saul-to-Azel names and keep ‘eleven begetting links from Saul to Azel’; if the הוליד-verb count is invoked as a separate measure, give eight tokens along the Saul line and note the ninth (v38) belongs to the Mikloth notice.

primary_reviews.rationale: Four runs, four exact matches, including the awkward doubled-athnach sequence in 10:1 which the row reproduces as the file has it rather than tidying it, which is good discipline. The samekh at 10:7 is genuine in pmarks, single-witness, undoubled, and cited as consistency rather than as a driver; the samekhs that also stand at 10:4 and 10:5 inside the span are correctly left out of the argument. I can confirm the inclusio claim lexically, since the flight root carries both edges, וַיָּ֑נָס in v1 and וַיָּנֻ֔סוּ in v7. The day-shift at v8 is a real formula and the seam it marks is where the row puts it. What fails is the identification of the opening signal itself: the row calls 10:1 'a scene-launching wayyiqtol clause' and then quotes a string whose first clause is not one. That matters, because the opening edge is the thing an original-language reviewer is asked to test, and the correct label makes the boundary argument better rather than worse.

challenges.claim: 'Ch. 10 opens with a scene-launching wayyiqtol clause' misidentifies the form. The verse opens וּפְלִשְׁתִּ֖ים נִלְחֲמ֣וּ: waw-conjunctive, fronted subject, then a niphal qatal third common plural. A wayyiqtol would require the consecutive prefix pattern, which is what the next clause actually shows, וַיָּ֑נָס. The row's own quoted string contains both forms, so the label contradicts the evidence it cites.
challenges.suggested_action: Relabel 10:1 as waw plus fronted subject plus perfect, and note that this backgrounding setting clause is a stronger discourse-initial signal than a plain wayyiqtol continuation would be, which strengthens the 9:44/10:1 seam the row is defending.

primary_reviews.rationale: The inclusio the row claims between v1's flight-from-the-Philistines clause and v7's abandon-and-flee clause is a genuine shared-root repetition rather than a stretch, and v8's 'וַיְהִי֙ מִֽמָּחֳרָ֔ת' is exactly the kind of day-shift formula that legitimately marks a scene edge under this book's own device matrix. The row keeps its samekh citation in a purely corroborating role rather than leaning on it to do the boundary's real work.

Morphology now matches the witness: נִלְחֲמ֣וּ is a niphal qatal 3cp behind a fronted plural subject, and the first consecutive in the chapter is indeed the וַיָּ֑נָס that follows it on the same OSHB line, so the relabel is faithful and the added remark about a fronted-subject perfect being the stronger opening signal is a fair reading rather than a rescue. Every Hebrew string in the row resolves byte-for-byte to the verse the prose names (10:1, 10:6, 10:7, 10:8), and the day-shift formula וַיְהִי֙ מִֽמָּחֳרָ֔ת does open 10:8, so the far edge is soundly argued on tier-1 grounds. Two repair-side defects survive. The prose carries a literal doubling of one sentence, which a window scan across this cluster finds nowhere else and which therefore looks like edit damage. And the marker treatment runs one way only: the samekh after 10:7 is invoked, while the samekhs recorded after 10:4 and 10:5, both interior to the span, go untagged on refs the row itself lists.

The verb form does not change at the seam; what changes is the causal complement and the two relative clauses, אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹא שָׁמָ֑ר among them.
