primary_reviews.rationale: The rewrite concedes the morphological point cleanly and rebuilds the far edge on material that the OSHB lines really do confine to v13: a beth-of-cause phrase, a relative clause on the unkept word, and the necromancy notice, none of which has a counterpart in the stripping-and-burial report of 10:8-12. All eleven Hebrew strings collate exactly to the verses named, including the pair of consecutives quoted from 10:14. The near edge at 10:8 is carried by the day-shift formula, which is tier-1 and uncontested. My one reservation is a gloss that drops a word: the three-element string quoted from 10:13 is rendered with only two of its elements, and the element left untranslated is the very root that 10:14 turns on, so a lexical tie which would strengthen this row's own far-edge case is not visible to a reader of the gloss. I note also that the phrase labelled 'the relative clause' is in fact a prepositional phrase carrying a relative clause; since the gloss supplied for it is accurate, I treat that as wording rather than a separate item.

challenges.claim: The necromancy quotation is glossed incompletely. וְגַם לִשְׁא֥וֹל בָּא֖וֹב לִדְרֽוֹשׁ holds two infinitives construct, לִשְׁא֥וֹל and לִדְרֽוֹשׁ, but the row's rendering 'and also to inquire of a spirit of the dead' accounts for the first and silently absorbs the second; WEB keeps both ('asked counsel of one who had a familiar spirit, to inquire'). The omission matters here because לִדְרֽוֹשׁ shares its root with דָרַ֥שׁ in the negated clause opening 10:14 -- a verse this row cites for its consecutives -- so the strongest lexical bond holding 13-14 together as the block this row excludes is neither glossed nor named.
challenges.suggested_action: Restore the second infinitive to the gloss and add a half-sentence noting that the root of לִדְרֽוֹשׁ recurs at 10:14 in דָרַ֥שׁ, which binds 13-14 to each other and away from 10:8-12, sharpening rather than weakening this row's far edge.

primary_reviews.rationale: Near and far edges both verified from the Hebrew. The relocation wayyiqtol at v4 does the work the device matrix predicts for a location change, and the unit's close on a growth/favor notice at v9b is a distinct closural type from the register-superscription vocabulary that opens v10 -- not a formula echo, but a genuine change in what kind of sentence is being written. My reservation is not about the span but about which rival the row treats as strongest. A book-wide consonantal sweep shows the closing formula of v10, עִם כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְהַמְלִיכ֑וֹ, occurs only three times in 1 Chronicles: here, at 11:3 as כִּדְבַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה בְּיַד שְׁמוּאֵֽל, and once far away at 15:15 as כִּדְבַ֣ר יְהוָ֑ה. challenges.claim: The row says the v15 phrase 'continues the same Three collective the heading introduced', but neither half of that holds. The heading it cites, וְאֵ֛לֶּה מִסְפַּ֥ר הַגִּבֹּרִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר לְדָוִ֑יד, introduces haggibborim, not a Three; the ranking immediately after it is רֹ֚אשׁ השלושים הַשָּׁ֣לִישִׁ֔ים, where the witness carries an unpointed ketiv (the thirty) beside a pointed qere (the officers) - in either reading the measure is not 'the three'. The first Three in the unit appears only at v12, הָאֲחוֹחִ֑י ה֖וּא בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֥ה. And the v15 form the row leans on, שְֽׁלוֹשָׁה֩ מִן הַשְּׁלוֹשִׁ֨ים, is anarthrous and partitive out of the thirty, not the three. The definite anchor the argument actually needs sits three verses later at וַיִּבְקְע֨וּ הַשְּׁלֹשָׁ֜ה.

Ten strings, all exact. The flaw is that the rewrite applies its own definiteness test unevenly at one point: it calls 11:12 the first definite occurrence of the Three while calling the morphologically parallel numeral at 11:15 anarthrous. I note separately a wording tangle carried over from the challenge text -- the row says the rank title 'carries an undisclosed ketiv/qere split' and then that 'the split is disclosed here' -- which reads as self-contradiction; I flag it here rather than as its own item because the intent is recoverable.

challenges.claim: The row's own definiteness test convicts one of its own claims. It writes that 'the first definite occurrence of the three as such comes one verse later, at v12's ה֖וּא בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֥ה הַגִּבֹּרִֽים'. The determined forms in this span are הַשְּׁלֹשָׁ֜ה at 11:18 (article, with dagesh in the shin) and the true construct chain שְׁלֹ֖שֶׁת הַגִּבּוֹרִֽים at 11:19 -- note the construct שְׁלֹ֖שֶׁת there against the absolute בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֥ה at 11:12 and again at 11:24. Calling 11:12 the first definite instance therefore contradicts the criterion by which the row reaches 11:18, the anchor the cure installed.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Three challenges land on this row, and two of them -- LF's and OL's first -- converge on the identical defect from independent angles, which the brief asks me to fold into a single remedy rather than adjudicate twice. Both correctly see that v24's positive clause is mispaired against v21's negative one in the frozen rationale; the true positive match for v24's וְלוֹ שֵׁ֖ם בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֥ה הַגִּבֹּרִֽים is v20's own וְלוֹ שֵׁ֖ם בַּשְּׁלוֹשָֽׁה, and the true negative match for v21's וְעַד הַשְּׁלוֹשָׁ֖ה לֹֽא בָֽא is v25a's וְאֶל הַשְּׁלוֹשָׁ֖ה לֹא בָ֑א, a clause the frozen row never quotes. primary_reviews.rationale: Collation is clean across this row's three forms -- the MT 12:17 opener plus the Amasai clause and the reception clause, both drawn from MT 12:19 -- with consonants, pointing and accents all matching source. Numbering holds too: WEB 12:16, 12:17, 12:18 and 12:19 answer to MT 12:17, 12:18, 12:19 and 12:20. The row's central form-claim invited a chapter-wide test, and the test upholds and sharpens it. Scanning the clause-initial element of every group-introduction in MT ch 12 gives: וְאֵ֗לֶּה הַבָּאִ֤ים at 12:1 and וְ֠אֵלֶּה מִסְפְּרֵ֞י at 12:24, both nominal; וּמִן הַגָּדִ֡י נִבְדְּל֣וּ at 12:9 and וּמִֽמְּנַשֶּׁ֞ה נָפְל֣וּ at 12:20, both fronted partitives; בְּלֶכְתּ֣וֹ אֶל צִֽיקְלַ֗ג נָפְל֣וּ at 12:21, a fronted temporal infinitive; and וַיָּבֹ֗אוּ at 12:17. Only 12:17 places a finite verb clause-initially. So this arrival is not merely formula-free, as the row puts it -- it is the sole verb-initial opener among the chapter's six group-introductions, a firmer tier-1 basis for the near edge than the row claims for itself. On the oracle clause, לָבְשָׁ֗ה אֶת עֲמָשַׂי֮ is a qal third feminine singular perfect governing its object with the accusative particle, so rendering it as the Spirit clothing Amasai is defensible and is correctly flagged as a gloss. The closing mark is typed accurately: pmarks gives PE at MT 12:19 (single-witness), which is what the row names, and the row properly demotes it to background agreement. A samekh stands after MT 12:18 (single-witness), between David's challenge and the reply, entirely inside the span; being tier-3 and non-driving, its omission is not a fault.

Moving from list to scene at 12:16 WEB is well argued: the bare wayyiqtol וַיָּבֹ֗אוּ carries none of the register-head machinery that opens the flanking Gad and Manasseh notices, and David's challenge plus Amasai's Spirit-borne reply is a genuine tier-1 speech frame that neither neighboring roster has.

primary_reviews.rationale: Quotation and arithmetic are both sound here: the three forms sit byte-exact in MT 12:20, 12:21 and 12:23, and all five dual-cites resolve correctly. Testing the substance separates two good arguments from one bad use of a third. First good one, and stronger than the row knows: a consonantal sweep places the verb at only 5:22, 12:20 and 12:21 across the whole book, and because the 5:22 attestation is pausal (נָפָ֔לוּ) the fully pointed and accented נָפְל֣וּ is unique to this pair of verses. Inside the chapter the lexeme therefore marks precisely the two notices being bound and nothing else. Second: MT 12:23 begins כִּ֚י לְעֶת י֣וֹם בְּי֔וֹם יָבֹ֥אוּ, a subordinating particle over an iterative yiqtol, and such a clause attaches backward, so keeping the generalization in this row rather than letting it head the census is syntactically correct. I also found unused corroboration: עַל דָּוִ֖יד occurs in this chapter at MT 12:20, 12:23 and 12:24 only, so נָפְל֣וּ עַל דָּוִ֗יד at the row's first verse and יָבֹ֥אוּ עַל דָּוִ֖יד at its last form a prepositional bracket enclosing the span. What fails is the third argument, where the same closing verse is made to do two incompatible jobs. The span itself I do not dispute; the medium confidence is honest.

challenges.claim: The rationale puts the closing verse to two uses that cannot both stand. It calls web:1Chr.12.22 = oshb:1Chr.12.23 (MT) "a summary bracket for the whole 12:1-22 accession section, not only for Manasseh", and it also cites that same verse as the reason the two Manasseh notices constitute one row because they "are resolved by one shared closing generalization". A closure reaching over all of MT 12:1-23 is shared equally with the Benjaminite archers (MT 12:1-8), the Gadites (MT 12:9-16) and the Benjamin-Judah band (MT 12:17-19); it therefore cannot individuate MT 12:20 against MT 12:21-22. The tier-1 evidence that does individuate the pair is lexical, and the row does not lean on it: נָפְל֣וּ stands at web:1Chr.12.19 = oshb:1Chr.12.20 (MT) and web:1Chr.12.20 = oshb:1Chr.12.21 (MT), a consonantal book-wide sweep returning only 5:22, 12:20 and 12:21, with the 5:22 attestation in the pausal form נָפָ֔לוּ so that the exact pointed shape is unique to this pair; and עַל דָּוִ֖יד brackets the span at web:1Chr.12.19 = oshb:1Chr.12.20 (MT) and web:1Chr.12.22 = oshb:1Chr.12.23 (MT).
challenges.suggested_action: Retire the shared-closure appeal as a unity ground and rest the row on the chapter-level confinement of נָפְל֣וּ together with the עַל דָּוִ֖יד bracket. Retain the section-wide reading of MT 12:23 only as a description of what that verse does, not as evidence for this particular span. No span change is sought and medium confidence remains appropriate.

primary_reviews.rationale: Binding the two Manasseh notices under one shared closing generalization is the right structural call, and the row is candid that splitting at 19/20 is defensible rather than pretending the case is airtight; the one weakness is in how the closing verse's causal force gets argued, not in the boundary itself.

primary_reviews.rationale: The repair holds where it matters. A consonantal sweep of the whole book returns the qatal only at oshb:1Chr.5.22, oshb:1Chr.12.20 and oshb:1Chr.12.21, and at the pointed level נָפְל֣וּ is confined to the two Manasseh notices alone, 5:22 carrying the pausal נָפָ֔לוּ instead — so the row's new unity ground is stronger than it claims and the retired closure appeal is genuinely gone. Every dual cite in the row resolves correctly under the WEB 12:5-40 = MT 12:6-41 offset, and the pe the row cites does sit at the end of MT 12:23. What the rewrite left behind is a smaller slip in the עַל דָּוִ֗יד paragraph, filed below: a pointed string that occurs once is described as recurring twice, and both recurrences are placed at the wrong end of their verses. One further wording note that I do not file: 'a book-wide sweep finds it in only one other place, 5:22's pausal' mixes two sweep levels in a single clause, since at the pointed level 5:22 is not a hit at all; the conclusion drawn from it is nevertheless correct.

challenges.claim: The corroboration paragraph misstates both the form and the position of its phrase. It quotes עַל דָּוִ֗יד from web:1Chr.12.19 = oshb:1Chr.12.20 (MT) and then says the phrase 'recurs at the close of v22' and 'opens the very next verse too'. The positions are wrong as well: inside MT 12:23 the phrase stands at words six and seven of thirteen, the verse closing on כְּמַחֲנֵ֥ה אֱלֹהִֽים; and inside MT 12:24 it stands at words six to eight, after the register head וְ֠אֵלֶּה מִסְפְּרֵ֞י רָאשֵׁ֤י הֶֽחָלוּץ֙ לַצָּבָ֔א, so it opens nothing. Since the row offers this as corroboration alongside the scarcity argument, the corroboration should at least be described accurately.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Two challenges target this row's use of web:1Chr.12.22 = oshb:1Chr.12.23 (MT) from different angles that converge on one repair. LF-M8-1Chr-075-1 is correct as stated: the rationale's English paraphrase of a causal, 'day by day' force is never demonstrated from the verse's own opening clause, כִּ֚י לְעֶת י֣וֹם בְּי֔וֹם יָבֹ֥אוּ עַל דָּוִ֖יד לְעָזְר֑וֹ — only the verse's tail is sliced in the row. OL-M8-1Chr-075-1 is right in substance and goes deeper: it shows the rationale asks that same verse to do two incompatible jobs, a whole-section summary and the specific warrant binding the two Manasseh notices, and a closure spanning all of MT 12:1-23 cannot individuate one sub-pair against its neighbors. I confirmed OL's replacement evidence independently: an exact-word sweep of נפלו across the entire book returns only three hits — the pausal נָפָלוּ at oshb:1Chr.5.22, and נָפְלוּ at web:1Chr.12.19 = oshb:1Chr.12.20 (MT) and web:1Chr.12.20 = oshb:1Chr.12.21 (MT) — so the identical pointed form is unique to this pair, a genuine tier-1 individuating signal the row does not use. The companion עַל דָּוִיד 'bracket' claim is the one particular needing correction: that phrase also opens the very next verse, web:1Chr.12.23 = oshb:1Chr.12.24 (MT), governed by a different verb (בָּאוּ ... חֶבְרוֹנָה, arrival at Hebron) — so it is not a clean two-point inclusio exclusive to this span, only looser corroboration alongside the exclusive נָפְלוּ match. Both challenges point to one reconciled repair: retire the shared-closure appeal as the unifying warrant, keep the section-wide reading of v23 as description only, and individuate the row primarily by נָפְלוּ's scarcity. No span change is at issue; medium confidence stands correct under either primary's account.

primary_reviews.rationale: Every Hebrew form in this row is byte-clean against MT 12:24, 12:28, 12:29 and 12:38, and its five dual-cites are arithmetically right. Of the row's four checkable assertions, two survive and two do not. Surviving: the enumeration really does comprise twelve tribal or regional entries -- Judah at MT 12:25, then Simeon, Levi, Benjamin, Ephraim, half-Manasseh, Issachar, Zebulun, Naphtali, Dan, Asher and the Transjordan block at MT 12:38. Surviving, and better evidenced than stated: the priestly elaboration carries no heading whatever, since MT 12:28 and MT 12:29 begin וִיהוֹיָדָ֖ע and וְצָד֥וֹק, waw plus a personal name, with neither an aleph-lamed-he formula nor a partitive, so nothing marks the aside off and the decision to keep it inside is correct. Failing: the identification of the opening head as "the exact device" of 11:10 and 12:1, and the description of the tally as running "uniformly". Both are book-scope assertions and both are refuted by sweep; I file them separately below. One further matter I deliberately do not double-charge: this row's far edge is the same seam as M8-1Chr-077's near edge, which I challenge there on the Hebron inclusio. Should the mesh accept that challenge, the natural consequence is an extension of this span to WEB 12:38, so the two items should be adjudicated together.

challenges.claim: The row states that its head matches "the exact device that opened 11:10 and 12:1". A consonantal sweep of the whole book locates the aleph-lamed-he plus mem-samekh-pe-resh combination at two places only, oshb:1Chr.11.11 and web:1Chr.12.23 = oshb:1Chr.12.24 (MT). The distinctive element of the quoted head, מִסְפְּרֵ֞י, therefore pairs with 11:11 (וְאֵ֛לֶּה מִסְפַּ֥ר הַגִּבֹּרִ֖ים), not with 11:10 (וְאֵ֨לֶּה רָאשֵׁ֤י הַגִּבּוֹרִים֙) or 12:1 (וְאֵ֗לֶּה הַבָּאִ֤ים), which share only the generic waw-plus-aleph-lamed-he opener. The counterexample is the load-bearing part: 11:11 carries this very formula one verse inside the mighty-men register without opening a unit at all, which shows the formula by itself does not discriminate a row boundary.
challenges.suggested_action: Recast the head as the generic waw-plus-aleph-lamed-he register opener shared with 11:10 and 12:1, disclose the 11:11 near-twin that does not open a unit, and let the boundary rest on the accompanying content shift -- the Hebron goal בָּ֥אוּ עַל דָּוִ֖יד חֶבְר֑וֹנָה and the kingdom-transfer purpose -- which is what actually distinguishes MT 12:24.

challenges.claim: "The tally runs uniformly ('of the children of X: N thousand ...')" does not describe the series accurately. Its first member, web:1Chr.12.24 = oshb:1Chr.12.25 (MT), reads בְּנֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה with neither the partitive nor a conjunctive waw, unlike web:1Chr.12.25 = oshb:1Chr.12.26 (MT) (מִן בְּנֵ֣י שִׁמְע֗וֹן) and the entries after it; three further members (MT 12:26, 12:27, 12:34) take the partitive but no waw. Only eight of the twelve entries actually exhibit the waw-plus-partitive shape the formula implies. The deviation is benign and in fact favours the row -- an asyndetic, non-partitive first item is what a governing register head predicts -- but a uniformity claim used to justify holding fifteen WEB verses together should describe the series correctly.
challenges.suggested_action: Qualify the pattern: a head-governed asyndetic first entry at MT 12:25, partitive entries thereafter, with waw present on eight of twelve. Present the deviation as reinforcing the near edge instead of asserting one invariant shape across all twelve members.

primary_reviews.rationale: The census row's own opening, וְ֠אֵלֶּה מִסְפְּרֵ֞י רָאשֵׁ֤י הֶֽחָלוּץ֙, is exactly the register-head device the book strategy names for 12:23, and keeping the Jehoiada/Zadok elaboration inside the tally rather than carving it out correctly applies the inset-stays-inside default; a supporting comparison the rationale draws to two other passages, though, does not hold up as cleanly as claimed.

challenges.claim: The rationale states the tier-1 register head at web:1Chr.12.23 = oshb:1Chr.12.24 (MT) is 'matching the exact device that opened 11:10 and 12:1', but oshb:1Chr.12.1 reads וְאֵ֗לֶּה הַבָּאִ֤ים אֶל דָּוִיד֙ (gloss: and these are the ones who came to David), an אֵלֶּה + participle arrival notice, not the אֵלֶּה + רָאשֵׁי (heads/chiefs) census-head construction that oshb:1Chr.12.24's וְ֠אֵלֶּה מִסְפְּרֵ֞י רָאשֵׁ֤י הֶֽחָלוּץ֙ shares with oshb:1Chr.11.10's וְאֵ֨לֶּה רָאשֵׁ֤י הַגִּבּוֹרִים֙. Only 11:10 is genuinely the same device; 12:1 is not.
challenges.suggested_action: Drop 12:1 from the 'exact device' comparison or soften the claim to 'the same אֵלֶּה-opening pattern' rather than an exact structural match across all three verses.

primary_reviews.rationale: Morphologically this is the best-repaired row in the cluster: I checked all twelve tribal entries of MT 12:25-38 against the text and the row's arithmetic is exactly right, including the treatment of וִיהוֹיָדָ֖ע הַנָּגִ֣יד לְאַהֲרֹ֑ן and its neighbour as an inset rather than a thirteenth and fourteenth entry. The far edge is also factually correct — the last figure מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֖ים אָֽלֶף closes the numeric series at MT 12:38 and the following verse carries no count. Three things still need attention. The rewrite brought six comparanda into the prose, two of them byte-quoted, without mirroring any of them in boundary_evidence_refs. The far edge is asserted in a single clause at confidence high, while the partner row across the same seam now grades it medium and calls the rival genuinely live. And the WLC's dense samekh field inside the span goes unmentioned, including at the two verses of the priestly inset whose separateness the rejected alternative denies.

The rationale quotes וְאֵ֛לֶּה מִסְפַּ֥ר הַגִּבֹּרִ֖ים from oshb:1Chr.11.11 and names oshb:1Chr.11.10, yet neither appears in the ref list; and the new morphology breakdown quotes בְּנֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה (web:1Chr.12.24 = oshb:1Chr.12.25 (MT)), מִן בְּנֵ֣י שִׁמְע֗וֹן (web:1Chr.12.25 = oshb:1Chr.12.26 (MT)), מִן בְּנֵי֙ הַלֵּוִ֔י (web:1Chr.12.26 = oshb:1Chr.12.27 (MT)) and מִזְּבֻל֞וּן (web:1Chr.12.33 = oshb:1Chr.12.34 (MT)) without listing any of the four. All six entered the row through the repair itself, so this is a defect the rewrite created rather than one it inherited.

primary_reviews.rationale: Mechanically this row is in order -- both MT 12:39 strings and the MT 12:41 string collate exactly, and the four dual-cites are correct -- so my objection is not to its craft but to what it claims the summary formula governs. The row reads כָּל אֵ֜לֶּה אַנְשֵׁ֣י מִלְחָמָה֮ as reaching across the chapter's whole accession narrative, and on that basis dismisses the rival attachment of WEB 12:38 to the census as resting on "'all these' alone". The Hebrew does not permit the wide reading. What completes the subject in this verse is בָּ֣אוּ חֶבְר֔וֹנָה, and the directional חֶבְר֔וֹנָה occurs in 1 Chronicles four times in all (11:1, 11:3, 12:24, 12:39), within this chapter only at the census head and at this verse. Every earlier contingent is positioned somewhere else: לְצִ֣יקְלַ֔ג at MT 12:1, לַמְצַ֨ד מִדְבָּ֜רָה at MT 12:9, עַד לַמְצָ֖ד at MT 12:17, אֶל צִֽיקְלַ֗ג at MT 12:21. Men who came to Ziklag or to the stronghold cannot be the referent of a summary predicating arrival at Hebron. The one clause that does widen the frame, וְ֠גַם כָּל שֵׁרִ֧ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל, widens it laterally to the un-mustered remainder of Israel, not backward over MT 12:1-23. The span may still be correct on the enumeration-to-feast shift, but its stated ground is wrong and the rejected alternative is materially stronger than conceded. I record for completeness that the tier-3 field is silent between MT 12:38 and MT 12:41 (single-witness) and place no weight on it, since a marker-only argument is insufficient evidence whichever way it points.

challenges.claim: This row treats the summary at web:1Chr.12.38 = oshb:1Chr.12.39 (MT) as "reaching back over the chapter's entire accession narrative rather than only the tally just closed". The verse's own predicate refutes that scope. כָּל אֵ֜לֶּה אַנְשֵׁ֣י מִלְחָמָה֮ is completed by בָּ֣אוּ חֶבְר֔וֹנָה, and חֶבְר֔וֹנָה stands in this chapter at web:1Chr.12.23 = oshb:1Chr.12.24 (MT) (בָּ֥אוּ עַל דָּוִ֖יד חֶבְר֑וֹנָה) and here alone -- four attestations book-wide (11:1, 11:3, 12:24, 12:39). The groups of MT 12:1-22 are located explicitly elsewhere: לְצִ֣יקְלַ֔ג at web:1Chr.12.1 = oshb:1Chr.12.1 (MT), לַמְצַ֨ד מִדְבָּ֜רָה at web:1Chr.12.8 = oshb:1Chr.12.9 (MT), עַד לַמְצָ֖ד at web:1Chr.12.16 = oshb:1Chr.12.17 (MT), אֶל צִֽיקְלַ֗ג at web:1Chr.12.20 = oshb:1Chr.12.21 (MT). They cannot be swept into a summary whose predicate is arrival at Hebron. Further, the widening clause וְ֠גַם כָּל שֵׁרִ֧ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל extends the frame to the remainder of Israel, not to the earlier accession notices. The verb-plus-goal repetition between MT 12:24 and MT 12:39 is a tier-1 lexical inclusio binding the summary to the census head, which makes the rejected alternative -- attaching WEB 12:38 to the census row -- considerably stronger than the "'all these' alone" the row allows it.

primary_reviews.rationale: Three forms quoted, three exact matches at MT 13:1, 13:4 and 13:5. Chapter 13 lies outside both offset zones -- I confirmed fourteen verses in each witness -- so the bare original-language references this row uses are the correct citation form and no dual-cite is owed. The near-edge characterisation was worth a book-wide test and passes without qualification: וַיִּוָּעַ֣ץ is a hapax in 1 Chronicles, attested at 13:1 and nowhere else, so calling it a fresh deliberative verb is literally true rather than impressionistic. The two-stage audience is present as described, שָׂרֵ֧י הָאֲלָפִ֛ים וְהַמֵּא֖וֹת at 13:1 giving way to לְכֹ֣ל קְהַ֣ל יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל at 13:2, and the closing decision idiom כִּֽי יָשַׁ֥ר הַדָּבָ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֥י כָל הָעָֽם is transcribed without drift. I pressed the one internal device capable of dividing the span -- the speech frame וַיֹּ֨אמֶר דָּוִ֜יד at 13:2, a tier-1 class in the book strategy -- and it does not divide: a consultation announced in 13:1 requires its reported content, and וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ כָֽל הַקָּהָ֖ל at 13:4 answers that content, so 13:2-3 is subordinate to the frame rather than a competing head. One wording caveat I decline to escalate, because it does not bear on this row's edges: describing 13:5 as "a different mustering verb" has no antecedent mustering verb anywhere in 13:1-4. The substantive lexical problem at that seam belongs to M8-1Chr-079, whose rationale advances it as a positive contrast, and I file it there.

primary_reviews.rationale: Transcription is faultless -- the 13:5 opener, the complete instrument series of 13:8 and the 13:9 pivot all answer to source exactly -- and the far edge is well drawn, since וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ עַד גֹּ֣רֶן כִּידֹ֑ן is a genuine locative turn and nothing between 13:5 and 13:8 competes with it. The trouble is at the near edge, where the row's reasoning inverts the evidence it appeals to. It says 13:5 swaps a deliberative assembly-gathering for a mustering-for-journey verb. Root distribution in this chapter says the reverse: qoph-he-lamed supplies קְהַ֣ל at 13:2 and הַקָּהָ֖ל at 13:4, both lying inside the preceding row, and וַיַּקְהֵ֤ל at 13:5 is the hiphil of that same root, whereas the gathering root genuinely abandoned at the seam is qoph-beth-tsade, present once at 13:2 in וְיִקָּבְצ֖וּ אֵלֵֽינוּ. The deliberative lexeme is thus retained and verbalised precisely at the boundary, not exchanged. That is a cohesion signal cutting against the seam, and the row owes it an answer rather than an assertion of its opposite. The boundary may well survive on the independent grounds the row also supplies -- a fresh main-line wayyiqtol after the evaluative clause closing 13:4, and the move from reported speech to narrated travel -- but as written the argument misdescribes the Hebrew. Noted without filing: both WEB citations in this row are cut off mid-sentence with no ellipsis, although the gloss on the 13:8 Hebrew does mark its elision properly.

challenges.claim: The near-edge argument -- that oshb:1Chr.13.5 "swaps the deliberative assembly-gathering for a mustering-for-journey verb" -- reverses the lexical facts. וַיַּקְהֵ֤ל at oshb:1Chr.13.5 is the hiphil of qoph-he-lamed, the identical root that furnishes the deliberative assembly in the row immediately preceding: לְכֹ֣ל קְהַ֣ל יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל at oshb:1Chr.13.2 and וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ כָֽל הַקָּהָ֖ל at oshb:1Chr.13.4. The gathering verb actually dropped at this seam is qoph-beth-tsade, occurring at oshb:1Chr.13.2 as וְיִקָּבְצ֖וּ אֵלֵֽינוּ. A book-wide sweep of qoph-he-lamed returns 13:2, 13:4, 13:5, 15:3, 28:1, 28:8, 29:1, 29:10 and 29:20, so all three chapter-13 attestations cluster immediately around the proposed boundary. Shared-root continuity straddling a seam is tier-1 counterevidence; the row neither discloses nor rebuts it, and instead asserts the contrary.
challenges.suggested_action: Replace the swap-of-gathering-verbs reasoning with the accurate contrast -- qoph-beth-tsade inside David's speech at 13:2 versus the hiphil of qoph-he-lamed at 13:5 realising the assembly named at 13:2 and 13:4 -- and disclose the shared root explicitly as a cohesion counter-signal. Rest the seam on the mode shift from reported speech to narrated travel together with the fresh main-line wayyiqtol following the evaluative close of 13:4. The recorded medium confidence is appropriate and should not be raised.

primary_reviews.rationale: Five Hebrew strings, five exact matches against MT 13:9, 13:10, 13:11, 13:12 and 13:14. The far-edge mark is typed correctly -- pmarks records PE at 13:14 (single-witness) -- and 14:1's Hiram embassy confirms a real topic change past it, so the row's outer frame is secure and the locative pivot at the near edge is genuine. Its rejection of a finer cut at 13:12 also reaches the right result. Where it falls short is in evidencing that rejection. The argument turns on 13:12 sharing the same deictic day as the death, yet the string the row quotes stops at בַּיּ֥וֹם and omits הַה֖וּא, which carries the whole anaphoric force; the full form is וַיִּירָ֤א דָוִיד֙ אֶת הָ֣אֱלֹהִ֔ים בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא. The omission matters more than usual here because the preceding verse ends on a contrasting demonstrative, עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה, an etiological formula pointing to the narrator's present rather than to story time. With two opposed day-deictics standing side by side, quoting the portion that is not distinctive fails to demonstrate the claim. The underlying reading is nonetheless correct -- בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא is attested at 13:12, 16:7 and 29:22, while the hazzeh formula occurs at 4:41, 4:43, 5:26, 13:11 and 17:5 -- so this is a demonstration failure rather than a false statement, and I grade it accordingly.

challenges.claim: The rejected-alternative argument depends on a demonstrative the quotation leaves out. The row cites וַיִּירָ֤א דָוִיד֙ אֶת הָ֣אֱלֹהִ֔ים בַּיּ֥וֹם from oshb:1Chr.13.12 and glosses it "David was afraid of God that day", but "that day" renders בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא and הַה֖וּא is absent from the quoted string; the verse actually reads וַיִּירָ֤א דָוִיד֙ אֶת הָ֣אֱלֹהִ֔ים בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא. This is not merely cosmetic: oshb:1Chr.13.11 closes with עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה, so two adjacent day-phrases point in opposite temporal directions -- narrator's present at 13:11 against story time at 13:12 -- and the row's cohesion argument for holding 13:12 with 13:9-11 depends on telling them apart. Book-wide, בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא stands at 13:12, 16:7 and 29:22, and the hazzeh formula at 4:41, 4:43, 5:26, 13:11 and 17:5.
challenges.suggested_action: Extend the quotation through הַה֖וּא and note the deliberate contrast with the etiological עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה at 13:11, so the anaphora that defeats a split at 13:12 is shown rather than asserted. No span change is warranted and the recorded confidence can stand.

primary_reviews.rationale: Running the Uzza death, the etiology, David's fear, and the Obed-Edom blessing together as one row is the harder but better call: the fear notice's 'that day' picks up the day just narrated rather than opening a fresh scene, and the row is upfront that a 9-11/12-14 split is a real, though rejected, rival.

The deictic contrast the repair was asked to demonstrate is real and now visible, and it does the work the row wants: בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא at 13:12 points into story time while עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה closes 13:11 in the narrator's present, so the fear notice is bound to the death and naming it follows. The pe at the end of MT 13:14 is correctly recorded and correctly labelled weak. Two items remain, both introduced by the rewrite. The book-wide attestation lists appended to the two formulas are stated of the pointed strings but only hold consonantally, and the row's two WEB-labelled quotations were retyped with straight apostrophes where the witness file has typographic ones — the same transcription failure that round one flagged on M8-1Chr-084 and that row now observes correctly.

challenges.claim: Both distribution claims are asserted of pointed strings that do not stand at three of the six loci named. The row says בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא is 'otherwise confined to oshb:1Chr.16.7 and oshb:1Chr.29.22', but 16:7 reads בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא; byte-collation puts the quoted string at 13:12 and 29:22 only. It likewise assigns עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה to 4:41, 4:43, 5:26 and 17:5, but 4:41 reads עַד הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה and 17:5 reads עַ֖ד הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה; the quoted string stands at 4:43, 5:26 and 13:11. A consonantal sweep does return the row's full lists, so the two-set contrast the argument rests on survives intact — only the level at which the sweep is claimed is wrong, and a row whose point is that two adjacent day-phrases must be told apart should be exact about pointing.

Whichever way the mesh decides, the row as written does not dispose of the seam it steps over, and it is silent about a parashah-class mark that falls inside its own span at exactly that point. For the record, I think the seam is defensible — but on evidence the row never cites.

primary_reviews.rationale: Collation is clean: the 16:1 opener, the v3 gift-list tail לְאִישׁ֙ כִּכַּר לֶ֔חֶם וְאֶשְׁפָּ֖ר וַאֲשִׁישָֽׁה and the 16:4 opener all reproduce 1Chr_oshb.txt character for character, and the WEB renderings quoted beside them match 1Chr_web_clean.txt without paraphrase. The trouble is that the two grammatical criteria the row names — “a new subject” at the opening and “its own new verb” at the close — are both inert here. Verses 16:1-4 form a single unbroken run of seven clause-initial wayyiqtol forms: וַיָּבִ֨יאוּ֙, וַיַּצִּ֣יגוּ and וַיַּקְרִ֛יבוּ in v1, וַיְכַ֣ל דָּוִ֔יד and וַיְבָ֥רֶךְ in v2, וַיְחַלֵּק֙ in v3, וַיִּתֵּ֞ן in v4. Not one disjunctive nominal clause interrupts them, so ‘its own new verb’ distinguishes v4 from v3 no more than it distinguishes v3 from v2. The subject criterion is equally uneven: the plural actors of v1 give way to David as singular subject from v2 onward, a participant change inside the span larger than any at the v3/v4 seam, where the subject does not change at all. What actually supports the row is semantic — a completed offering-and-meal event against a standing appointment — and that is worth stating as the sole ground. In chapter 16 the string כל הארץ occurs three times, at v14, v23 and v30; the third of those lies outside this span, in the preceding movement, as בְּכָל הָאָ֖רֶץ. primary_reviews.rationale: The four quoted strings all collate byte-exact and sit in the verses claimed. The mark this row leans on is genuine: pmarks assigns PE to 1Chr.18.8 (single-witness), which is where the rationale places it, and it is handled properly, as sub-pause texture rather than as a seam. challenges.claim: The binding device has two legs and only one is shown. v.6 is quoted; v.13 is merely characterised as 'the near-identical wording' with '(v.13, same sense)' and no Hebrew put on the record, which is exactly the assert-rather-than-demonstrate move the contract forbids. Sliced, the legs read וַיּ֤וֹשַׁע יְהוָה֙ לְדָוִ֔יד בְּכֹ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָלָֽךְ at v.6 and וַיּ֤וֹשַׁע יְהוָה֙ אֶת דָּוִ֔יד בְּכֹ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָלָֽךְ at v.13: identical except that the verb governs David with a preposition in v.6 and with the object marker in v.13. The alternation deserves disclosure, the more so because this book's only other occurrence of that verb form, at 11:14, takes a cognate accusative instead (וַיּ֥וֹשַׁע יְהוָ֖ה תְּשׁוּעָ֥ה גְדוֹלָֽה).
challenges.suggested_action: Quote v.13 byte-exact beside v.6 and disclose the prepositional versus accusative government of David. The refrain claim survives the fix, and in fact widens: both verses run garrison, servitude and victory clauses in the same order.

challenges.claim: A closural formula recurring inside a span is at least as good an argument for paneling as for bracketing, and the row never closes that gap. Its first occurrence ends the Damascus notice, whose own head is וַיָּ֤שֶׂם דָּוִיד֙ בַּאֲרַ֣ם דַּרְמֶ֔שֶׂק, and what follows is a fresh subject-initial clause, וַיִּקַּ֣ח דָּוִ֗יד; its second occurrence ends the Edom notice, headed by the matching וַיָּ֤שֶׂם בֶּֽאֱדוֹם֙ נְצִיבִ֔ים. On the row's own description the two verses are near-verbatim, which is what a panel-closing refrain looks like - so the evidence adduced for 'bracketing the whole catalogue' equally supports two refrain-closed panels at 18:1-6 and 18:7-13. The rationale asserts the unit reading without arguing why the first occurrence is non-terminal.
challenges.suggested_action: Argue the non-terminality of v.6 from the text - the Hadadezer thread runs on through the spoil notices of vv.7-8 and into the Tou embassy - or record 6/7 as an unresolved internal seam and drop confidence below high.

primary_reviews.rationale: The row pre-empts its own strongest internal threat by naming the pe after v.8 and defusing it correctly with v.9's own causal clause tying the Tou embassy back to the Zobah victory as sequel rather than a fresh notice; the v.6/v.13 refrain is honestly described as "same sense" instead of overclaimed as verbatim-identical wording.

Both items are discharged. v.13 sits on the record beside v.6 in full pointing, the alternation between the two governments of David is disclosed rather than smoothed away, and the book-wide count survives independent testing: the consonantal form ויושע occurs three times in 1Chr and only three, at 11:14, 18:6 and 18:13, the first taking a cognate accusative just as the row says. The paneling rival is answered from the text, so the rating is earned. What the repair carried in with it is a syntactic mislabel. The clause at 18:9 recruited to tie the embassy back to Zobah is called a causal clause, but following a verb of perception the particle introduces what was heard, and WEB renders it 'heard that David had struck'. That matters beyond terminology on two counts. The row's own point depends on the complement reading, since what binds the embassy to the Zobah victory is what Tou heard. And the sibling row on 19:1-5 in this very cluster was rewritten in this very round to draw exactly this distinction for the parallel construction after the verb of seeing, so the cluster now labels one construction two ways.

challenges.claim: 18:9 is described as the Tou embassy's own opening causal clause. Sliced, the verse reads וַיִּשְׁמַ֕ע תֹּ֖עוּ מֶ֣לֶךְ חֲמָ֑ת כִּ֚י הִכָּ֣ה דָוִ֔יד אֶת כָּל חֵ֖יל הֲדַדְעֶ֥זֶר מֶֽלֶךְ צוֹבָֽה: after the verb of hearing the particle is an object complementizer introducing what Tou heard, not a discourse-level causal connector, and WEB renders it 'When Tou king of Hamath heard that David had struck'. This is a regression introduced by the present round, because the sibling row M8-1Chr-104 in this same cluster was rewritten in the same round to name the identical construction correctly at 19:6, וַיִּרְאוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֔וֹן כִּ֥י, where it states the particle is the object complementizer completing the verb of seeing rather than a causal connector. The mislabel also weakens the row's own argument, since the back-reference to the Zobah victory is carried precisely by the complement.
challenges.suggested_action: Rename it a complement clause after the verb of hearing and align the wording with the formulation already adopted at M8-1Chr-104 for 19:6. The non-terminality argument for v.6 needs no other change and reads more cleanly on the corrected parse.

primary_reviews.rationale: v.13 is now quoted in full alongside v.6 with the ל/את government alternation disclosed, and the row argues v.6's non-terminality from the Hadadezer thread running into the Tou embassy rather than just asserting the bracket reading. No fresh defect found.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Two challenges target the refrain that this thirteen-verse span leans on hardest, and both improve the rationale without disturbing the reading. OL-102-1 is right that v.13 is paraphrased (‘same sense’) rather than quoted: I sliced both closes independently — v.6 ends וַיּ֤וֹשַׁע יְהוָה֙ לְדָוִ֔יד (dative ל), v.13 ends וַיּ֤וֹשַׁע יְהוָה֙ אֶת דָּוִ֔יד (object marker) — and a full-book sweep of that Hiphil-wayyiqtol form turns up exactly three occurrences total (11:14, 18:6, 18:13), with 11:14 taking a cognate accusative instead of a personal object, confirming the alternation OL flags is real and worth disclosing given how much argumentative weight the refrain carries. OL-102-2 raises a fair completeness gap rather than a wrong conclusion: a refrain that closes twice inside one span, once after the Damascus notice (v.6) and once after Edom (v.13), is at least as compatible with two panels as with one bracket, and the row asserts the bracket without arguing v.6’s non-terminality — though the row’s own v.9 move (tying Tou’s embassy back to the Zobah/Hadadezer defeat) already supplies most of that argument, it is simply never pointed at the 6/7 seam specifically. Both fixes make the row’s case for the span stronger, not weaker, so I record no confidence question here.

challenge_responses.response: Accepted. v.13 is now quoted in full — וַיּוֹשַׁע יְהוָה אֶת דָּוִיד בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר הָלָךְ — alongside v.6, with the ל/את government alternation disclosed; oshb:1Chr.11.14 is added as the book's only other occurrence of this Hiphil-wayyiqtol of ישע, which takes a cognate accusative instead of a personal object at all. Accepted. challenges.claim: The rival is defeated on the ground that v.14 changes 'syntax (title-clauses, not wayyiqtol battle notices)', but v.14 is itself wayyiqtol twice over: וַיִּמְלֹ֥ךְ דָּוִ֖יד opens it and וַיְהִ֗י עֹשֶׂ֛ה follows. peer_crosscheck.assessment: Two grammar-naming corrections arrive for this row, and the office-register finding itself is not shown wrong by either. Accepted. Every item in vv.15-17 is waw-coordinated (וְיוֹאָ֥ב, וִיהוֹשָׁפָ֥ט, וְצָד֧וֹק, וַאֲבִימֶ֥לֶךְ, וּבְנָיָ֨הוּ֙, וּבְנֵי); 'asyndetic' is replaced with 'polysyndetic, waw-coordinated verbless clauses.'

post_resolution_check.notes: Span 18.14-18.17 checked; the wayehi-oseh periphrastic argument and the three nakah-chain forms at 18.1/18.2/18.3 all collate correctly (18.2's 'vayakh' opens that verse exactly as quoted). primary_reviews.rationale: Four citations, four exact matches in the verses assigned. The opener claim verifies against the book: that campaign-report formula stands at 18:1, 19:1 and 20:4 and nowhere else in 1Chr, so 'the same device used at 18:1' is accurate. The left edge is therefore in good order. Disclosure for the record, since this row cites no marks at all: pmarks has PE keyed to 1Chr.19.3 inside the span and PE keyed to 1Chr.19.7 beyond it (both single-witness); as Writings tier-3 these can neither carry the seam nor be turned against it, and I use them for neither purpose. challenges.claim: The close at 5/6 sits inside an unbroken narrative chain, and the grammar cited for it is misnamed. From v.1 to v.7 the verbs run consecutively with nothing to interrupt them - וַיִּקַּ֨ח חָנ֜וּן at v.4, וַיֵּלְכוּ֩ וַיַּגִּ֨ידוּ at v.5 and וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ closing it, then וַיִּרְאוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֔וֹן כִּ֥י and וַיִּשְׁלַ֣ח חָ֠נוּן וּבְנֵ֨י עַמּ֜וֹן at v.6 - with no fronted constituent, no temporal notice and no new participant at the alleged seam, since Hanun and the Ammonites have been the actors since v.3. The particle the row twice calls causal, in 'a new causal wayyiqtol clause' and in "v.6's own 'saw that' causal clause", is an object complementizer after the verb of seeing, as the row's own gloss concedes; it does not mark a discourse hinge. Compare this row's left edge, which does carry a disjunctive frame, וַיְהִי֙ אַחֲרֵי כֵ֔ן. A high confidence is resting on a warrant the Hebrew does not supply.
challenges.suggested_action: Re-argue the close on the grounds actually available - the incident is resolved by the royal directive at the end of v.5, and v.6 reconfigures participant roles as Ammon turns from host to hirer of Aramean mercenaries - with the particle named correctly as a complementizer; failing that, lower confidence from high to medium.

primary_reviews.rationale: The comfort-mission-to-mutilation arc is a genuinely self-contained episode, and v.6's "saw that" causal clause is a real hinge into the mobilization sequence rather than a continuation of the embassy scene; checking v.4's own opening shows it is Hanun's direct narrative response to v.3's accusation, so no unargued seam hides between vv.3 and 4 despite a pe following v.3 in the marks data.

The most thorough repair in the cluster. The row concedes what it had been over-claiming, and the concession is accurate on my own reading of the verbs, since every verse from v.1 through v.7 opens with a consecutive preterite and there is indeed no grammatical break at the drawn seam. The particle at v.6 is now named correctly, the boundary is rebuilt on the directive settling the incident and on Ammon's move from host to hirer, and the rating comes down even though the item offered that only as a fallback. What is missing is the mark field. Once a seam rests on content alone, the tier-3 landscape becomes the only other evidence within reach, and this row reports it in one direction: 19:7 is annotated as a pe while 19:3, appearing on the same reference list, is not, even though that second entry marks a break between v.3 and v.4, well inside the unit as drawn, and no mark is mentioned in the prose at all. I am not treating the bare absence of a mark at 5/6 as telling against the boundary, which the rules forbid. The point is narrower: something present, interior, and already on this row's own citation list goes unlabelled while a more distant entry is labelled.

challenges.claim: The Masoretic marks in this stretch are disclosed asymmetrically. pmarks keys a pe to 1Chr.19.3 and another to 1Chr.19.7. The row annotates only the second, listing oshb:1Chr.19.3 with no mark note while giving oshb:1Chr.19.7 as pe and single-witness, and the rationale invokes neither. Taking those entries as the rest of this cluster takes them, with the break falling after whichever verse is named, 19:3 yields a pause between v.3 and v.4, interior to the span 19:1-5 as drawn. That is a datum present in the witness rather than an absence, and it bears on internal unity at just the point where the row has conceded it holds no grammatical warrant. The 19:7 pe conversely tells weakly against the rival's 1-9 block and is cited but never used.
challenges.suggested_action: Give oshb:1Chr.19.3 the same parenthetical annotation 19:7 already carries, and add one sentence putting both on the record: the 19:3 mark as weak tier-3 texture against internal unity that the content argument has to absorb, the 19:7 mark as weak texture against carrying the unit through v.9. Neither is decisive at tier 3, but both belong in view.

primary_reviews.rationale: The causal-particle mislabeling is fixed (כי renamed an object complementizer), the seam is re-argued on the directive's resolution and the host-to-hirer role shift, and confidence is lowered from high to medium as the challenge allowed. No fresh defect found; the unbroken wayyiqtol chain claim (v1-v7) checks out against the text.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: One challenge reaches this row, and it is the sharpest confidence concern in the cluster. Tracing the wayyiqtol chain from v.1 through v.7 myself turns up no break at the alleged seam: no fronted constituent, no temporal notice, no new participant crosses 5/6, since Hanun (introduced v.2) and the Ammonite princes (v.3) are still the actors when וַיִּרְאוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֔וֹן כִּ֥י opens v.6. The row twice calls that particle ‘causal’, but it is the object complementizer completing the verb of seeing (‘saw THAT’), not a discourse-level connector, and the row’s own English gloss already concedes the sense without naming the part of speech correctly. This is a genuine mismatch between the stated warrant and what the Hebrew supports, sitting under a high rating; the row does have available alternative grounds — the royal directive resolving the incident at the close of v.5, and v.6’s reconfiguration of Ammon from host to hirer of Aramean mercenaries (אֲרַ֨ם נַהֲרַ֜יִם, אֲרַ֤ם מַעֲכָה֙ and וּמִצּוֹבָ֔ה all confirmed as the hiring targets) — but whether those grounds sustain ‘high’ once substituted for the mislabeled particle, or should settle at ‘medium’ as the challenge suggests, is precisely the confidence question the author/boss round needs to weigh; I leave the rating as frozen.

Three repairs landed on this row and each carried a new defect out with it, which is the pattern this round exists to catch. challenges.claim: The row says v.19 "settles the whole Ammon/Aram conflict". The Hebrew settles Aram only: 19.19b reads "וְלֹא אָבָ֣ה אֲרָ֔ם לְהוֹשִׁ֥יעַ אֶת בְּנֵי עַמּ֖וֹן עֽוֹד" — a statement that Aram would no longer come to Ammon's aid. challenges.claim: 21.6 is called "a verbless, topic-fronted aside". It is not verbless. challenges.suggested_action: Narrow the lexical claim to 'first use of בֵּית in the temple-building sense' (or explicitly distinguish it from 21:17's idiomatic 'father's house'), rather than an unqualified 'first time in this arc,' so the rejected-alternative's lexical case is not overstated.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both docket items land, and the repair did not cost the row anything I can measure. Sweeping the consonantal skeleton actually puts the row on firmer ground than it claims for itself: the resumptive frame בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֔יא is not merely unused earlier in ch.21 but occurs at exactly two loci in the whole book, 21:28 and 21:29, so the repetition the row builds on is a closed pair rather than a common idiom. The lexical arithmetic checks out too - the house-lexeme is absent from 21:28, 21:29 and 21:30, stands once in 21:17, and returns in the building sense at 22:1 and 22:2. Mark handling is clean: pmarks records a samekh after 21:30 and after 22:1, the row reports both with the single-witness tag, states that the bracketing suits either reading, and declines to let it decide. Every Hebrew string collates byte-for-byte and the one WEB-tagged rendering is verbatim; the other parenthetical English is offered as gloss, not attributed to the translation. One observation I record without filing it: the quotation of v.30 stops before its own causal clause, כִּ֣י נִבְעַ֔ת מִפְּנֵ֕י חֶ֖רֶב מַלְאַ֥ךְ יְהוָֽה, which grounds David's inability in terror of the angel's sword rather than in the distance to Gibeon. That clause narrows the etiology rather than contradicting it, so the row's reading survives; a fuller quotation would simply be more candid.

A consonantal sweep of 21:17, 21:28-30, and 22:1-2 against 1Chr_oshb.txt confirms the repaired claim exactly: בית is absent from all three verses of the 28-30 span, present once at 21:17 in the idiomatic 'my father's house,' and present twice more at 22:1-2 in the temple sense. The rival lexical case is now stated at the strength it actually has, and the deictic argument for reading 22:1 as this arc's close still carries the row. No fresh defect surfaced in the repaired text.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: LF and OL caught the identical overreach independently, and I confirm it a third time directly against 1Chr_oshb.txt: the rationale's claim that בֵּית ('house') 'appears for the first time in this arc in 22:1' is false on its face, since oshb:1Chr.21.17 already carries the lexeme in וּבְבֵ֣ית אָבִ֔י ('and against my father's house'), eleven verses earlier and squarely inside the same census-plague-altar arc the row names for itself. What survives the check, and is what both challenges independently converge on as the fix, is the row's own adjacent, narrower clause -- that the temple-building sense of בֵּית, not the bare lexeme, is what genuinely debuts at 22:1, and that 21:28-30's own cultic vocabulary (מִשְׁכָּן, מִזְבֵּחַ) never uses the word at all. This is one defect with one remedy, not two competing ones: LF's suggested narrowing ('first use in the temple-building sense') and OL's ('absent from 21:28-30') are complementary phrasings of the same correction and should be merged rather than adjudicated against each other. Neither challenge touches the row's actual seam-driver -- the backward-pointing demonstratives זֶ֣ה/וְזֶה in 22:1, which still lack any antecedent inside 22:2ff -- so the deixis argument for closing at 22:1 stands untouched; only the rejected-alternative's lexical framing needs tightening. The samekh disclosures at 1Chr.21.30 and 1Chr.22.1 (both single-witness, tier-3) check out unchanged.

challenge_responses.response: Accepted per the reconciled LF/OL remedy: the unqualified 'first time in this arc' claim is replaced — בֵּ֖ית is disclosed as already present at 21:17 in a different sense (David's own household), and the rival's lexical case is narrowed to the temple-building sense debuting at 22:1, absent from 21:28-30's own וּמִשְׁכַּ֣ן/וּמִזְבַּ֥ח vocabulary.

Accepted; same reconciled fix as LF-114-1. The rival reading now rests on the verified narrow claim (absent from 21:28-30's cultic vocabulary; temple-building sense debuts at 22:1), not the falsified first-occurrence claim, and 21:17's earlier idiomatic use of the lexeme (וּבְבֵ֣ית אָבִ֔י) is disclosed rather than overlooked.

boss_ruling.reasoning: The convergent בית-claim repair is adopted: the lexeme stands at 21:17 in another sense, so the rival's lexical support is narrowed to the temple-building sense debuting at 22:1. The backward-attachment reading of the site declaration survives with its rival honestly weighed; medium_low stands for this strategy-flagged join.

post_resolution_check.notes: Span 21.28-22.1 checked; described by the row itself as the arc's most contested seam, and treated with the corresponding care -- the double-samekh bracket at 21.30 and 22.1 is disclosed on both sides, and the rival lexical reading (beit's temple sense debuting at 22.1) is argued rather than dismissed before the deictic evidence is preferred.

primary_reviews.rationale: Six runs, each one locating cleanly in its cited verse, and the mark work is sound: pmarks_1Chr.json gives PE at 1Chr.22.4, which puts the petuchah at the 4/5 seam as stated, and the row's refusal to let it divide v.5 from the materials list is well judged — v.5 closes on וַיָּ֧כֶן דָּוִ֛יד לָרֹ֖ב, which resumes the preparing verb governing the whole passage, so the reflection summarises rather than restarts. The closing edge at 5/6 is likewise secure, since v.6 introduces a summons with a new addressee. My reservation is confined to the opening edge, and it matters because this row claims high confidence. The stated ground — that 22:2 carries no deixis back to 22:1 — is correct so far as it reaches; 22:2 contains no demonstrative. But deixis is not the only formal relation across that seam, and the other one runs the opposite way.

challenges.claim: 1Chr.22.1 and 1Chr.22.2 begin with a byte-identical twenty-character string, וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֔יד , matching down to the munach on the verb and the zaqef qatan on the name; I verified this as the literal common prefix of the two verses in 1Chr_oshb.txt, not as a paraphrase. The same frame returns at 22:5 (וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֗יד) with only the accent on the name differing. This is tier-1 formal evidence and it is invisible in translation, since web:1Chr.22.1 renders 'Then David said' while web:1Chr.22.2 renders 'David gave orders'. The row places its boundary between the first and second occurrences of this formula while treating the interval from the second to the third as unit-internal, and never says why one repetition divides and the other binds.
challenges.suggested_action: Argue the differential from the Hebrew — 22:1's frame governs direct speech whereas 22:2's governs an infinitival order (לִכְנוֹס֙) — or lower the confidence from high, since the strongest formal signal standing at this row's opening edge is presently unaddressed.

primary_reviews.rationale: Reading v.5 as the passage's own summarizing rationale rather than a fresh beat is well-grounded: its closing clause restates exactly the gathering action vv.2-4 just narrated, and the shift to direct address only comes at v.6's summons. Treating the pe after v.4 as disclosed-but-non-driving is consistent with the campaign's Writings tier-3 policy.

The repair does what the docket asked and does it from the Hebrew, but it installs a criterion the row then declines to apply to its own interior. Having made 'wayyomer plus direct quotation opens, wayyomer plus infinitival directive continues' the reason the seam falls at 1/2, the row meets the identical configuration at 4/5 - v.5 is wayyomer plus direct quotation, on the row's own description - and overrides it on content grounds while a petuchah stands at that very seam in the single witness. The two signals that the row itself elevated both fire at 4/5 and are both set aside, yet confidence stays at high, which was the docket's stated fallback. Separately, the mark evidence is handled unevenly: pmarks puts a samekh after 22:1, which is precisely this row's opening edge and the one witness-side datum that supports the cut, and the reference list carries oshb:1Chr.22.1 with no annotation, while decision 114 in this same cluster tags the identical reference as a samekh. All Hebrew collates exactly and every WEB-tagged rendering is verbatim against 22:1, 22:2, 22:3, 22:4 and 22:5; the character count attached to the shared formula is the one number that does not verify.

challenges.claim: The repair makes a formal contrast the row's opening driver - v.1's וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֔יד introduces a direct declarative quotation, v.2's the infinitival לִכְנוֹס֙ - but the same contrast recurs unresolved inside the span. The row concedes that v.5 'recurs the same wayyomer-plus-direct-quotation pattern as v.1', which by the criterion just adopted marks an opening rather than a continuation, and pmarks independently records a petuchah after 22:4 at that identical seam (oshb:1Chr.22.4, pe, single-witness). Both signals are overridden by a content argument that v.5 summarises vv.2-4, while confidence remains 'high'. The content argument is also not one-directional: 22:2 closes on לִבְנ֖וֹת בֵּ֥ית הָאֱלֹהִֽים, which ties the gathering back to v.1's site declaration exactly as tightly as v.5 ties back to v.2.
challenges.suggested_action: Either state why the form criterion governs the 1/2 seam but yields to content at the 4/5 seam where a single-witness pe also stands, or take the docket's alternative and lower confidence from high.

challenges.claim: pmarks_1Chr.json records a samekh after 1Chr.22.1, which falls at this row's opening edge and is the only mark in the single witness that corroborates the 2/5 span's start. boundary_evidence_refs lists 'oshb:1Chr.22.1' with no mark annotation, whereas decision 114 in the same cluster lists the identical reference as 'oshb:1Chr.22.1 (samekh, single-witness)'. The row annotates the pe at 22:4 that cuts against it but leaves unannotated the samekh that supports it.
challenges.suggested_action: Annotate oshb:1Chr.22.1 as (samekh, single-witness) and disclose it in the rationale as tier-3 corroboration of the opening edge, matching decision 114's treatment of the same reference.

challenges.claim: The formula is described as a 'twenty-character formula' and quoted as וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֔יד. That string is nineteen code points. Twenty is the length of the literal common prefix of 22:1 and 22:2 including the word-final space that follows the name, which is not what the row prints.
challenges.suggested_action: Either write nineteen, or say 'twenty-character common prefix' and include the trailing space in what is quoted.

primary_reviews.rationale: The three-fold repetition of the opening formula is disclosed and resolved on its own grammatical terms rather than left as an unexplained asymmetry. v.5's function as the passage's summarizing close, restating the very gathering v.2 initiated, holds up against the text: v.5 ends on the same 'David prepared' idea that opened the unit.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Re-slicing 1Chr.22.1, 22.2, and 22.5 confirms OL's collation exactly: all three open with the speech-frame formula וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֔יד/וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֗יד, with 22:1 and 22:2 sharing an identical accent pattern (munach + zaqef qatan on the name) and 22:5 differing only by a revia. The book strategy's own device matrix lists speech-and-prayer frames as a tier-1 boundary signal, so this is not a cosmetic repetition -- it is exactly the kind of device the campaign treats as boundary-relevant elsewhere (e.g. the Nathan-oracle frame). The row's stated ground for opening at v.2 -- that v.2 carries no demonstrative pointing back to v.1 -- is accurate but incomplete: it never explains why the first recurrence of this formula (1|2) is where the row divides while the second recurrence, inside its own span (v.5), is not. The row's content-based reading of v.5 as this unit's summarizing close, rather than a fresh beat, is untouched by this gap and remains persuasive on its own terms (v.5 closes on the same preparing verb that governs vv.2-4). But the opening-edge argument as written rests on an incomplete accounting of the formal evidence at its own seam, which is worth the author/boss round weighing against the row's 'high' confidence label.

Added the formal differential: v.1's וַיֹּ֣אמֶר introduces a direct declarative quotation (the site-declaration already closed in decision 114) while v.2's וַיֹּ֣אמֶר governs an infinitival directive (לִכְנוֹס֙), opening fresh administrative content; v.5 is disclosed as formally echoing v.1's direct-quotation pattern but is kept in this unit because its content closes v.2's own gathering action (ending on the same וַיָּ֧כֶן verb) rather than opening new declaration, so confidence remains high with the opening-edge argument now made explicit.

post_resolution_check.notes: Span 22.2-22.5 checked; the nineteen-code-point vayomer-David formula recurrence across 22.1/22.2/22.5 collates exactly, and the samekh after 22.1 plus the pe after 22.4 are both correctly typed and disclosed as non-driving.

primary_reviews.rationale: Eight Hebrew runs, all of them sound against the source, and the mark the row discloses genuinely exists: pmarks_1Chr.json records SAMEKH at 1Chr.22.6, so the tradition did feel a division immediately before the direct discourse, and declining to follow it is the right call given how tightly the summons and the speech it introduces are bound. The unit-integrity case is broadly right — the narrative frame does not hand the floor to anyone else between v.6 and v.16, and ק֣וּם וַעֲשֵׂ֔ה at v.16 answers the commission of v.6. Two things are nonetheless inaccurate as written, one grammatical and one positional, and both fall squarely in my remit.

challenges.claim: The row asserts an address that “runs without a change of speaker or addressee all the way to v.16”. oshb:1Chr.22.8 embeds a quotation frame, וַיְהִ֨י עָלַ֤י דְּבַר יְהוָה֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר, after which the verbs are second masculine singular aimed at David (שָׁפַ֔כְתָּ, לֹֽא תִבְנֶ֥ה בַ֨יִת֙ לִשְׁמִ֔י, עָשִׂ֑יתָ) under a first-person divine speaker (לְפָנָֽי), and the divine voice continues through oshb:1Chr.22.9 (וַהֲנִח֥וֹתִי, אֶתֵּ֥ן) and oshb:1Chr.22.10 (וַהֲכִ֨ינוֹתִ֜י) until עַתָּ֣ה בְנִ֔י at v.11 restores the David-to-Solomon axis. Speaker and addressee do change at the embedded level. The inconsistency is internal to the row, which elsewhere cites the oracle-relay of 21:9 as the kind of frame that would count.
challenges.suggested_action: Restate the claim at the discourse level actually intended — no change in the outer frame's speaker or addressee — and name the lemor-framed quotation as the reason the oracle stays inside the host speech, rather than leaving it as an unexplained exception to the row's own criterion.

challenges.claim: The mark is localised as standing “at the seam between the summons and Solomon's name”. In pmarks_1Chr.json a mark keyed to verse X follows verse X, so this samekh stands after 22:6, at the 6/7 seam; Solomon's name occurs inside v.6 itself (לִשְׁלֹמֹ֣ה בְנ֑וֹ), well before the mark. As written the phrase invites a mid-verse reading of a mark that is not mid-verse. The row's alternative phrase, that the mark stands just before the direct discourse opens, is the accurate one, and the mark type (samekh = setumah) is correct.
challenges.suggested_action: Drop the first localisation and retain the second, so the mark cannot be read as falling inside v.6.

primary_reviews.rationale: David's charge to Solomon runs as one uninterrupted address from v.6's summons through v.16's closing imperative, and the internal pivots the decision names (the quoted oracle in vv.8-10, the resumed blessing at v.11, the stockpile inventory at v.14) are real but none of them changes speaker or addressee, so keeping this as one row rather than three is the harder-won and better-argued call. The rejected alternative isolates a single strongest rival instead of spreading itself across several candidate seams.

Both items are repaired and the discourse-level restatement is the right one: David speaks and Solomon listens from v.7 through v.16 without interruption at the outer frame, while vv.8-10 run a first-person divine speaker over 2ms verbs aimed at David, and עַתָּ֣ה בְנִ֔י at v.11 restores the original axis. The mark is now correctly located after the whole of v.6. What the repair leaves behind is a discriminator that cannot carry the weight put on it. The row says the oracle stays inside David's speech 'precisely because the lemor-frame marks it as a quotation David is himself relating', and contrasts that with 21:9 and with v.6. Checked against the witness, 22:8 and 21:9 both close their frame with the same lexeme, while 22:6 carries none at all, so the presence or absence of lemor tracks neither category. The property that does the work is the one the row states in the same breath and then subordinates: 22:8's frame verb is itself inside David's first-person speech, whereas 21:9's is a narrative wayyiqtol at the outer level. Hebrew collation is clean throughout and the WEB-tagged strings at 22:6, 22:8 and 22:16 are verbatim.

challenges.claim: The repair rests the embedding argument on the quotation frame: the oracle stays inside the host speech 'precisely because the lemor-frame marks it as a quotation David is himself relating', unlike the oracle-relay of 21:9 or the summons of v.6. The lexeme does not sort the three cases. oshb:1Chr.22.8 ends its frame with לֵאמֹ֔ר and oshb:1Chr.21.9 ends with לֵאמֹֽר - the same word, differing only in accent - while oshb:1Chr.22.6 (וַיִּקְרָ֖א לִשְׁלֹמֹ֣ה בְנ֑וֹ) contains no such frame at all. So the row's contrast case shares the feature and its other contrast case lacks it.
challenges.suggested_action: Rest the embedding on the feature that actually discriminates and that the row already states - 22:8's frame verb stands inside David's own first-person speech, marked by the 1cs prepositional phrase, whereas 21:9's is a narrative-level wayyiqtol - and demote lemor to an accompanying feature rather than the reason.

primary_reviews.rationale: Distinguishing outer-frame continuity from embedded-level speaker shift is the right fix, and the row now draws the comparison to 21:9's genuine oracle-relay accurately: that verse opens a new communication event (Yahweh to Gad) rather than reported speech inside David's own address, which is the actual test the row is applying.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Both OL points are precision corrections to the row's own wording rather than challenges to its outcome, and both check out. First, the row's topic sentence -- that the David-to-Solomon address 'runs without a change of speaker or addressee all the way to v.16' -- is stated too absolutely: oshb:1Chr.22.8's לֵאמֹר-framed quotation genuinely shifts to a first-person divine speaker addressing David in the second person (שָׁפַ֔כְתָּ, תִבְנֶ֥ה, עָשִׂ֑יתָ) through v.10, before עַתָּ֣ה בְנִ֔י at v.11 restores the outer frame -- an embedded-level change the row's own next sentence half-concedes by naming 'quoted oracle' as one of the 'real internal movements,' which is exactly the tension OL flags. Second, the samekh at 1Chr.22.6 (single-witness) is correctly typed but mis-located: per the pmarks generation convention a mark keyed to verse X follows that verse's text, so it falls at the 6/7 seam, after Solomon's name and the whole charge-to-build clause, not 'between the summons and Solomon's name' as the row's first phrasing has it -- both sit inside v.6, ahead of the mark. The row's own second phrasing ('just before the direct discourse opens') is the accurate one and needs no fix. Neither point disturbs the row's central and well-supported claim that the outer frame never changes hands from v.6 to v.16.

challenge_responses.response: Accepted. Restated the claim at the outer-frame level (speaker David, addressee Solomon, unchanged through v.16); disclosed the embedded first-person divine speaker in the לֵאמֹ֔ר-framed quotation at vv.8-10, and named the לֵאמֹ֔ר-frame as the reason it stays inside the host speech rather than counting as a new communication event.

Accepted. Corrected the mark's location: the samekh falls after all of v.6 (summons, Solomon's name, and the charge to build), immediately before v.7's direct discourse, not 'between the summons and Solomon's name'; the row's own second phrasing is retained as the accurate one.

rulings.remedy: Rest the embedding argument on the feature that actually discriminates -- 22:8's frame verb stands inside David's own first-person recollection ('God said TO ME'), whereas 21:9's is a narrator-level wayyiqtol addressed to Gad -- and demote the לֵאמֹר-frame to an accompanying feature rather than the stated reason, since 21:9 also ends its frame with a form of לאמר (differing from 22:8's only in cantillation/metheg) and 22:6 carries no such frame at all.

boss_ruling.reasoning: The speaker-constancy claim is restated at the outer-frame level with the embedded divine speech (v.8's לאמר frame) disclosed, and the samekh locations corrected to the follows-verse convention. Medium holds.

post_resolution_check.notes: Span 22.6-22.16 checked; the embedded-oracle argument (vv.8-10 nested inside David's own recollection versus 21.9's narrator-level address to Gad) is sound, and the samekh after 22.6 verifies correctly. One low-severity gap: the row compares the cantillation of 21.9's lemor against 22.8's lemor in fine detail (confirmed genuinely different: meteg versus zaqef qatan) but does not add 21.9 to its own refs.

primary_reviews.rationale: Quotation is clean across all four runs. The addressee change this row leans on is grammatically real, and in fact sharper than the row states: 22:7-16 addresses Solomon throughout in the second masculine singular (עִמָּ֑ךְ, אֱלֹהֶֽיךָ, תִּשְׁמ֗וֹר, וְעִמְּךָ֤), whereas 22:18-19 switches wholesale to the plural (אֱלֹֽהֵיכֶם֙, עִמָּכֶ֔ם, לְבַבְכֶם֙, תְּנ֤וּ, וְק֗וּמוּ וּבְנוּ֙). That number shift is the decisive tier-1 signal at the opening edge and it holds without qualification; the row quotes plural forms but never names the shift as the discriminator. A pe stands at oshb:1Chr.22.19 per pmarks_1Chr.json (tier-3, single-witness), consistent with the closing edge though incapable of driving it. The closing edge is where this row's reasoning goes wrong, because it is not argued from 1 Chronicles at all.

challenges.claim: The row closes with “This span is the end of the assigned range; no further seam is argued past v.19.” An assignment range is a production artifact, not a signal in the text, and under the contract tier-4 metadata may not do boundary work in either direction; boundary_evidence_refs correspondingly stop at 1Chr.22.19 with no reference to the following verse, so the closing edge carries no textual warrant at all. Grounds do exist and go uncited: oshb:1Chr.23.1 opens waw-plus-subject with a nominal predicate, וְדָוִ֥יד זָקֵ֖ן וְשָׂבַ֣ע יָמִ֑ים, rather than continuing the wayyiqtol chain, which is a tier-1 disjunctive opening, and a pe stands at oshb:1Chr.22.19 (tier-3, single-witness, corroboration only).
challenges.suggested_action: Replace the range statement with the disjunctive-clause argument for the 22:19|23:1 edge and add web:1Chr.23.1 and oshb:1Chr.23.1 to boundary_evidence_refs.

challenges.claim: The row distinguishes this charge from the Solomon charge by “a distinct argument-shape”. Lexically the two are built to the same pattern: each pivots on the same temporal adverb (oshb:1Chr.22.11 עַתָּ֣ה בְנִ֔י; oshb:1Chr.22.19 עַתָּ֗ה תְּנ֤וּ) and each climaxes on an imperative of the same root joined to an act-or-build verb (oshb:1Chr.22.16 ק֣וּם וַעֲשֵׂ֔ה; oshb:1Chr.22.19 וְק֗וּמוּ וּבְנוּ֙). The shape is shared, not distinct; what actually differs is grammatical number and addressee.
challenges.suggested_action: Drop the argument-shape claim and rest the distinction on the 2ms-to-2mp shift, which the row already quotes and which no rival reading can absorb.

primary_reviews.rationale: The addressee shift from a private father-son charge to a public address to 'all the princes of Israel' is unambiguous, and the argument-shape that follows — a rhetorical question grounding the command, then a renewed imperative — is distinct from the Solomon charge's shape. Ending at v.19 is forced by the assigned span rather than an invented seam, which the decision states plainly.

This is the cleanest repair in the cluster on the two items themselves. The range statement is gone, replaced by a genuine textual argument: 23:1 opens waw-plus-subject with a nominal predicate instead of continuing the wayyiqtol chain, the pe after 22:19 is flagged as weak single-witness support, and the missing references were added. The shape claim is not merely softened but abandoned, and the person-and-number contrast that replaces it holds against the text - the four plural forms cited all stand in v.19 and v.18 supplies two more, against the 2ms run of vv.7-16. What no longer holds unremarked is the opening edge. The row prints the Hebrew of v.17 beside a WEB rendering that ends 'saying,'. primary_reviews.rationale: This row withstands every test I can put to it. Its four citations slice byte-exact (five runs once the ellipsis is split), and that ellipsis elides exactly one word, the object marker אֶת, and is marked rather than silent, so nothing is smuggled past the reader. The two WEB lines it reproduces match web:1Chr.23.1 and web:1Chr.23.2 word for word, and its v.3 rendering is offered as paraphrase rather than as WEB text. The syntax bears out the opening: v.1 is waw-plus-subject with a nominal predicate, וְדָוִ֥יד זָקֵ֖ן וְשָׂבַ֣ע יָמִ֑ים, a disjunctive opening rather than narrative continuation, and the succession wayyiqtol then follows inside the same verse exactly as the row describes, which is why fusing the two notices in one row is right. The closing at 2/3 is at least as strong as claimed: v.3 opens on וַיִּסָּֽפְרוּ֙, a niphal that my sweep of all 943 MT verses finds exactly once in 1 Chronicles, so the counting verb genuinely inaugurates something instead of prolonging the gathering. I also tested the rejected alternative's book-wide assertion that the census formula is independently attested as its own device, and it survives: counting-noun loci appear at 1Chr.7.2, 1Chr.7.40, 1Chr.21.2, 1Chr.21.5, 1Chr.23.24 and 1Chr.23.27 among eighteen in total. No mark is claimed for 23:1-3 and none exists in pmarks_1Chr.json; the row correctly builds nothing on that silence. No dual-cite obligation attaches, since ch 23 aligns one-to-one across the witnesses.

Fusing the aged-king notice with the succession act in v.1 and closing this unit at v.2's gathering, rather than folding in v.3's census, is well-supported: the census formula that opens v.3 recurs independently elsewhere in the book, so treating it as the next unit's opener is a documented pattern rather than an assumption.

primary_reviews.rationale: The three runs collate without fault, and the seam the row chooses at 5/6 is the right one: וַיֶּֽחָלְקֵ֥ם at v.6 does install a different organising principle, and nothing in vv.3-5 anticipates the clan names. I would add that the opening is stronger than the row realises, since the niphal at v.3 occurs once in the entire book. But two of the supporting claims are assertions about the text that the text contradicts, and the first is precisely the class of claim the campaign requires to be swept before it is written.

challenges.claim: The row identifies 23:3 as carrying “the same age-and-count pattern used for the Reuben/Gad musters earlier in the book”. Sweeping the consonantal skeleton of all 943 MT verses for the age formula returns exactly two loci, oshb:1Chr.23.3 (מִבֶּ֛ן שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה וָמָ֑עְלָה) and oshb:1Chr.23.24 — both inside ch 23. The Reuben/Gad/half-Manasseh muster at oshb:1Chr.5.18 carries no age formula whatever but a capability list, נֹשְׂאֵ֨י מָגֵ֤ן וְחֶ֨רֶב֙ וְדֹ֣רְכֵי קֶ֔שֶׁת וּלְמוּדֵ֖י מִלְחָמָ֑ה, and David's own census at oshb:1Chr.21.5 counts by אִישׁ֙ שֹׁ֣לֵֽף חֶ֔רֶב. The stated comparandum does not exist in 1 Chronicles.
challenges.suggested_action: Strike the Reuben/Gad comparison and put in its place what the sweep does establish — that the counting verb of v.3 is a book-wide hapax and the age formula recurs only at 23:24 — which supports the same conclusion on firmer ground and additionally bears on the 23:24-32 relation flagged as low-confidence in the book strategy.

challenges.claim: vv.4-5 are called “David's quoted speech” and the functional-breakdown argument leans on that status. No speech frame introduces them: v.3 ends on its total (אָֽלֶף), v.4 opens on מֵאֵ֗לֶּה, and no verb of speaking occurs anywhere in vv.4-5. The sole first-person marker in the stretch is עָשִׂ֖יתִי at v.5. web:1Chr.23.4-5 supplies quotation marks, but translator punctuation is tier-4 and cannot establish a Hebrew speech frame. The attribution is an inference from one 1cs verb, presented as a datum.

primary_reviews.rationale: The functional four-way breakdown in David's speech is argued to sum to the v.3 total, and it genuinely does — 24,000 + 6,000 + 4,000 + 4,000 equals 38,000 — so the row's central numeric claim is demonstrated, not merely asserted. The companion claim, that vv.3-5's vocabulary never overlaps with the Gershon/Kohath/Merari clan names that follow, also holds on direct inspection.

Both items were acted on, and the arithmetic the repair now leans on holds: v.3 totals thirty-eight thousand, and the four functional figures of vv.4-5 - twenty-four thousand, six thousand, four thousand, four thousand - sum to exactly that, so the 'breaks the total into four named functions' claim is sound in both witnesses. The hapax claim also verifies: the consonantal counting verb of v.3 returns nowhere else in the book, and עָשִׂ֖יתִי at v.5's close really is the only first-person form in vv.4-5. Two things the repair introduced do not verify. The recurrence sentence names a specific string and then exhibits a different one in its own parenthesis, so as written it asserts something a sweep refutes; what the sweep supports is a recurrence of the frame with a changed numeral. And the account of what WEB contributes at vv.4-5 is too narrow - the translation supplies words, not punctuation - which matters because this row's entire point is what each witness does and does not carry at this seam.

challenges.claim: The replacement claim is that 'the age formula מִבֶּ֛ן שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה וָמָ֑עְלָה recurs exactly once more in the book, at 23:24', with the parenthesis then giving מִבֶּ֛ן עֶשְׂרִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה וָמָֽעְלָה. primary_reviews.rationale: Quotation is accurate throughout — five runs, all sound, with the single ellipsis in the v.11 citation eliding only the clause וִיע֤וּשׁ וּבְרִיעָה֙ לֹֽא הִרְבּ֣וּ בָנִ֔ים. Mark handling is the best in the cluster: pmarks_1Chr.json records SAMEKH+SAMEKH at 1Chr.23.6, the verse is one of the ten doubled loci enumerated in the book strategy, and the row both discloses the doubling and confines it to tier-3 corroboration without letting it drive anything. The difficulty is structural. This row names its rival explicitly — 23:6-23 as one undifferentiated three-clan list — and answers it with a single discriminator, that only the Gershon material carries internal closing tallies. I swept 23:6-23 for those devices and the discriminator does not hold; and separately, the register head formula the row uses to justify its closing edge occurs three times inside the span without comment.
